title: ThreatLocker Portal Administration
summary: The admin's daily loop inside a Zero Trust endpoint platform: organizations, computers, agents, and policies, plus agent health monitoring, deployment states, and the reports that carry compliance conversations. You will learn to read the portal the way an operator reads a cockpit — knowing at a glance what is healthy, what is drifting, and what needs you.
objectives: Explain the portal hierarchy — organizations, computers, agents, policies — and how policy inheritance flows through it.
Run a daily admin loop: agent health triage, deployment-state review, pending approvals, and Detect alert review.
Diagnose common agent health states and decide the correct remediation for each.
Move a policy through its lifecycle — draft, test ring, staged rollout, monitor — without breaking production.
Build reports that answer compliance questions with evidence, not adjectives.
Design a clean organization structure for a multi-site client base that stays manageable at scale.

notes.title: The portal's mental model: organizations, computers, agents, policies
notes.body:
Every endpoint protection platform has a mental model, and your speed as an admin depends on holding it clearly. At the top sits the organization — the tenant boundary. Under a managed service provider, one portal holds many organizations, one per client, so that Client A's policies can never leak into Client B's fleet. Inside an organization you group computers, usually by site, department, or role: front office, warehouse, servers, executives. Each computer runs an agent — the software on the endpoint that enforces policy and reports home. Policies are the rules: what may execute, what an allowed app may do, who may elevate, what storage may connect. Policies attach at any level of the tree and inherit downward, with more specific levels overriding or refining what they inherit.

Worked example: you administer Harborlight IT, a fictional MSP with three clients — a dental practice (18 endpoints), a law firm (45 endpoints), and a warehouse (60 endpoints plus 4 servers). You create three organizations. Inside the law firm you create groups: Attorneys, Paralegals, Front Desk, Servers. The base allowlisting policy attaches at the organization level so every machine gets it. The Servers group gets an additional hardened policy layered on top. When the warehouse asks for USB barcode scanners, you attach a Storage Control exception at the warehouse organization level only — the dental practice never sees it. The rule of thumb: attach a policy at the highest level where it is universally true, and push exceptions down to the narrowest group that needs them.

Common gotchas: the classic beginner mistake is attaching everything at the computer level because it feels precise. Six months later you have 200 snowflake machines and no one can answer 'what policy does this fleet run?' Another is forgetting that a deny inherited from a parent still applies when a child policy allows something — deny-by-default platforms resolve conflicts conservatively, so test the effective policy on a real machine, not just in your head. Finally, name groups for what they are, not who sits there today: 'Front-Desk' survives reorgs better than 'Maria-PCs'.

Here is the drill that makes inheritance concrete: pick any computer in your tree and trace its effective policy set by hand. Start at the organization level, list each policy attached there, then walk down through each group to the machine, noting where a lower level refines or overrides. Do this for three machines — one per client — and write down the results. Then compare against what the portal reports as effective policy. If they match, your mental model is correct; if not, you have found either a misunderstanding or a misconfiguration, and both are worth more than the ten minutes the drill took. Make this a quarterly exercise, and require it of every new admin before they touch a production policy. Inheritance you cannot trace by hand is inheritance you cannot troubleshoot at 2 AM.

notes.title: The admin's daily loop: health, pipeline, review
notes.body:
Operators who thrive do not stare at dashboards all day; they run a loop. A solid daily loop has four passes and takes about twenty minutes. Pass one: agent health. How many agents checked in recently, how many are stale, how many are on an old version? A fleet where 5 percent of agents are stale is normal noise; a fleet where stale agents cluster at one site is a network or deployment problem. Pass two: the policy pipeline. What changed in the last 24 hours, who changed it, and is anything sitting in a test ring waiting for promotion or stuck halfway through a rollout? Pass three: pending approvals. Users who requested an application approval are waiting on you; every hour of delay trains them to resent the platform. Pass four: Detect alerts. Which indicators of compromise were blocked, and do any of them suggest a real intrusion attempt rather than background noise?

Worked example: it is 8:40 AM and you open the portal for the law firm. Health: 43 of 45 agents checked in within the hour; 2 are stale — both in the Front Desk group, both went quiet Friday at 6 PM. That pattern says 'machines powered off for the weekend,' not 'agent broken.' You note them and move on. Pipeline: yesterday you pushed a Ringfencing tightening for the billing app to the test ring of 5 machines; no block complaints overnight, so you schedule the wider rollout for tonight. Approvals: 3 pending — a PDF tool, a dictation app, a browser extension. You recognize the PDF tool from the firm's approved software list and approve it; the other two need a quick check with the office manager. Detect: 4 alerts overnight, all the same blocked script execution attempt on one paralegal's machine at 2 AM. That one earns a deeper look in module 11's troubleshooting workflow.

Operator gotchas: the loop fails when it becomes ritual without judgment — clicking through alerts to clear them instead of asking 'does this pattern mean something?' Keep a one-line daily log; when an incident happens Thursday, your Monday-to-Wednesday notes become the timeline.

The daily loop has weekly and monthly siblings. Weekly: review the exception inventory for anything expiring, check version drift across the fleet, and read the week's Detect alerts as a set — patterns invisible day-to-day emerge weekly. Monthly: run the four compliance reports, review the change log for entries you cannot understand, and walk the group tree for cruft. The daily loop keeps you alive; the weekly and monthly loops keep the fleet healthy. Put all three on the calendar as recurring blocks, because loops that live only in your head die the first time you have a busy week — and busy weeks are when you need them most.

notes.title: Agent deployment states and health monitoring
notes.body:
An agent is a small program with a big job, and like any software it has states. Think in four buckets rather than memorizing labels. Healthy: checking in on schedule, running the current policy version, all modules reporting. Stale or offline: not checking in — the machine may be off, the network may be down, or the agent may be broken; the distinction matters because your response differs completely. Version-mismatched: checking in but running an old agent build, which means it may lack current protections or report fields you expect. Policy-pending: healthy and communicating, but a policy change has not applied yet — perhaps the machine needs a reboot, or the change is staged for a maintenance window.

Worked example: three machines need you. Machine A, a warehouse kiosk, has not checked in for 14 days. You check with the site lead: the kiosk was unplugged during a remodel and sits in a closet. Remediation: reinstall or reimage when it returns to service, and meanwhile it is not protected — note it in the risk log. Machine B, an attorney laptop, checks in fine but runs an agent two versions behind. The auto-update ring skipped it because the user keeps postponing reboots. Remediation: coordinate a reboot, verify the version afterward. Machine C, a new front-desk PC, shows policy-pending on the Storage Control policy. The policy requires a service restart the user deferred. Remediation: schedule the restart tonight, confirm applied tomorrow. Three states, three different fixes — none of them 'reinstall the agent and hope.'

Common mistakes: treating every unhealthy agent as an agent problem. Most stale agents are powered-off machines, and most version mismatches are deferred reboots. Also, do not confuse 'offline' with 'unprotected' in reports to management — an offline machine cannot be attacked over the network, but it also cannot receive policy; say exactly which one you mean. Finally, watch for the slow drift: a fleet that loses one percent of healthy agents per week to neglect will be at eighty percent in five months. Health is a trend, not a snapshot.

Turn health into a number you manage: define a fleet-hygiene target — for example 98 percent of agents healthy and current — and track it weekly on a simple trend line. When the line dips, investigate the cause class: is it one site (network or power), one machine type (imaging breaking updates), or random (user behavior)? Each class has a different fix, and the trend tells you which class you are fighting. Report the number monthly to whoever owns the risk, with every gap explained by name. A single tracked number, honestly reported, builds more trust than any dashboard — and it makes slow drift visible before it becomes a crisis.

notes.title: The policy lifecycle: draft, test ring, staged rollout, monitor
notes.body:
Policies are code that runs on every endpoint, so they deserve a software-like lifecycle. Draft: write the policy against a documented requirement, in a non-production scope, with a clear name and description that says what it does and why it exists. Test ring: apply it to a small, representative set of machines — your own workstation and a few volunteers who will actually report problems. Staged rollout: expand in waves, pausing between waves to watch for breakage. Monitor: after full deployment, watch block events and ticket volume for at least a full business cycle before calling it done.

Worked example: the dental practice wants USB drives blocked except for the encrypted drives used for X-ray image transfers. Draft: you write a Storage Control policy that denies removable storage by default and permits the two known encrypted drive models for the Imaging group only. Test ring: you apply it to your own test machine plus the office manager's PC for three days. Day two, the office manager reports her personal flash drive stopped working — expected, and you confirm the encrypted drive still works. Staged rollout: week one, the Imaging group (6 machines); week two, the whole practice (18 machines), announced in advance. Monitor: for two weeks you watch block events for removable storage. You see a handful of denied personal drives in week one, zero by week two — users adapted. You document the outcome and close the change.

Operator gotchas: the most expensive mistake is skipping the test ring because 'it is just a small change.' Small changes break payroll systems. The second is rolling out on Friday afternoon — if it breaks, you discover it Monday, or worse, the night-shift discovers it Saturday with no one to call. The third is vague policy names. 'USB Policy v3' tells the next admin nothing; 'Storage-DenyUSB-AllowEncryptedImaging' tells them everything. Name policies like the next admin is reading them at 2 AM during an incident — because someday they will be.

Version your policies like code: every change gets a version note — what changed and why — and the previous version stays restorable with one action. Never edit the production policy in place to try something; clone it, test the clone in the ring, then promote. Keep a staging scope — a group of test machines mirroring production's variety — permanently available, so there is always somewhere safe to try the risky change. The discipline feels slow until the day a bad edit takes thirty seconds to revert instead of three hours to reconstruct from memory. Policies are infrastructure; treat them with the change hygiene infrastructure deserves.

notes.title: Reports that carry compliance conversations
notes.body:
Sooner or later someone with authority asks: 'prove our endpoints are protected.' Auditors, cyber-insurance underwriters, and client executives all ask versions of this question, and 'trust us, we have a great platform' is not an answer. Reports are how you answer with evidence. The reports that matter in practice: agent health and coverage (what percentage of the fleet is protected right now), denied executions (what the platform stopped, by category), policy change history (who changed what, when — your audit trail), and exception inventory (every deliberate hole you have opened, with owner and expiry). Together these four tell a story: we are covered, the controls fire, changes are governed, and exceptions are tracked.

Worked example: the law firm's cyber-insurance renewal asks for evidence of application control. You pull four numbers for the last 90 days. Coverage: 45 of 45 agents healthy, 100 percent. Denied executions: 312 blocked application launches, of which 289 were unapproved installers users tried to run, 21 were scripts blocked by Ringfencing, and 2 were flagged for review — both turned out to be a legitimate macro the firm then approved. Change history: 11 policy changes, all with named authors and timestamps. Exceptions: 4 active, each with a business owner and a review date. Your one-page summary writes itself: 'In 90 days the platform denied 312 unauthorized executions with zero successful malware executions reported; all policy changes are logged; 4 exceptions are active and reviewed quarterly.' That is a compliance conversation you win.

Common mistakes: reporting raw counts without context — 'we blocked 10,000 things' sounds either impressive or terrifying depending on the audience, so always pair counts with what they were and what happened next. Another is generating the report the morning it is due and discovering the data has gaps; run your key reports monthly as a habit so the quarterly fire drill is just a re-export. Finally, never hand an auditor a report you have not read. If there is an ugly number in it, you want to find it before they do, with an explanation ready.

Prepare for the questions auditors actually ask, because they are sharper than 'are you protected?' They ask: show me a denied execution from last month and walk me through what happened next. Who approved this exception, and where is the business justification? Your change log shows a policy edit at 2 AM — who authorized it? Two agents are unhealthy — why, and what is the plan? Rehearse these with your own reports before the auditor arrives: pull one denied execution and narrate the triage, open the exception inventory and read the justifications aloud, account for every unhealthy agent by name. The audit is a performance, and the rehearsal is what makes it boring — boring audits are the ones you pass.

notes.title: Designing organization structure for a multi-site client base
notes.body:
Structure is destiny: the group tree you build on day one determines whether policy management stays easy at 50 endpoints or collapses at 500. Design for three properties. First, separation: different clients, and different trust levels within a client, must not share policy scope accidentally. Second, inheritance efficiency: common policies attach high, exceptions attach low, so a change in one place propagates correctly. Third, readability: a new admin should be able to look at the tree and predict where a given machine's policy comes from.

Worked example: back to Harborlight IT's three fictional clients. Dental practice (one site, 18 endpoints): flat — one organization, groups for FrontDesk, Operatories, and a single Server group. The practice is small enough that department groups suffice. Law firm (one site, 45 endpoints, higher risk): organization with groups Attorneys, Paralegals, FrontDesk, Servers, plus an Executives group with stricter Storage Control because partners travel with laptops. Warehouse (two buildings, 60 endpoints, 4 servers): organization with site-level groups — BuildingA and BuildingB — each containing Office and Floor subgroups, plus Servers. The scanner exception attaches at the warehouse organization level; a kiosk lockdown policy attaches at the Floor subgroups. Naming convention: CLIENT-SITE-ROLE, so 'LAW-MAIN-ATTORNEY' is unambiguous in every report and alert.

Common gotchas: over-nesting — seven levels of groups feels organized and becomes unmaintainable; three levels handle almost every real client. Under-grouping is the opposite failure: one flat group per client means every exception becomes per-machine, which is how you end up with 200 snowflakes. And never structure around people ('John's laptop') — people change roles and leave; structure around function, because function is what the policy actually governs. Review the tree quarterly: if you cannot explain a group's purpose in one sentence, merge it.

Design for the acquisition you have not had yet. Sooner or later a client acquires a company, or your MSP onboards a client with an existing mess, and your clean tree meets reality. The pattern: create the new organization or group branch as a quarantine zone with a restrictive baseline policy, run Learning Mode baselining on its machines, and migrate them into your standard structure group by group — never by dumping them into production groups on day one. The quarantine zone is the ring structure applied to mergers: observe, categorize, then integrate. Document the migration the same way you document a rollout, because in six months nobody will remember which machines came from the acquisition — except the tree, if you built it right.

notes.title: Operator gotchas: inheritance, timing, and the human factor
notes.body:
Most portal disasters are not platform bugs; they are operator habits. Inheritance surprises: you tighten a policy at the organization level on Monday, and Tuesday the warehouse calls because scanners stopped working — you forgot the scanner exception lived two levels down and your change overrode its scope. The fix is a pre-change habit: before modifying any policy, list every group that inherits it and ask 'who breaks if I am wrong?' Timing: pushing policy changes during business hours is how you learn what 'change window' means. Even a correct policy can require a service restart or reboot; schedule changes for evenings and tell users what to expect. The human factor: users experience deny-by-default as the computer saying no. If the first time they hear about the platform is a blocked application with no explanation, you have lost them. Every rollout needs a plain-language announcement: what is changing, why, what to do if something legitimate gets blocked, and how fast you will respond.

Worked example: you need to tighten Ringfencing on the billing application at the law firm — block it from launching script interpreters. Before touching the portal, you write the change note: what, why, rollback plan. You check inheritance: the billing policy is attached at the organization level, inherited by all 45 machines, and the billing app is used by 6 people in the Paralegals group. You apply the change to a test ring of 3 machines Tuesday evening, verify the billing app still runs its normal workflow Wednesday morning, then roll out to the firm Wednesday evening with a note to the office manager. Thursday: zero complaints, and the Detect feed shows two blocked script-launch attempts from a malicious attachment someone opened — the exact attack you were preventing. That is what good operations looks like: boring on the surface, decisive underneath.

Final discipline: every change gets four lines in the log — what changed, why, who approved, and how to undo it. When something breaks at 2 AM, those four lines are worth more than any dashboard. Operators are remembered not for the policies they write but for the incidents they prevent and the calm they bring to the ones they cannot.

Protect against your own absence: the bus factor. If you were unavailable tomorrow, could your successor run the fleet from your documentation alone? Test it: hand your design document, runbooks, and change log to a peer and ask them to perform the daily loop and trace three machines' effective policies. Every question they ask is a documentation gap; fix them. Keep credentials, vendor contacts, and escalation paths in the team vault, not your head. The ultimate operator gotcha is not a technical mistake — it is being the single point of failure for the entire security posture. Heroes document themselves into replaceability; that is what makes the fleet survive them.

cards.front: What are the four levels of the portal hierarchy, top to bottom?
cards.back: Organization, groups (sites/departments/roles), computers, agents — with policies attaching at levels and inheriting downward.

cards.front: What is Allowlisting (Application Control) in one sentence?
cards.back: Deny-by-default application control: the platform learns the application environment, permits what users use, and denies everything else.

cards.front: What does Ringfencing restrict?
cards.back: What allowed applications are permitted to do — blocking them from executing other apps or processes, editing the registry, reading/writing files, or opening network sessions.

cards.front: What problem does Elevation Control solve?
cards.back: It removes standing local admin rights and grants just-in-time elevation delegated to specific applications via policy.

cards.front: What does Storage Control govern?
cards.back: Granular policies over storage devices, file paths, and shares — used to block data theft and exfiltration via removable media.

cards.front: What does Network Control do at the endpoint?
cards.back: Acts as an endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs that open and close ports, blocking lateral movement and command-and-control traffic.

cards.front: What is ThreatLocker Detect?
cards.back: The alerting layer that surfaces indicators of compromise that the modules blocked — your review queue for real attack attempts.

cards.front: What is Configuration Manager used for?
cards.back: Centralized configuration of Microsoft Defender across the fleet from the portal.

cards.front: What are the four passes of the daily admin loop?
cards.back: Agent health, policy pipeline review, pending approvals, Detect alert review.

cards.front: What are the four agent health buckets?
cards.back: Healthy, stale/offline, version-mismatched, policy-pending — each with a different remediation.

cards.front: What are the four stages of the policy lifecycle?
cards.back: Draft, test ring, staged rollout, monitor — with a full business cycle of monitoring before calling it done.

cards.front: What four reports carry a compliance conversation?
cards.back: Agent health/coverage, denied executions, policy change history, and the exception inventory with owners and review dates.

quiz.q: Two agents in the Front Desk group went stale Friday at 6 PM and it is now Monday morning. What is the most likely explanation and the right first step?
choices: The agents are corrupted; reinstall them immediately on all front-desk machines.
The machines were likely powered off for the weekend; verify with the site contact before treating it as an agent problem.
The portal is down; open a severity-1 ticket with the vendor.
The policies were revoked; re-push all policies to the group.
quiz.explain: Stale agents that share a time and group pattern usually mean powered-off machines, not broken agents. Confirming with the site contact takes two minutes and prevents a pointless reinstall campaign — most stale agents are off machines or deferred reboots, not agent failures.

quiz.q: You need a USB exception for barcode scanners at one warehouse client. Where should the exception policy attach?
choices: At the computer level on each scanner workstation, for precision.
At the warehouse client's organization level, so it covers current and future scanner machines without touching other clients.
At the MSP portal root, so all clients benefit.
Nowhere — exceptions should never be created.
quiz.explain: Attach at the highest level where the need is universally true (the warehouse org) and no higher. Computer-level attachment creates snowflakes; portal-root attachment leaks a warehouse exception into the dental practice and law firm.

quiz.q: During a staged rollout, the test ring reports no issues for three days. What is the correct next step?
choices: Push to the full fleet immediately; three clean days is proof.
Expand to the next wave on schedule, pausing between waves to watch for breakage.
Skip the remaining waves to save time.
Roll back the test ring to be safe.
quiz.explain: A clean test ring earns you the next wave, not the whole fleet. Staged rollouts exist because some breakage only appears at scale or in untested workflows — pausing between waves is the control that catches it.

quiz.q: An auditor asks for evidence of application control over the last 90 days. Which set of reports answers completely?
choices: A screenshot of the portal dashboard.
Agent coverage, denied executions by category, policy change history, and the exception inventory with owners and review dates.
The vendor's marketing whitepaper.
A list of installed applications.
quiz.explain: Compliance wants evidence of coverage, enforcement, governance, and tracked exceptions. A dashboard screenshot proves nothing about history; the four reports together show the controls fire, changes are logged, and every deliberate hole has an owner.

quiz.q: A policy change at the organization level breaks an application that had an exception two levels down. What went wrong?
choices: The platform has a bug in exception handling.
The operator did not check inheritance — the parent-level change overrode or conflicted with the narrower exception's scope.
Exceptions expire after 30 days automatically.
The agent was offline.
quiz.explain: Deny-by-default platforms resolve conflicts conservatively, so a broad parent change can neutralize a narrow child exception. The pre-change habit is listing every inheriting group and asking who breaks if you are wrong.

quiz.q: Why should policy rollouts avoid Friday afternoons?
choices: The portal is slower on Fridays.
Breakage discovered over the weekend hits users with no admin available, and some changes need reboots users will postpone.
Licenses expire on weekends.
Agents do not check in on weekends.
quiz.explain: A Friday change that breaks something means a weekend of blocked users or a Monday-morning fire. Evening change windows mid-week give you the next business day to detect and fix issues with staff available.

quiz.q: An agent shows 'policy-pending' on a new Storage Control policy. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The policy was deleted.
The agent is communicating but the change has not applied yet — possibly awaiting a service restart or reboot.
The machine is infected.
The license expired.
quiz.explain: Policy-pending means the agent is reachable but the change has not taken effect. Many policy changes need a service restart or reboot to apply, so the fix is scheduling that restart and confirming afterward — not reinstalling.

quiz.q: A user complains their personal flash drive stopped working after your Storage Control rollout, but the approved encrypted drive works. How do you classify this?
choices: A false positive that must be fixed immediately.
Expected behavior — the policy is working as designed; explain and document it.
An agent malfunction.
A reason to roll back the entire policy.
quiz.explain: Deny-by-default means personal drives are supposed to stop working. Calling designed behavior a false positive trains the organization to distrust the platform; instead, confirm the approved workflow functions and document the outcome.

quiz.q: What is the single most valuable habit when modifying any policy?
choices: Taking a screenshot before and after.
Writing the four-line change log: what changed, why, who approved, and how to undo it.
Notifying the vendor.
Doing it quickly before anyone notices.
quiz.explain: The four-line log is what saves you at 2 AM: what, why, who approved, and the undo path. Screenshots help, but only the log tells the next operator whether the change was intentional and how to reverse it safely.

quiz.q: Your group tree has seven nesting levels and groups named after individual employees. What is the structural problem?
choices: There is no problem; more detail is always better.
Over-nesting becomes unmaintainable and people-named groups rot when staff change roles; structure around function at two to three levels.
The portal cannot handle seven levels.
Groups must be named after employees for accountability.
quiz.explain: Structure around function, not people, and keep nesting shallow. People change roles and leave; functions persist. If you cannot explain a group's purpose in one sentence, it should be merged.

items.explain: Twenty focused minutes beats eight hours of dashboard staring.

items.prompt: An agent is stale but its group-mates went quiet at the same Friday 6 PM time. Likely cause?
items.answer: Machines powered off for the weekend — verify with the site contact.
items.explain: Shared time-and-group patterns point to environment, not agent corruption.

items.prompt: Name the four stages of the policy lifecycle.
items.answer: Draft, test ring, staged rollout, monitor.
items.explain: Policies are code on every endpoint — ship them like software.

items.prompt: What four lines go in every change log entry?
items.answer: What changed, why, who approved, how to undo it.
items.explain: The undo path is what saves you at 2 AM.

items.prompt: You tighten a Ringfencing policy at the organization level Monday; Tuesday the warehouse's scanners stop working. Diagnose.
items.answer: The parent-level change conflicted with the narrower scanner exception two levels down — an inheritance surprise from skipping the pre-change impact check.
items.explain: Always list inheriting groups and ask who breaks before modifying a shared policy.

items.prompt: Detect shows the same blocked script execution on one machine at 2 AM three nights running. Next step?
items.answer: Investigate as a potential real intrusion attempt — check the process chain, the file's origin, and whether the user was active; do not just clear the alerts.
items.explain: Repeated off-hours blocks on one machine are the pattern that separates noise from an actual attempt.

items.prompt: The office manager needs a new dictation app approved and is waiting. It is not on the approved software list. What do you do?
items.answer: Do not approve blindly — verify legitimacy and business need with the office manager first, then approve or deny with a documented reason.
items.explain: Pending approvals are a security decision, not a speed contest; every hour of delay is weighed against the risk of approving blindly.

items.prompt: A client asks you to prove 100% of endpoints are protected right now. What do you pull?
items.answer: Agent health/coverage report: count of healthy vs stale vs mismatched agents, with the stale ones explained (powered off, pending reinstall).
items.explain: Never claim 100% without the data — report the real number and account for every non-healthy agent by name.

items.prompt: You inherit a portal where every policy is attached at the computer level across 200 machines. What is your remediation plan?
items.answer: Inventory the per-machine policies, consolidate common ones to group/org level, migrate in waves with a test ring, and document the new structure — never big-bang it.
items.explain: Snowflake fleets are fixed by consolidation in waves, with the same lifecycle discipline as any policy change.

items.prompt: A policy change needs a reboot to apply, and users keep postponing. How do you handle it?
items.answer: Set a maintenance window, communicate it in advance, and enforce the reboot — then verify policy-pending clears the next morning.
items.explain: Policy-pending agents are a compliance gap; indefinite postponement is not an option, but surprise reboots destroy trust.

handsOnLab.title: Design a portal organization structure for a fictional 3-site MSP client base
handsOnLab.brief: On paper or in a document, architect the full portal hierarchy for a fictional MSP with three clients across multiple sites: groups, policy attachment points, naming conventions, and the daily-loop checklist you would run against it. You produce the design artifacts a real admin would hand to their successor.
steps: Invent your three fictional clients: a 20-endpoint dental practice (1 site), a 45-endpoint law firm (1 site), and a 60-endpoint warehouse (2 buildings). Write one paragraph per client covering business, risk level, and special needs (scanners, travel laptops, servers).
Draw the organization tree for all three clients: organizations, then groups. Keep nesting to three levels maximum and name every group by function, not by person.

Decide policy attachment points: list each policy you would create (base allowlisting, ringfencing tiers, storage control, network control, elevation) and mark exactly which level each attaches to and why.
Write the naming convention document: define the CLIENT-SITE-ROLE pattern with three correct and two incorrect examples, and explain why the incorrect ones fail.
Design the exception strategy: list every exception each client needs (scanners, encrypted drives, travel laptops), with the narrowest group each attaches to and a named business owner.
Write the daily-loop checklist as a one-page runbook: the four passes, what 'normal' looks like for this fleet, and the thresholds that trigger escalation.
Draft the plain-language user announcement for the warehouse scanner exception rollout: what changes, why, what to do if something legitimate is blocked, and your response-time commitment.
Create the change-log template with the four required lines, and fill in one realistic example entry for the storage policy rollout.
Build the monthly compliance one-pager template: the four report sections, where each number comes from, and the sentence you would write to an auditor for each.
Review your own tree with fresh eyes: for three random computers, trace which policies apply by inheritance and write down the effective set. Fix anything surprising.
Write a 'handoff note' to a successor admin: the three things most likely to confuse them about your structure and where the bodies are buried.
Save everything as org-design.md in a lab folder, with clear section headers matching the steps above.

title: Cyber Hero Support Operations
summary: The support and triage discipline behind the 'Cyber Hero' team: ticket intake that captures what matters, severity classification you can defend, escalation paths that work under pressure, and communication that keeps customers calm. This is the team you would join on October 13 — learn to operate like you already belong to it.
objectives: Explain what 'hero' support means operationally: speed, accuracy, and documentation as a single discipline.
Run a complete ticket intake that captures the six facts every escalation needs.
Classify tickets into a severity matrix and defend the classification to a customer and a manager.
Decide when and how to escalate, with the right context packaged for the next tier.
Communicate status under pressure without over-promising or going silent.
Write ticket documentation that lets the next hero pick up exactly where you left off.

notes.title: What 'hero' support means operationally
notes.body:
Every security vendor claims great support; few define what it means in operations. Strip away the branding and 'hero' support is three measurable behaviors. Speed: first response in minutes, not hours, because a blocked user is a user finding workarounds — and workarounds are how security dies. Accuracy: the first diagnosis is usually right, because the hero reads the block event before guessing, asks the clarifying question before acting, and fixes the cause rather than the symptom. Documentation: every ticket leaves a trail so the customer never repeats themselves and the next hero never starts from zero. Speed without accuracy is just fast damage; accuracy without documentation is brilliance that evaporates at shift change.

Worked example: two responses to the same ticket — 'Our design app stopped opening after your update.' Response A, five minutes later: 'We pushed a fix, try now.' The app opens. Two days later it breaks again, worse, because Response A approved the updater binary globally and the real problem — a Ringfencing rule blocking the app's new helper process — was never diagnosed. Response B, twelve minutes later: 'I can see our Ringfencing policy blocked your app's new helper process after the update. I have allowed that specific process for your design group and verified the app launches. I am watching for similar blocks across your fleet today.' Response B was seven minutes slower and infinitely better: correct cause, narrow fix, verified, with monitoring attached. Heroes are measured by resolution quality and recurrence rate, not just response time.

Common gotchas: confusing responsiveness with resolution — replying 'looking into it' every hour is not support, it is narration. Another is the hero complex itself: the tech who hoards knowledge and becomes the single point of failure is not a hero, they are a risk. Real heroes write things down precisely so they are replaceable. Finally, speed has a floor: a thoughtful twelve-minute response beats a careless two-minute one. The discipline is to be fast without being hasty, which is a skill you build by practicing the intake and classification workflows in this module until they are reflex.

Measure what matters and distrust what is easy to game. Response time is easy to measure and easy to game — a stream of 'looking into it!' updates proves nothing. Track instead: reopen rate (did the fix stick?), time-to-correct-diagnosis (when did you actually know the cause?), and customer effort (how many times did they repeat themselves?). A hero with a twelve-minute response and a tiny reopen rate beats a two-minute responder with chronic reopen churn on every metric the business actually feels. Review these monthly as a team, and celebrate the low-reopen techs publicly — what you celebrate is what the team optimizes for.

notes.title: Ticket intake: capturing the six facts
notes.body:
Most bad support outcomes are decided in the first three minutes, at intake. An intake that misses key facts sends the tech down the wrong path; an intake that captures them makes the diagnosis almost mechanical. The six facts: who is affected (user, machine, group — is it one person or a pattern?), what exactly happens (the precise symptom, in the user's words plus your translation), when it started (timestamp, and what changed just before — updates, new software, policy pushes), what is blocked versus what is broken (is the platform denying an action, or is something else failing?), business impact (who cannot work and what it costs per hour of delay), and what has already been tried (so you do not repeat it and so you learn what did not work).

Worked example — bad intake: 'User says app blocked. Called at 10. Will look into it.' This tells the next person nothing; they will call the user back and ask everything again, and the user will conclude support is incompetent. Good intake: 'Affected: Maria Santos, workstation LAW-MAIN-042, Paralegals group — single user so far. Symptom: billing application fails to launch, error says the action was blocked; started this morning ~8:15 AM. Changed just before: Ringfencing tightening pushed to the firm last night (change log entry 2026-10-06). Blocked vs broken: platform deny — Detect shows the billing app's helper process denied at launch. Impact: Maria cannot generate invoices; billing team of 6 unaffected so far. Tried: rebooted, same result; user has not tried workarounds. Next: verify against test ring, prepare narrow exception for the helper process.' The good intake already contains the diagnosis; the fix is ten minutes away.

Operator gotchas: the fact users omit most often is 'what changed just before' — they do not connect their problem to an update, so you must ask directly: 'Did anything update, install, or change yesterday?' The fact techs skip most often is business impact, because it feels like sales talk — but impact is what sets your severity, and severity sets your response clock. Write the intake as if the person reading it is you, at 2 AM, with the customer on hold. Because someday it will be.

The vague ticket — 'internet is slow,' 'computer is acting weird' — needs a funnel, not a guess. Start wide: when did you first notice it, and is it constant or intermittent? Then narrow: is it one application or everything, one machine or several, wired or wireless? Then test: can you try this specific action right now and tell me exactly what happens? Each answer eliminates a branch; three questions usually isolate it to an app, a machine, or the network. Write the funnel answers into the intake as you go — 'slow internet' becomes 'intermittent latency on wireless, all apps, two laptops in Building B, started Tuesday after the access-point firmware update.' The vague ticket was never vague; it was just unasked.

notes.title: Severity classification: a matrix you can defend
notes.body:
Severity is not a feeling; it is a contract. When you mark something SEV-1, you are committing the organization's fastest resources and telling the customer this is all-hands. The classification has to be defensible in both directions — to the customer who thinks everything is urgent, and to your manager when you wake people up. A workable four-level matrix: SEV-1, critical business function down with no workaround, or active security incident — respond immediately, update every 15 to 30 minutes. SEV-2, major function degraded or single critical user blocked, workaround exists but painful — respond within the hour, update hourly. SEV-3, minor function affected or single non-critical user blocked — respond same business day, update daily. SEV-4, question, request, or cosmetic issue — respond within one to two business days.

Worked example — classify these four. One: ransomware-style encryption behavior blocked on a file server at 2 AM, Detect firing repeatedly. SEV-1: possible active incident, no workaround for 'maybe breached.' Two: the billing app blocked for one paralegal, five colleagues fine, invoices due Friday. SEV-2: single user, workaround is a colleague's machine, but revenue-adjacent. Three: a user's personal flash drive blocked by the new storage policy, approved encrypted drive works. SEV-3 or even 4: designed behavior, no business impact, needs explanation not a fix. Four: office manager asks how to run the monthly compliance report. SEV-4: a question, however politely urgent it sounds on the phone. Notice that severity follows impact and workaround availability, not volume or tone — the shouting caller with a SEV-4 gets calm handling, not an escalation.

Common mistakes: letting the customer's urgency set your severity — empathize with their frustration while classifying by impact. Another is severity inflation to get faster internal help; it works once, then nobody trusts your SEV-1s, which is dangerous when a real one arrives. And severity can change: a SEV-3 that turns out to affect a whole department gets reclassified upward with a note explaining why. The matrix is a living judgment, not a label you are stuck with.

Severity disputes are inevitable: the customer insists their SEV-4 is a SEV-1, or your manager thinks your SEV-2 is really a SEV-3. Handle both with the matrix, not authority. To the customer: acknowledge the impact, state your committed response plan, explain the classification in impact facts, and name the trigger that would reclassify upward immediately. To the manager: present the impact facts and the matrix, not your feelings. The matrix is the shared language that depersonalizes the disagreement. And when you are wrong — the SEV-4 that becomes a SEV-1 — say so plainly and reclassify fast; defending a wrong call to save face is how small incidents become big ones.

notes.title: Escalation paths: when, to whom, with what
notes.body:
Escalation is not failure; it is a tool. The failure is escalating late, escalating to the wrong tier, or escalating with no context so the next person starts over. Escalate when: you have exhausted your diagnostic steps, the issue exceeds your authority (a global policy change, a customer-wide exception), the severity demands skills you do not have, or the clock demands parallel effort. Escalate to: the next tier defined in your runbook — typically senior support, then engineering, then vendor escalation — never by guessing who might know. Escalate with: the six intake facts, what you tried and the results, your current hypothesis, the business impact and severity, and exactly what you need from the next tier.

Worked example — an escalation done right: 'Escalating ticket 4821 to senior support. SEV-2. Affected: 6 of 18 machines in the dental Imaging group; imaging software fails to launch since this morning's agent update. Intake facts attached. Tried: verified the block is our Ringfencing policy denying the app's new helper process; test exception on one machine did not resolve it — the helper now launches but crashes, suggesting the update changed more than the process name. Hypothesis: the vendor update altered the application's behavior beyond the process identity, possibly new file paths. Impact: the practice cannot take X-rays; patients being rescheduled. Need: help determining what the updated application now requires — permission to pull detailed process telemetry, or a joint call with the application vendor.' The senior tech can act in five minutes. Compare the bad version: 'Imaging app broken after update, please help.' That escalation buys a round of clarifying questions and an hour of delay.

Operator gotchas: the most common escalation failure is waiting too long — techs treat escalation as admitting defeat and burn two hours before calling for help on a SEV-1. Set a personal rule: if a SEV-1 or SEV-2 is not meaningfully progressing in 30 minutes, escalate. Another is escalating upward but not sideways: sometimes the fastest help is a peer who saw this exact issue last month — check the ticket history and team chat before going up the chain. And always tell the customer you are escalating and what it means: 'I am bringing in our senior team now; you will hear from us within 30 minutes.' Silence during escalation feels like abandonment.

Escalate sideways before you escalate up. The peer who fixed this exact issue last month is faster than the senior tier's queue — check the ticket history for similar symptoms and reach the resolving tech directly with your context package. Keep a team channel where stuck techs post the five-element package; make it culturally safe to ask early by celebrating the quick ask, not the lone-wolf grind. Upward escalation is for authority and capacity; sideways escalation is for knowledge. Most stuck tickets need knowledge, not rank — and the team that shares freely resolves faster than the team of brilliant silos.

notes.title: Communication under pressure
notes.body:
When systems are down, communication is the product. The customer cannot see you working; they only see what you tell them. The discipline has four rules. One: acknowledge fast, even before you have answers — 'We see it, we are on it, next update in 30 minutes' beats silence every time. Two: update on a cadence you announce in advance, and keep it even when there is no news — 'no change yet, still diagnosing, next update at 11:00' maintains trust. Three: never promise what you do not control — no ETAs you invented, no 'it will be fixed soon.' Promise communication, not resolution: 'I will update you every 30 minutes until this is resolved.' Four: translate, do not dump — the customer needs to know what is happening to their business and what they should do, not the internal ticket ID and process names.

Worked example — the 3-line status update during an outage. Bad: 'We are experiencing a service disruption affecting some users. Our engineers are working on it.' This says nothing and commits to nothing. Good: 'What is happening: our 2 AM policy push is blocking the imaging application on 6 machines at your practice — X-rays cannot be taken right now. What we are doing: our senior team is diagnosing the exact block and we have a rollback ready if needed. What you should do: reschedule morning X-ray appointments if possible; we will update you by 9:30 AM with either a fix or a workaround.' Three lines: situation, action, customer guidance, plus a committed next-update time. Write it, read it as the customer, then send it.

Common mistakes: going silent while you 'focus on the fix' — the customer experiences silence as abandonment and starts calling everyone they know, which multiplies the chaos. Another is the premature all-clear: 'looks fixed, let me know if it happens again' without verification — verify with the customer on a real workflow before closing. And never, ever blame the customer or the platform in writing: 'you clicked the wrong thing' and 'our product has a bug' both create enemies. Describe facts and next steps; assign no blame in the moment.

The incident ends, but the communication is not over. Send the follow-up within 24 hours: what happened in one paragraph with no blame, what you fixed, what you changed so it does not recur, and an invitation for feedback. For SEV-1s, add the timeline: detected at, acknowledged at, mitigated at, resolved at. This message does three jobs: it closes the emotional loop for the customer, it creates the written record the post-mortem needs, and it demonstrates the systemic improvement that justifies their trust. Customers forgive outages; they do not forgive being left wondering. The follow-up is where a bad day becomes a trust-building story.

notes.title: Documentation discipline: notes that save the next hero
notes.body:
A ticket without documentation is a story that never happened — the customer will call back in a month with the same issue and nobody will remember the fix. Good documentation has a fixed shape: the intake facts, the diagnostic steps in order with results, the root cause in one sentence, the fix with exact scope, verification that it worked, and follow-ups (monitoring, review dates, related risks). Write it during the ticket, not after — memory degrades fast, and 'I will document it later' means never.

Worked example — a ticket note written well: 'Ticket 4821, SEV-2, resolved. Cause: vendor update renamed the imaging app's helper process; existing Ringfencing policy denied the new process name. Diagnosis: Detect showed deny events for the new process at launch; confirmed on test machine that old process name no longer exists post-update. Fix: narrowed policy exception updated to the new process identity, scoped to Imaging group, applied 10:42 AM. Verified: launched imaging app on 3 affected machines, took test X-ray, confirmed save to network share. Follow-up: watching Detect for similar denies across fleet today; added vendor-update check to the pre-rollout checklist; exception review date set for 90 days. Customer confirmed operational at 11:15 AM.' Anyone reading this in six months knows exactly what happened and why. The note also feeds the knowledge base: the next tech with a renamed-helper-process issue finds this ticket instead of rediscovering the diagnosis.

Operator gotchas: documenting only the fix and not the diagnosis — 'updated the policy' helps no one next time. Another is private knowledge: the fix that lives in your head or in a DM thread might as well not exist; if it is not in the ticket, it did not happen. And document the dead ends briefly: 'checked network share permissions — not the cause' saves the next person from re-walking that path. Documentation is how a support team gets smarter instead of just older.

Turn ticket notes into a knowledge base, or the knowledge dies in the ticket archive. Monthly, harvest the best-resolved tickets: extract the symptom-diagnosis-fix triple into a searchable article, tag it by application and error, and link the source tickets. When the same issue recurs, the next tech finds the article in seconds instead of rediscovering the diagnosis. Assign article ownership — someone keeps each one current as software updates. A support team with a living knowledge base gets faster every quarter; a team without one solves the same problems forever. The documentation discipline from this module compounds only if you build the harvesting habit on top of it.

notes.title: Talking about support in the October 13 interview
notes.body:
You are interviewing for an IT Infrastructure Specialist role with a company famous for its support culture, so expect support-flavored questions even for an infrastructure title. They will probe three things: how you handle pressure, how you communicate with non-technical users, and whether you document. Prepare two or three STAR stories — Situation, Task, Action, Result — drawn from real experience: a time you fixed something under time pressure, a time you dealt with a frustrated user, a time your documentation saved someone. The STAR format matters because it forces the result: interviewers remember outcomes, not processes.

Worked example — a STAR story built from this module's material: 'Situation: at my last role I supported a small office where the billing application stopped launching for the whole billing team on a Monday morning — invoices due that week. Task: I was the only support available and needed them working within the hour. Action: I checked the endpoint protection console first instead of guessing, found our policy blocking the app's updated helper process, applied a narrowed exception to just the billing group, and verified invoicing worked on two machines before telling the team. I then documented the cause and added a vendor-update check to our change process. Result: the team was billing again within 40 minutes, and the same issue never recurred because the checklist caught the next update in testing.' Notice the structure: pressure, methodical action, verified result, systemic improvement. That last clause — 'and it never recurred because...' — is what separates operators from firefighters.

Common mistakes: telling war stories with no result ('and then it was really crazy') — always land the outcome with a number or a concrete improvement. Another is badmouthing past users or employers, even lightly; the panel hears how you will talk about them. And do not claim experience you do not have — if your support background is thin, say so plainly and show the discipline instead: 'I have not run enterprise support, but here is exactly how I would handle your SEV-1 call, step by step.' Panels hire judgment and honesty over inflated resumes.

Prepare questions for them, because the panel scores curiosity too. Ask: what does the escalation path look like from this role — when would I pull in engineering? How does the team balance fast approvals against careful verification? What is the most common breakage pattern new hires struggle with? Each question shows you already think like an operator: you are asking about the real job, not the perks. Avoid questions the job posting already answers, and never ask anything suggesting you skipped basic research. End with: what would make someone exceptional in this role in the first 90 days? Then listen carefully, because they just handed you the grading rubric.

quiz.q: A customer calls shouting that everything is down. You check: one user's personal flash drive is blocked by policy; their approved drive works. What is the severity and the right handling?
choices: SEV-1 — the customer is shouting, so treat it as critical.
SEV-3/4 — designed behavior with no business impact; calmly explain, verify the approved workflow, document.
SEV-2 — any block event is at least SEV-2.
Ignore it; the user is overreacting.
quiz.explain: Severity follows impact and workaround availability, never tone. This is designed deny-by-default behavior with a working approved path — it needs a calm explanation and documentation, not an escalation. Empathize with frustration while classifying by fact.

quiz.q: Which intake is actionable?
choices: 'App blocked for user, looking into it.'
'Maria Santos, LAW-MAIN-042, billing app fails to launch since ~8:15 AM after last night's Ringfencing push; Detect shows helper-process deny; 1 of 6 affected; reboot tried; invoices due Friday.'
'User unhappy with the new security software.'
'Something changed last night, not sure what.'
quiz.explain: The second intake has all six facts: who, what, when/what-changed, blocked-vs-broken, impact, tried. It practically contains the diagnosis. The others force the next tech to start over and call the user back.

quiz.q: It is 25 minutes into a SEV-1 and you are stuck. What do you do?
choices: Keep working alone; escalating now would look bad.
Escalate immediately with the full context package, and tell the customer you are bringing in senior help with a 30-minute update commitment.
Tell the customer to wait until you figure it out.
Downgrade the severity so the clock stops.
quiz.explain: The 30-minute rule exists because stuck time on a SEV-1 is the most expensive time in support. Escalation is a tool, not an admission of failure — and the customer must hear what is happening, not silence.

quiz.q: During an outage you have no fix yet and the next update is due. What do you send?
choices: Nothing — wait until there is real news.
'No change yet; still diagnosing the block. Next update at 11:00.'
'It will be fixed soon.'
A dump of internal ticket IDs and process names.
quiz.explain: Keep the announced cadence even with no news — silence reads as abandonment. Never promise resolution timing you do not control; promise communication. And translate: the customer needs situation, action, and their next step.

quiz.q: A fix works on your test machine. Before telling the customer it is resolved, you must:
choices: Close the ticket immediately to protect your resolution-time metric.
Verify on the customer's real workflow — have them launch the app and complete the actual task — then document and close.
Assume it works everywhere and push the change fleet-wide.
Ask the customer to reboot and call back if it still fails.
quiz.explain: The premature all-clear is a classic trust-killer. Verification means the customer's real workflow succeeding on affected machines, witnessed or confirmed — then the ticket gets its documentation and closure.

quiz.q: Your escalation note says 'Imaging app broken after update, please help.' What is missing?
choices: Nothing; senior support will figure it out.
Everything that makes escalation work: intake facts, steps tried with results, hypothesis, impact/severity, and exactly what you need from the next tier.
A more urgent tone.
The customer's phone number only.
quiz.explain: A context-free escalation buys a round of clarifying questions and an hour of delay. The five-element package lets the next tier act in minutes — escalation quality is a core hero skill.

quiz.q: A SEV-3 ticket turns out to affect an entire department. What do you do?
choices: Keep it SEV-3; the classification was already set.
Reclassify upward with a note explaining why, and adjust the response clock.
Close it and open a new ticket.
Wait for the customer to complain louder.
quiz.explain: Severity is a living judgment. When the impact picture changes, reclassify and note the reason — the audit trail of why severity changed is itself valuable documentation.

quiz.q: Which ticket note will help the team in six months?
choices: 'Fixed the policy.'
'Updated exception; user confirmed working.'

'Cause: vendor update renamed the imaging helper process; Ringfencing denied the new name. Fix: narrowed exception updated to the new process identity for the Imaging group, verified on 3 machines with a test X-ray. Follow-up: watching Detect today; added vendor-update check to the pre-rollout checklist.'
'Customer happy now.'
quiz.explain: The useful note has cause in one sentence, fix with exact scope, verification, and follow-ups. In six months, the next tech with a renamed-process issue finds this ticket instead of rediscovering the diagnosis from zero.

quiz.q: In the interview you are asked about a time you failed a customer. What is the strongest approach?
choices: Say you have never failed a customer.
Give a real STAR story: the situation, your action, the honest result including what went wrong, and the systemic fix you made so it could not recur.
Blame the previous employer’s tools.
Deflect to a story about a difficult coworker.
quiz.explain: Panels know everyone has failed a customer; they are testing honesty and growth. A real failure plus a systemic fix ('and it never recurred because...') demonstrates exactly the operator mindset they hire for.

quiz.q: Two techs handle the same ticket. Tech A replies in 2 minutes with a guess that is wrong; Tech B replies in 12 minutes with the correct diagnosis, a narrow fix, and monitoring. Who performed better and why?
choices: Tech A — response time is the primary metric.
Tech B — accuracy and resolution quality beat raw speed; a wrong fast guess creates recurrence and rework.
They are equal; both responded.
Neither; both were too slow.
quiz.explain: Speed without accuracy is fast damage. Heroes are measured by resolution quality and recurrence rate — Tech B's twelve minutes included diagnosis, a scoped fix, verification, and monitoring, which is what actually ends the ticket.

handsOnLab.title: Run a simulated support shift
handsOnLab.brief: You are the hero on shift. Work a fictional queue of ten tickets end to end: intake, severity classification, diagnosis, customer communication, one escalation, and a shift handoff document. Everything is written — the discipline is in the writing.
steps: Create ten fictional tickets spanning the range: a blocked payroll app, a personal USB complaint, a suspected malware block at 2 AM, a how-to question, a whole-department outage, a printer issue, an approval request for unknown software, a repeat of last week's issue, a VIP with a minor problem, and one vague 'internet is slow' report.
For each ticket, write the six-fact intake. Where the fictional user gives you too little, write the clarifying question you would ask — do not invent their answer.
Classify all ten into SEV-1 through SEV-4 using the matrix, and write one sentence defending each classification.
Write the diagnosis for each ticket: what you would check first, what the likely cause is, and the fix with exact scope. Mark which two you would verify on a test machine before touching production.

Draft the customer-facing response for four tickets: the SEV-1, the shouting VIP with a SEV-4, the personal-USB complaint, and the vague 'internet is slow.' Each must include situation, action, and the customer's next step.
Choose one ticket to escalate. Write the full five-element escalation package: intake facts, steps tried with results, hypothesis, impact/severity, and exactly what you need from the next tier.
Write the 3-line outage status update for the department-wide outage: what is happening, what you are doing, what the customer should do — plus the committed next-update time.
Write complete ticket notes for three resolved tickets using the six-element shape: intake, diagnostics, root cause in one sentence, fix with scope, verification, follow-ups.
Build a STAR story from the simulated shift's hardest ticket, written as you would deliver it in the October 13 interview — with a concrete result.
Write the shift handoff document: open tickets with severity, next action, and owner; watch items; and anything the next hero must know in the first five minutes.
Re-read your handoff as if you are the incoming hero at 2 AM. Fix anything unclear.
Save everything as shift-log.md with clear sections per step above.
handsOnLab.deliverable: shift-log.md containing ten intakes with severity defenses, diagnoses, four customer responses, one escalation package, one outage status update, three ticket notes, one STAR story, and the shift handoff document.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every ticket has a severity with a one-sentence defense, a next action, and an owner; the escalation package lets a senior act in five minutes; the handoff is readable at 2 AM.
