title: Policy Troubleshooting & Break-Fix
summary: When allowlisting breaks a legitimate application, the operator's job begins: a diagnosis workflow that finds the exact denied action, reads block events like evidence, handles the classic breakage patterns — updaters, installers, macros — and applies exceptions with change-control discipline. You will build a break-fix runbook you could actually use on shift.
objectives: Run the four-step diagnosis workflow: identify the blocked action, check the policy, test the exception, document.
Read a block event's fields — process, parent, action, target — and reconstruct what the application tried to do.
Diagnose and fix the three classic breakage patterns: updaters/installers, macros/scripts, and removable media.
Write exceptions that are narrow, time-bounded, owned, and reviewed — never broad permanent holes.
Test exceptions safely in a canary ring before fleet-wide rollout.
Prove whether a breakage is the policy or something else by isolating variables.

notes.title: The diagnosis workflow: blocked action, policy, exception, document
notes.body:
Every break-fix follows the same four steps, in order, no skipping. Step one: identify the blocked action precisely. Not 'the app is blocked' — which process, launched by which parent, attempted which action against which target, at what time. The block event or Detect alert gives you this; the user's description does not. Step two: check the policy. Which policy denied it, at which level of the tree, and was the denial correct per the policy's intent? Sometimes the policy is working exactly as designed and the answer is user education, not an exception. Step three: test the exception. If a policy change is warranted, make the narrowest change that resolves the legitimate need, test it on a canary machine, and verify the real workflow. Step four: document. The cause, the change with exact scope, who approved it, verification, and the review date.

Worked example: 9:04 AM, ticket — 'Nobody in billing can open the invoice app since this morning.' Step one: you pull the block events. At 8:47 AM, on six billing machines, the invoice application's helper process was denied execution — parent process the invoice app itself, action 'execute,' target the helper binary. The helper's file hash differs from last week: the vendor pushed an update overnight. Step two: the Ringfencing policy for the billing group permits the invoice app but the helper process identity changed with the update, so the denial is policy-correct but business-wrong. Step three: you update the narrowed exception to the new helper identity, scoped to the billing group only, apply it to two canary machines, and watch a user generate and print a test invoice. Clean. Then roll out to the group. Step four: you log the cause, the change, the approver, verification, and set a 90-day review — plus a note to add vendor-update checks to the pre-rollout checklist.

Common mistakes: starting at step three — pushing an exception before identifying the exact blocked action. This produces broad, sloppy exceptions that accumulate into Swiss cheese. Another is skipping step two's judgment call: not every denial needs an exception; some need the user to use the approved path. And the classic: fixing it, telling the user 'try now,' and never documenting — which guarantees the next update breaks it again and nobody remembers why. The workflow is a loop, and documentation is what makes the loop compound instead of repeat.

Time-box each step so diagnosis does not become archaeology. Identification: fifteen minutes — if you cannot name the blocked action from the events in that time, escalate with what you have. Policy check: fifteen minutes — read the denying rule and judge its intent. Exception and test: the canary test starts within the hour for SEV-2 and above. Documentation: written before you close the ticket, no exceptions. The time-boxes are not about rushing; they are about recognizing when you are stuck. A tech who escalates at minute thirty with clean notes outperforms the hero who emerges at hour three with a fix and no trail — because the next identical ticket takes the first tech ten minutes and the second tech another three hours.

notes.title: Reading block events like a detective
notes.body:
A block event is a witness statement: it tells you who did what to whom, and your job is to reconstruct the story. The fields that matter: the process (what was blocked — name, path, hash), the parent process (what launched it — this is often the real story), the action (execute, write file, read file, registry edit, network connection), the target (what it tried to touch), the policy that denied it (which rule, at which level), and the timestamp plus machine and user. Read them in relationship, not isolation: a blocked 'powershell.exe' means nothing until you see its parent was 'winword.exe' and its target was a network connection — that is a malicious document, not an admin script.

Worked example: Detect shows a deny at 2:14 AM on workstation LAW-MAIN-031. Process: powershell.exe. Parent: winword.exe — Microsoft Word launched PowerShell in the middle of the night. Action: network connection attempt. Target: an external IP address. Policy: the Ringfencing rule that stops Word from spawning script interpreters and reaching the network. User: an attorney who was not at work at 2 AM. Reconstruction: someone opened a malicious document — likely a phishing attachment — and Word tried to launch PowerShell to reach an external server. The platform did exactly its job. Your response is not an exception; it is incident response: isolate the machine, find the document, check whether anything else executed. Contrast with a daytime event: parent is the IT admin's remote tool, action is a registry edit on a managed machine, user is you. Same blocked action, opposite meaning. Context is everything.

Operator gotchas: the number-one misread is treating the blocked process as the culprit instead of following the parent chain upward. Always ask 'who launched this, and who launched them?' until you reach a user action or a system service. Another is ignoring the timestamp: a block at 2 AM on an unattended machine means something very different from the same block at 10 AM with the user active. And watch for the 'legitimate parent, malicious child' pattern versus 'malicious parent, legitimate child' — both exist, and the remediation differs completely. When in doubt, reconstruct the full chain before touching any policy.

Correlate across machines: a single block event is a ticket, but the same block on twenty machines is an incident with a different response. When you see a deny, ask 'who else?' — query the event feed for the same process, parent, or target across the fleet in the same window. The payroll-helper block on six machines meant a vendor update, not six individual problems; the fix was one policy change, not six tickets. Fleet-wide correlation also catches the attack: the same malicious pattern on five machines is a campaign, and your response shifts from break-fix to incident response. Train yourself to zoom out before you zoom in — the pattern across machines usually reveals the cause faster than any single event's details.

notes.title: Breakage pattern: updaters and installers
notes.body:
Updaters are the number-one source of allowlisting breakage, and understanding why makes you fast at fixing them. An updater breaks policy in up to four ways at once. New hashes: the updated binary has a different file hash than the approved one, so hash-based approval stops matching. New paths: the installer drops files into temp directories or versioned folders the policy never saw. New helper processes: the updated app spawns child processes with new names, tripping Ringfencing rules. New behaviors: the updater itself needs to write to protected locations or reach the network, which the base policy denies. Any one of these produces a 'the app stopped working after the update' ticket; a major version update can produce all four.

Worked example: the design team's browser auto-updates overnight. Morning: the browser will not launch. Block events show the new browser binary denied — hash changed. You also see the updater's temp installer denied execution, and the browser's new helper process denied by Ringfencing. The fix, done properly: first, verify the update is legitimate — check the vendor's release notes and confirm the hash against the vendor's published value or your software deployment tool's copy. Then update the approval to the new binary identity, permit the updater's behavior narrowly (the specific updater process, writing to its install path, during the update), and update the Ringfencing rule for the renamed helper. Test on two canary machines: launch, browse, verify the helper runs. Then roll out. What you do NOT do: approve the temp installer's hash globally, or turn off Ringfencing for the browser 'until the dust settles' — both are holes that outlive the incident.

Common mistakes: approving by hash alone for applications that update frequently — you will be approving every week. For frequently-updating apps, the sustainable answer is usually approving the vendor's signed updater process and its defined install behavior, not chasing hashes. Another is forgetting the updater needs network access to fetch the update while the app itself should not have it — Ringfencing lets you split those permissions per process, which is exactly the granularity the feature exists for. And always ask: should this app auto-update at all? For critical line-of-business software, managed updates through your deployment tool beat surprise auto-updates that break Monday mornings.

Make the managed-versus-unmanaged decision explicitly for every application class. Managed updates — pushed through your deployment tool on your schedule — give you testing, timing control, and known identities; they are the right answer for line-of-business software where a surprise break costs real money. Auto-updates are acceptable for low-risk, frequently-patched software where the security cost of delay exceeds the breakage risk — but then your policy must approve the updater's behavior, not chase hashes. Unmanaged per-user installs are the enemy of both: no testing, no timing, no inventory. Write the decision down per application class, because 'we will figure out updates later' is how Monday mornings get ruined.

notes.title: Breakage pattern: macros and scripts
notes.body:
Macros and scripts live in the exact territory Ringfencing was built to control: legitimate automation that is also the favorite weapon of attackers. A macro is code inside a document; a script is code run by an interpreter like PowerShell or a Windows script host. The platform's stance is deny-by-default: Word does not get to launch PowerShell, Excel macros do not get to write executables, scripts do not run unless explicitly permitted. When a legitimate business process depends on a macro, the breakage feels personal — 'you broke my spreadsheet' — but the rule exists because malicious documents use the identical mechanism.

Worked example: the finance team has a monthly close spreadsheet with macros that pull data and generate reports. After the Ringfencing tightening, the macros are blocked — Excel cannot launch the data tool the macro calls. Diagnosis: block events show excel.exe as parent, the data tool as the blocked child process, action execute. The macro itself is legitimate — you verify with the finance lead, check the spreadsheet's origin, and confirm it has been in use for a year. The fix: a narrowed exception permitting Excel to launch that specific data tool, for the finance group only, with the spreadsheet's location restricted to the finance share. You do not permit Excel to launch arbitrary processes, and you do not permit macros fleet-wide. Verification: run the month-close workflow end to end on a canary machine. Documentation notes the business owner and sets a review date — because the day that spreadsheet gets a malicious copycat, you want the scope to be as small as possible.

Operator gotchas: the dangerous shortcut is 'allow macros for the finance team' as a blanket permission — that is not an exception, it is surrendering the control. Exceptions must name the specific parent, the specific child, and the specific scope. Another is the unsigned-macro problem: if the business macro is unsigned, anyone can modify it and the exception still applies — push the business toward signing macros or storing them in a controlled location. And never forget the alternative: sometimes the right fix is not an exception but a better workflow — a small script run by the IT team on a schedule can replace a fragile user macro entirely.

The sustainable answer for macro-heavy businesses is trusted locations plus signing, not per-macro exceptions forever. Designate controlled shares where macro-enabled files live; the policy permits macro execution only for files in those locations, and only those locations are writable by the document owners — not by email attachments or downloads. Push the business toward signing macros: a signed macro from a known publisher is verifiable in a way an unsigned one never is. The migration path: inventory current macros, move them to trusted locations, sign what matters, and set a date after which unsigned macros outside trusted locations stop working. It is a project, not a ticket — but it ends the endless exception treadmill for macros.

notes.title: The exception discipline: narrow, temporary, owned, reviewed
notes.body:
Every exception is a deliberate hole in a deny-by-default wall, so exceptions need the discipline of a bank vault log. A proper exception has five attributes. Narrow: the smallest scope that solves the problem — specific process, specific action, specific group, never 'allow everything for everyone.' Temporary: an expiry or review date, because today's legitimate need is tomorrow's forgotten hole. Owned: a named business owner who can answer 'do you still need this?' Owned by a person, not a department. Justified: the business reason written down, so the next admin does not have to guess. Reviewed: a calendar date when the exception gets re-examined, and a default action if the owner does not respond — usually removal or re-approval.

Worked example — an exception request done right: 'Request: permit the imaging application's updater process to write to the program install path and reach the vendor update server. Scope: Imaging group, 6 machines, updater process identity only. Business justification: the imaging software updates monthly; without this, each update breaks the app and blocks X-ray appointments. Owner: Dr. Patel, practice owner. Expiry: 12 months, with quarterly verification that the updater identity has not changed unexpectedly. Approved by: [you], after verifying the updater's signature against the vendor. Rollback: remove the exception; the app continues running on its current version.' Compare the bad version: 'Allowed imaging updater.' One of these survives an audit; the other is a mystery hole.

Common mistakes: permanent exceptions with no review date — they accumulate until the policy is decorative. Overly broad scope — 'allow for the whole organization' when six machines needed it. Missing owners — 'the finance team' cannot answer an email; a named human can. And the meta-mistake: no exception inventory. If you cannot produce a list of every active exception with owner and review date in five minutes, you do not have exception discipline — you have exception folklore. Build the inventory from day one; module 9's compliance report depends on it.

Run the exception review as a real meeting, quarterly, with the owners in the room. The agenda is mechanical: for each active exception, the owner answers 'do you still need this?' in thirty seconds. Still needed: confirm the scope is still minimal and reset the review date. Not needed: remove it now, verify nothing breaks, document the removal. Owner absent: default to removal after one grace cycle — exceptions without advocates are the ones that rot. The meeting takes an hour for a healthy inventory and pays for itself the first time it kills a years-old exception nobody remembered. Publish the minutes: the inventory, the removals, the renewals. Visibility keeps exceptions deliberate instead of folkloric.

notes.title: Testing exceptions in a canary ring
notes.body:
An exception is a policy change, and policy changes get the lifecycle: test before fleet-wide rollout. The canary ring is a small set of representative machines — your own workstation, one or two volunteers per affected group, covering the machine types and software combinations in scope. The test plan has three parts: the positive test (the legitimate workflow now works — launch the app, run the real task, confirm the output), the negative test (the things that should still be blocked are still blocked — try the adjacent bad action and confirm the deny), and the soak (leave it for at least one full business cycle, watching block events for surprises).

Worked example: the finance macro exception from the last note. Canary ring: your test VM, plus two finance workstations whose owners agreed to test. Positive test: open the month-close spreadsheet, run the macros, verify the report generates and the data tool launches. Negative test: from Excel, try to launch an unapproved process — confirm it is still denied. Try modifying the macro to call something new — confirm denied. Soak: three business days, watching the block feed for the finance group. Day two: you see a deny for a different helper the macro occasionally calls during quarter-close — not in your exception. You add it narrowly, re-test, and extend the soak. Only then do you roll out to the full finance group. The soak caught what the lab test missed, which is exactly why the soak exists.

Operator gotchas: canary machines that are not representative — testing only on your pristine admin workstation misses the weird software combinations of real user machines. Include at least one 'messy' machine. Another is the too-short soak: testing for an hour catches syntax errors, not behavioral surprises; a full business cycle is the minimum. And the negative test is the one everyone skips and the one that matters most — an exception that accidentally permits more than intended is worse than no exception, because it is invisible. Prove the deny still works, every time.

Choose canaries for representativeness, not convenience. Cover the axes of variation: machine types (laptop versus desktop versus kiosk), OS and driver versions (the driver-variant miss from the deployment module is the cautionary tale), software combinations (the machine with the weird legacy app), and user behaviors (the power user who exercises edge features). Five machines spanning the variation beat twenty identical ones. Recruit volunteers explicitly — they get fixes first and a direct line to support — and rotate them so nobody burns out. Document the canary set per application class, because the right canaries for the billing app differ from those for the warehouse scanners. Representativeness is the whole game.

notes.title: When it is not the policy: isolating variables
notes.body:
The hardest break-fix skill is proving a negative: demonstrating that the policy is NOT the cause, so you stop changing security controls and start fixing the real problem. Users blame the security platform for everything — it is the newest, most visible change, and 'the security thing did it' is cognitively easy. Your job is bisection: change one variable at a time until the cause is isolated. The method: reproduce the problem, check the block events for that exact timeframe — if there is no deny event for the failing action, the policy is probably not the cause. Then test on a machine outside the policy scope, or temporarily move a test machine to a permissive test policy, and see if the problem persists. If it persists without the policy, the policy is innocent.

Worked example: 'The invoice app is broken since your update.' You check block events for the affected machines across the failure window: zero deny events for the invoice app or its helpers. The policy did not fire. Next, you test on a machine in the IT group that never received the billing policy: same failure. The policy is innocent — twice proven. Now you look elsewhere: the vendor pushed an app update the same night, and the app's own log shows a database connection failure. The real cause is a database credential rotation that the app update mishandled. You hand the evidence to the app vendor instead of carving exceptions into a policy that was never the problem. Imagine the alternative: you had 'fixed' it with a broad exception, the app still failed, and now you have both a broken app and a hole in your policy.

Common mistakes: the correlation trap — 'it broke after the policy push, therefore the policy broke it.' Post hoc reasoning is the number-one cause of unnecessary exceptions. Another is testing without a control: changing two things at once and not knowing which one mattered. And the political mistake: telling the user 'it is not our policy' without evidence. Bring the evidence — the empty block log, the failing test outside policy scope — and the conversation stays professional. 'Here is the proof it is not the policy, and here is what I found instead' makes you the hero, not the obstacle.

Build the 'not the policy' evidence package as a habit, because you will present it weekly. The package: the block-event query for the failure window showing zero denies for the failing action, the reproduction on a machine outside the policy scope failing identically, and your alternate hypothesis with its own evidence — the vendor's update notes, the application's error log. Present it as help, not defense: 'I have ruled out the policy with these two tests — here is what I found instead, and here is my recommended next step.' Users who see this package twice stop blaming the platform reflexively; they start bringing you better symptoms. The evidence package does not just win the argument — it trains the organization to troubleshoot with you instead of against you.

notes.title: Change control for people who hate paperwork
notes.body:
Change control has a reputation problem: it sounds like bureaucracy, so operators skip it, and then nobody knows why the policy looks the way it does. The fix is making the control lighter than the chaos it prevents. For routine exceptions, the control is four lines: what changed, why, who approved, how to undo it — written before the change, not after. For standard changes (the tenth identical updater exception), a pre-approved template: fill in the blanks, no meeting required. For emergency changes (the 2 AM SEV-1), the control is 'act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow' — the paperwork follows the fix, but it still happens. What never happens: an undocumented change. The day you cannot explain a policy line is the day you have lost control of the fleet.

Worked example — the emergency change log entry: 'EMERGENCY 2026-10-07 02:14 — What: rolled back last night's Ringfencing tightening on the billing group to the previous version. Why: SEV-1, billing app blocked on 6 machines, root cause not yet isolated, business impact immediate. Approved by: on-call lead (verbal, 02:10). Undo of the undo: re-apply the tightening after root-cause diagnosis in the test ring. Follow-up: post-mortem scheduled today 10 AM; the tightening stays in the test ring until then.' Forty seconds to write, and it answers every question the morning shift, the manager, and the auditor will ask. Compare: no entry, and Monday's admin finds a policy that does not match Friday's documentation, with no idea why.

Operator gotchas: change control theater — a three-page form for a one-line change just teaches people to bypass the process. Match the weight of the control to the risk of the change. Another is the approval bottleneck: if every exception needs a manager's signature, exceptions pile up and users suffer — pre-approve the routine patterns and reserve human approval for the novel and the broad. And review the change log itself monthly: if you find entries you cannot understand, the process is failing even if everyone is filling in the form. The goal is a fleet whose every policy line has a reason, an owner, and an undo path.

Audit the change log monthly, because the process rots silently. Read every entry and ask: do I understand what changed and why? Is the approver named? Is there an undo path? Flag the entries that fail — not to punish, but to find where the process is too heavy (people bypass heavy processes) or too vague (the template needs better prompts). Track two numbers: what fraction of policy changes have complete log entries, and how many emergency changes got their within-the-hour documentation. A process with total bypass is not a process; lighten it until compliance is the path of least resistance. Change control that people actually follow beats perfect change control that everyone routes around.

quiz.q: Ticket: 'Nobody in billing can open the invoice app since this morning.' What is your FIRST step?
choices: Push an exception allowing the invoice app everywhere.
Pull the block events for the billing machines this morning and identify the exact blocked process, parent, action, and target.
Roll back last night's policy push immediately.
Reinstall the invoice app on all billing machines.
quiz.explain: Step one of the workflow is identifying the blocked action precisely — process, parent, action, target. Everything else (policy check, exception, rollback) depends on knowing exactly what was denied. Acting before identifying produces sloppy, over-broad fixes.

quiz.q: Block event: powershell.exe blocked, parent winword.exe, 2:14 AM, network connection to an external IP, user not at work. What is the correct response?
choices: Create an exception so Word can launch PowerShell; the user probably needs it.
Treat as a potential incident: isolate the machine, find the document, investigate — do not create an exception.
Ignore it; the platform blocked it so there is no problem.
Uninstall Word from the machine.
quiz.explain: The parent chain (Word launching PowerShell at 2 AM to reach an external IP) is the classic malicious-document pattern. The platform did its job; your job is incident response. An exception here would legalize the attack path.

quiz.q: After a browser auto-update, the browser will not launch: new binary hash denied, temp installer denied, new helper process denied by Ringfencing. What is the disciplined fix?
choices: Approve the temp installer's hash globally and disable Ringfencing for the browser until things settle.

Verify the update is legitimate, update approvals to the new identities, narrowly permit the updater's defined behavior, update the Ringfencing rule for the renamed helper, test on canaries, then roll out.
Tell users to stop updating the browser.
Reimage all affected machines.
quiz.explain: Each breakage mode gets a narrow, verified fix: new identities approved after legitimacy verification, updater behavior permitted narrowly, Ringfencing updated for the renamed helper, canary-tested. Global approvals and disabling controls trade a morning's inconvenience for permanent holes.

quiz.q: Finance has a legitimate macro that needs Excel to launch one specific data tool. What is the correct exception scope?
choices: Allow macros for the entire finance team.
Permit excel.exe to launch that specific data tool, for the finance group only, with the spreadsheet restricted to the finance share — and push toward signed macros.
Allow Excel to launch any process for finance.
Disable Ringfencing for the finance group.
quiz.explain: Exceptions name the specific parent, the specific child, and the narrowest scope. Blanket macro permission is surrendering the control; the narrowed exception preserves both the business workflow and the security boundary.

quiz.q: You test an exception: the legitimate workflow works. What critical test remains before rollout?
choices: Nothing — the positive test is sufficient.
The negative test: confirm adjacent bad actions are still denied, then soak for a full business cycle watching block events.
Ask the user if they are happy.
Immediately roll out to the whole fleet to save time.
quiz.explain: The negative test proves your exception did not accidentally open more than intended — an invisible over-permission is worse than no exception. The soak catches behavioral surprises that lab tests miss, like the quarter-close helper in the worked example.

quiz.q: 'The app broke after your policy push' — but there are zero deny events for the app in the failure window, and it also fails on a machine outside the policy scope. What do you conclude?
choices: The policy is guilty; the logging must be broken.
The policy is innocent — twice proven. Stop changing security controls and investigate the real cause (e.g., the vendor's own update).
Add an exception anyway, just in case.
Re-push the policy to fix the logging.
quiz.explain: Bisection proved it twice: no deny in the window, and failure without the policy. Changing controls now would create holes without fixing anything. Bring this evidence to the user and the vendor — it keeps the conversation professional and factual.

quiz.q: Which exception request is audit-proof?
choices: 'Allowed imaging updater.'

'Permit the imaging updater process to write to the install path and reach the vendor update server; scope: Imaging group, 6 machines; owner: Dr. Patel; expiry 12 months with quarterly verification; approved after signature check; rollback: remove the exception.'
'User needed it, approved.'
'Temporary fix, will review later.'
quiz.explain: The audit-proof exception has all five attributes: narrow scope, expiry/review, named owner, written justification, and a rollback path. 'Will review later' without a date means never.

quiz.q: It is 2 AM, a SEV-1 policy breakage is blocking a business function, and the cause is unclear. What is the change-control-correct move?
choices: Wait until morning when the change board meets.
Roll back to the last known-good policy now to restore service, document within the hour, and hold a post-mortem review before re-applying.
Make no changes; document the outage instead.
Disable the agent on affected machines.
quiz.explain: Emergency change control is 'act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow.' Rolling back to known-good restores service fastest; the documentation and post-mortem preserve governance. Waiting for a morning meeting trades hours of outage for process theater.

quiz.q: Your canary test uses only your pristine admin workstation. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing — the admin workstation is the most important machine.
Canaries must be representative: include volunteer machines from the affected group, including at least one 'messy' real-world machine, or you will miss real-world software combinations.
Canary testing is unnecessary for small changes.
You should test on the CEO's machine instead.
quiz.explain: A pristine admin workstation does not represent the fleet's software combinations. The canary ring exists to catch what the lab misses — it must include real user machines from the affected groups.

quiz.q: A user demands you 'just turn off the blocking' for their department because exceptions take too long. How do you respond?
choices: Agree — user satisfaction comes first.
Explain what the control protects them from, commit to a fast verification timeline for their legitimate need, and offer the narrowed exception path — while documenting the request.
Refuse and close the ticket.
Turn it off quietly and turn it back on later.
quiz.explain: Disabling a control for a department is surrendering the security boundary for convenience. The operator move is empathy plus discipline: acknowledge the friction, speed up the legitimate path, keep the control intact — and document the request in case the pattern repeats.

items.prompt: Recite the four break-fix steps in order.
items.answer: Identify the blocked action, check the policy, test the exception, document.
items.explain: No skipping — acting before identifying produces sloppy exceptions.

items.prompt: Name the six key fields of a block event.
items.answer: Process, parent process, action, target, denying policy/level, timestamp + machine + user.
items.explain: Read them in relationship — the parent chain is often the real story.

items.prompt: Name four ways updaters break allowlisting.
items.answer: New hashes, new paths, new helper processes, new behaviors.
items.explain: A major version update can produce all four at once.

items.prompt: What are the five attributes of a proper exception?
items.answer: Narrow, temporary, owned, justified, reviewed.
items.explain: Every exception is a deliberate hole — log it like a vault entry.

items.prompt: What are the three parts of a canary test?
items.answer: Positive test, negative test, soak for a full business cycle.
items.explain: The negative test proves the deny still works; the soak catches behavioral surprises.

items.prompt: How do you prove the policy is NOT the cause?
items.answer: Check block events for the failure window, then reproduce outside policy scope — if it still fails, the policy is innocent.
items.explain: Bisection beats the correlation trap.

items.prompt: What is the emergency change-control rule?
items.answer: Act now, document within the hour, review tomorrow.
items.explain: The paperwork follows the fix but still happens.

items.prompt: Block events show the billing helper denied at 8:47 AM on six machines; the helper's hash changed overnight. Walk the workflow.
items.answer: Step 1: identified — helper process, parent the billing app, action execute, hash changed by vendor update. Step 2: policy correct per intent but business-wrong. Step 3: narrow exception to the new helper identity for the billing group, canary-test with a real invoice. Step 4: document cause, change, approver, verification, 90-day review.
items.explain: The full loop: identify precisely, judge policy intent, narrow exception, verify on a real workflow, document.

items.prompt: A macro exception request says 'allow macros for finance.' What do you do?
items.answer: Refuse the blanket scope; rewrite it narrowed — specific parent (excel.exe), specific child (the data tool), finance group only, share-restricted, with owner and review date.
items.explain: Blanket macro permission surrenders the control the platform exists to provide.

items.prompt: During the soak you spot a deny for a different helper the macro calls only at quarter-close. What happened and what do you do?
items.answer: The lab test missed a behavioral path — exactly what the soak is for. Add the helper narrowly, re-test, extend the soak before fleet rollout.
items.explain: This is the soak earning its keep; do not skip it or shorten it after a surprise.

items.prompt: The user insists 'your update broke it' but there are no deny events and it fails off-policy too. Script your reply.
items.answer: 'I checked the block logs for the failure window and tested outside the policy — the policy did not fire and the failure happens without it, so the cause is elsewhere. Here is what I found instead [vendor update / credential issue], and here is my next step.'
items.explain: Evidence, not argument: the empty block log plus the off-policy reproduction keeps it professional.

items.prompt: You need an exception for a one-time vendor remote session tonight. Write the exception attributes.
items.answer: Narrow: vendor's remote tool process, this machine only, tonight's window. Temporary: expires tomorrow morning. Owned: named requester. Justified: vendor support case number. Reviewed: auto-expiry plus verification the session ended.
items.explain: One-time needs get the tightest scope of all — time-boxed to the session window.

items.prompt: A department head asks for a permanent exception 'so we never have this problem again.' How do you respond?
items.answer: Explain that permanent exceptions accumulate into decorative policies; offer a 12-month exception with quarterly reviews and a named owner instead — and suggest fixing the underlying workflow if the need is truly permanent.
items.explain: Permanent means forgotten. Time-boxed with reviews keeps the hole deliberate and visible.

handsOnLab.title: Build a break-fix runbook with five realistic scenarios
handsOnLab.brief: Write the runbook you would want open on your second monitor during a shift: five realistic breakage scenarios, each with symptoms, diagnosis steps, the policy check, an exception draft, a test plan, and a rollback — plus the blank templates you would reuse for scenario six.
steps: Set up your runbook document with five scenario sections plus a templates appendix. Each scenario gets the same headings: symptoms, diagnosis, policy check, exception draft, test plan, rollback, documentation.

Scenario 1 — the blocked payroll run: write the symptoms (payroll app fails Friday morning), the block-event fields you would pull, and the exact narrowed exception you would draft for the payroll group.

Scenario 2 — the updater breakage: a design app auto-updates overnight and will not launch. Write the four updater breakage modes to check, the legitimacy verification steps, and the canary test plan including the negative test.

Scenario 3 — the macro block: finance's month-close spreadsheet macros are denied. Write the diagnosis (parent/child chain), the narrowed exception with all five attributes, and the argument for pushing the business toward signed macros.

Scenario 4 — the USB block: a warehouse scanner's storage is denied after a Storage Control tightening. Write the inheritance check (which level broke the scanner exception), the fix, and the user communication.
Scenario 5 — the false alarm: 'the app broke after your policy push' with zero deny events. Write the bisection procedure, the evidence you would gather, and the professional reply script.
For each scenario, write the rollback: the exact undo action if your fix makes things worse.
Build the blank templates appendix: the four-line change log, the exception request form (five attributes), the canary test plan (positive/negative/soak), and the escalation package.

Add a 'triage cheat sheet' page: the four workflow steps, the six block-event fields, and the three questions to ask every caller ('what changed just before?', 'show me the exact error', 'who else is affected?').
Review all five scenarios for scope creep: flag any exception you wrote that is broader than necessary and narrow it.
Have a peer (or your future self) read scenario 3 cold and attempt the diagnosis from your written steps alone. Fix anything they stumble on.
Save the runbook as break-fix-runbook.md and note the date of your next self-review.
handsOnLab.deliverable: break-fix-runbook.md with five complete scenarios (symptoms, diagnosis, policy check, exception draft, test plan, rollback, documentation), the templates appendix, and the triage cheat sheet.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Each scenario traces symptom to root cause to verified fix; every exception draft has all five attributes; the cheat sheet fits on one page; a cold reader can execute scenario 3.
