mockTask.q: Panel question: 'You pushed a policy change Friday at 4:55 PM. Monday morning the helpdesk queue is on fire. Walk me through what happened and what you do now.'
choices: Immediately roll back the change, then investigate calmly: pull block events from the weekend, identify the exact denied actions, and explain the Friday-afternoon timing mistake and the change-window discipline you will follow.
Blame the users for not reporting issues over the weekend.
Push a broad exception allowing everything the helpdesk mentions to quiet the queue fast.
Deny that the policy change could be related since it worked on your machine.
mockTask.explain: The panel is testing ownership and method. The strong answer owns the timing mistake (Friday changes are an operator error), restores service first via rollback, then diagnoses with evidence — and names the systemic fix: evening change windows, canary rings, no Friday pushes. Deflection or broad exceptions fail the judgment test.

title: ThreatLocker Deployment Projects
summary: Rolling out deny-by-default across a real organization: pilot rings, Learning Mode baselining, stakeholder communication, go/no-go gates, rollback plans, and the success metrics that prove the project worked. You will write a complete 90-day deployment plan for a 200-endpoint fictional company.
objectives: Design pilot rings for a staged rollout and explain what each ring proves.
Run a Learning Mode baselining window and turn its output into initial policies.
Write stakeholder communications — the exec one-pager and the user announcement — that prevent rollout panic.
Define go/no-go gates with measurable criteria for each rollout wave.
Build a rollback plan that fits deny-by-default semantics: revert policy, not panic.
Track the success metrics that prove the deployment worked: coverage, blocks, exceptions, ticket trends.

notes.title: Rollout phases and pilot rings
notes.body:
You do not deploy deny-by-default to 200 endpoints on a Monday. You deploy in rings — concentric waves of machines where each ring proves something the previous one could not. Ring 0 is IT and the project team: your own machines, where breakage is embarrassing but not business-stopping, and where you learn the platform's behavior. Ring 1 is friendly volunteers across departments: real workflows, cooperative users who will report problems instead of working around them. Ring 2 is half the fleet: scale effects appear here — the weird software combinations, the forgotten legacy app, the department with the unusual workflow. Ring 3 is everyone: by now the policies are proven and the support team has seen most breakage patterns.

Worked example: Meridian Logistics, a fictional 200-endpoint company — 150 office staff, 40 warehouse, 10 servers. Ring 0: the 8-person IT team, week 1-2. You discover the ticketing system's updater needs a Storage Control exception — caught with zero business impact. Ring 1: 20 volunteers across office and warehouse, week 3-4. The warehouse volunteers surface the barcode scanner need; the office volunteers surface a dictation app. Both get narrowed exceptions. Ring 2: 90 more machines, week 5-7. Scale reveals a legacy label printer whose driver installer trips the policy on 12 machines — one exception, applied once at the warehouse group level, fixes all twelve. Ring 3: the remaining 82, week 8-9, plus the 10 servers in their own hardened track. Total breakage tickets: 31, all resolved within the ring that found them. Nobody in Ring 3 ever experiences a surprise, because Rings 0-2 already paid for the lessons.

Common mistakes: rings that are too small to be representative — five IT machines do not represent the warehouse. Rings that move too fast — the point of pausing between rings is the soak, watching for the problems that only appear over a business cycle. And the political mistake: skipping rings because an executive wants it done this quarter. The rings ARE the schedule; compressing them does not save time, it moves the breakage from the pilot into production, where it costs ten times more.

Run servers on a separate, slower track — never in the user rings. Servers have different risk profiles (availability is critical, change windows are narrow), different software (fewer apps, each one load-bearing), and different blast radius (one bad policy halts the business, not just one user). The server track mirrors the ring shape — lab, one canary server, then the fleet — but on maintenance-window scheduling with explicit rollback rehearsals. Harden server policies beyond the workstation baseline: servers run fewer applications, so their allowlists can be shorter and their Ringfencing stricter. The most expensive deployment failures are server policies pushed with workstation assumptions; the separate track makes that mistake structurally impossible.

notes.title: Learning Mode baselining: listening before enforcing
notes.body:
Deny-by-default has a cold-start problem: on day one, the platform does not know what 'normal' looks like for this specific organization. Learning Mode solves it by observing first and enforcing later. During the baselining window, the agent watches which applications execute, which processes they spawn, what files and network resources they touch — and records it all without blocking. At the end of the window, you review the learned baseline and convert it into initial policies: the applications people actually use become the allowlist, and everything else remains denied. The baselining window must cover a full business cycle — at least two weeks, ideally including a month-end or equivalent peak — because the payroll app that runs monthly will not appear in a three-day sample.

Worked example: Meridian's Ring 1 baselining runs for three weeks. The learned data shows 214 distinct applications across the 20 volunteers. Reviewing, you categorize: 160 are standard business apps and OS components — approved. 22 are department-specific tools (dictation, label software, scanner utilities) — approved with group scoping. 18 are updaters and installers — handled via updater rules, not individual approvals. 9 are personal or redundant (three different PDF readers, two music apps, a game) — not approved; users get the standard alternatives. 5 are unknown — investigated, two turn out to be a forgotten remote-access tool that gets removed, three are vendor utilities that get approved narrowly. The baseline review is where you discover what the organization actually runs versus what IT thought it ran — the gap is always embarrassing and always valuable.

Operator gotchas: the too-short window — baselining for a long weekend and missing the monthly processes, which then break on day one of enforcement. The unreviewed baseline — approving everything learned without categorization just allowlists the organization's bad habits, including that forgotten remote-access tool. And baselining during abnormal periods: if you baseline over the holidays or during a migration, 'normal' is wrong. Time the window for a representative business period, review every category with a human, and remember that the baseline is a starting point — policies keep evolving after enforcement begins.

Run the baseline review as a working meeting, not a solo task. Attendees: you, one person from IT who knows the software inventory, and a representative from each major department. Walk the categorized list — approve, scope, updater-rule, reject, investigate — making decisions out loud and recording each with its rationale. The department reps catch what IT misses ('we still use that old label tool twice a year'), and their presence builds the buy-in you will need at enforcement. Time-box the investigate items: each gets an owner and a 48-hour deadline, not an indefinite parking lot. End with the approved baseline signed off — that signature turns 'IT's project' into 'our policy.'

notes.title: Stakeholder communication: the exec one-pager and the user announcement
notes.body:
Deployments fail on communication more often than on technology. Two documents carry the rollout: the exec one-pager and the user announcement. The exec one-pager answers the three questions leadership actually has: what are we doing and why (in business terms — fewer ransomware incidents, cleaner audits, not 'implementing Ringfencing'), what will it cost in disruption (honest: expect some blocked-application tickets in the first weeks, here is the support plan), and what do you need from them (visible sponsorship when someone important complains). The user announcement answers the user's three questions: what is changing on my computer, what do I do when something legitimate gets blocked, and how fast will you fix it.

Worked example — the user announcement for Meridian's Ring 2: 'Starting Monday, your computer will block applications that are not on our approved list — this is how we stop ransomware. What changes: if you try to install something new, you will see a block message instead of an installer. Most of your daily apps are already approved and will work normally. What to do: if a work application you need gets blocked, call the helpdesk at extension 4357 or click the request button in the block message — include what you were trying to do. We will respond within 2 hours during business hours. What not to do: please do not try workarounds like portable apps from USB drives; they will also be blocked, and you will just lose time. Why: last year a single malicious email attachment cost us three days of downtime. This prevents that.' Notice what it does: sets expectations, gives a clear action, states the response commitment, explains the why in one sentence, and preempts the workaround impulse.

Common mistakes: the technical announcement — 'we are deploying application allowlisting with Ringfencing policies' means nothing to users and frightens them. The missing why — without the ransomware sentence, the rollout reads as IT power-tripping. The absent executive sponsor — when a VP's favorite unapproved tool gets blocked and they escalate over your head, you need leadership to have already signed the one-pager. And announcing once: repeat the message at each ring, because Ring 3 users were not paying attention during the Ring 1 announcement.

If leadership will not sponsor visibly, do not launch — a rollout without air cover fails at the first executive escalation, and you will own the political damage. When the one-pager comes back unsigned, diagnose the objection: cost, disruption fear, or disbelief in the threat? Answer with the matching evidence — pilot block data for disbelief, the ring structure and rollback plan for disruption fear, incident-cost math for cost objections. Offer a smaller commitment: sponsor just the pilot, with a go/no-go they control. Most resistance melts after Ring 1 produces real numbers. But if sponsorship is truly absent, say so plainly and pause — launching deny-by-default into an unsupportive executive team is a career-limiting move dressed as initiative.

notes.title: Go/no-go gates between waves
notes.body:
Each ring ends at a gate, and gates have criteria — otherwise 'the pilot went fine' is a feeling, not a fact. A go/no-go gate checks four things. Breakage rate: how many blocking tickets per machine in the ring, and is the trend falling? If Ring 1 generated 40 tickets on 20 machines, something is wrong with the policies, not the users. Resolution time: are break-fix tickets closing within the committed window? A growing backlog means the support team is underwater and the next ring will drown them. Exception quality: are the exceptions created narrow, owned, and reviewed — or is the team punching holes to keep up? User sentiment: a quick pulse survey — do users understand what to do when blocked? If they are working around the platform instead of requesting approvals, the communication failed. Go means all four are healthy; no-go means pause, fix, and re-gate — never 'go and hope.'

Worked example — Meridian's Ring 1 gate review. Breakage: 14 tickets on 20 machines over two weeks — high, but 11 were the scanner and dictation issues now fixed with exceptions; the trend is falling. Resolution: average 3 hours, within the 4-hour commitment. Exceptions: 6 created, all narrow with owners and review dates — quality good. Sentiment: pulse survey, 16 of 20 say they understand the block message and the request process; 4 are confused about USB drives — communication gap to fix before Ring 2. Decision: conditional GO — proceed to Ring 2 after sending the USB clarification to all staff and adding the scanner exception to the baseline. The gate did its job: it caught the USB confusion before it became 90 confused users instead of 4.

Operator gotchas: gates without teeth — if the answer is always 'go,' you do not have gates, you have ceremonies. Define the criteria before the ring starts, when you can still be objective. Another is the sunk-cost push: 'we have spent six weeks, we cannot pause now' — pausing for one week to fix policies is always cheaper than a failed Ring 3. And document every gate decision with its data; when the post-mortem asks why Ring 2 went ahead, 'the numbers supported it, here they are' is the answer that ends the discussion.

Document every gate decision with its data, and write the no-go recovery plan before you need it. The gate record: the four metrics, the decision (go, conditional go, no-go), any conditions, and the signatures. The no-go plan, written in advance: what gets fixed, who owns each fix, the re-gate date, and what the held rings do meanwhile. A no-go without a recovery plan becomes an indefinite stall — the project loses momentum and dies quietly. A no-go with a dated recovery plan is just a delay with a purpose. Teams that handle their first no-go well earn the credibility that makes every subsequent gate honest; teams that never say no-go eventually ship a failure.

notes.title: Rollback plans under deny-by-default
notes.body:
Rollback in a deny-by-default world does not mean uninstalling the platform in a panic — it means reverting policy to the last known-good state, which is fast, controlled, and does not surrender the security boundary. Your rollback plan has three tiers. Tier 1, policy revert: the previous policy version is one action away — you restore it for the affected group and the breakage stops. This handles 90 percent of bad pushes. Tier 2, ring halt: stop the rollout wave, keep completed rings on the new policy if they are healthy, hold the rest. This contains a wave-specific problem. Tier 3, enforcement pause: for a truly catastrophic misconfiguration, temporarily relax enforcement to monitor-only for the affected scope while you diagnose — the platform still sees everything, it just stops blocking. Note what is NOT on the list: mass uninstallation, which destroys your visibility exactly when you need it most.

Worked example: during Meridian's Ring 2, a Ringfencing tightening for the label software goes out Tuesday evening. Wednesday morning, 12 warehouse machines cannot print shipping labels — the tightening blocked the driver's new helper process, which the canary ring missed because the canary machines had a different driver version. Tier 1 response: revert the label policy to the previous version for the warehouse group — 10 minutes, labels printing again. Then diagnose calmly: the driver version difference explains the miss. Fix: update the policy for both driver versions, test on both, re-push Wednesday evening. The rollback was boring and fast, which is the entire point — because the plan existed before the incident, nobody had to invent it under pressure.

Common mistakes: no rollback plan at all — the team discovers during the incident that nobody knows how to revert. The untested rollback — reverting has its own steps and they should be rehearsed, not read for the first time at 2 AM. And the pride trap: refusing to roll back because 'the policy is correct, the users need to adapt' — if the business cannot ship labels, the policy is wrong for now regardless of its theoretical merit. Roll back, fix, re-deploy. Speed of recovery is the metric, not stubbornness.

Rehearse the rollback before Ring 1 — a game day, not a document review. Pick a test group, push a deliberately breaking policy change, and execute the Tier 1 revert under time pressure: who authorizes, what gets clicked, how you verify service restored, how you communicate. Time it. The rehearsal always reveals something: the revert needs a permission nobody has, the verification step is vague, the communication template is missing. Fix all of it now, while the stakes are zero, and write the lessons into the runbook. The team that has rolled back on purpose rolls back calmly in the incident; the team meeting the revert button for the first time at 2 AM does not.

notes.title: Success metrics: proving the deployment worked
notes.body:
A deployment project ends with evidence, not a feeling. Track five metrics from day one so the final report writes itself. Coverage: percentage of the fleet with healthy agents and current policy — the goal is effectively 100 percent, and every gap gets a named reason. Block volume: denied executions per week by category — this should spike at enforcement start (the platform discovering the organization's shadow IT) then settle to a low baseline. Exception inventory: count of active exceptions with owners and review dates — growing slowly and deliberately, never exploding. Ticket trends: break-fix tickets per week — high in early rings, falling steadily; a rising trend means policies or communication are failing. Time-to-approve: how fast legitimate requests get approved — this measures whether security is enabling or obstructing the business.

Worked example — Meridian's 90-day numbers. Coverage: 198 of 200 agents healthy (two machines in storage, documented). Block volume: week 1 of enforcement saw 412 denied executions — mostly unapproved installers and personal software users tried to run; by week 8 the baseline is ~15 per week, mostly updater edge cases. Exceptions: 23 active, all narrow, all owned, earliest review date in 60 days. Tickets: Ring 1 averaged 7 per week, Ring 3 averaged 2 per week — the trend the gates demanded. Time-to-approve: median 45 minutes against a 2-hour commitment. The executive summary: 'In 90 days we moved 200 endpoints to deny-by-default. The platform denied 1,900+ unauthorized executions with zero reported malware incidents. Twenty-three deliberate exceptions are tracked and reviewed. Approval median is 45 minutes. Two machines await reimaging.' That is a project that gets funded again.

Operator gotchas: vanity metrics — 'we blocked 10,000 things' without categories or outcomes impresses nobody who matters. The missing baseline — if you did not measure ticket volume before the project, you cannot prove the trend improved; start measuring in week one. And the metric nobody tracks: user workaround attempts. If Storage Control blocks are falling but USB-related helpdesk calls are rising, users may be finding ways around the control — investigate the behavior, not just the numbers.

Build the dashboard in a spreadsheet before you automate anything — the manual version teaches you which numbers actually matter. One tab per metric, one row per week: coverage with gap explanations, block volume by category, exception inventory with review dates, tickets per week with the ring annotated, time-to-approve median. Add a notes column for context ('Ring 2 wave 1 started,' 'holiday week'). Review it at every gate and monthly in steady state. Only automate after three months of manual tracking, when you know exactly which numbers you read and which you ignore. The spreadsheet-first discipline prevents the classic failure: an expensive automated dashboard of metrics nobody reads, while the number that matters lives in someone's head.

notes.title: The 90-day plan: putting it all together
notes.body:
A deployment plan is a narrative with dates: it tells everyone what happens, when, and what proves each phase worked. The 90-day shape for a 200-endpoint rollout: days 1-14, foundation — portal structure built, naming conventions set, Ring 0 (IT) deployed, Learning Mode baselining begins on Ring 1 volunteers. Days 15-35, pilot — Ring 1 under enforcement, baseline reviewed and converted to policies, first gate review, user announcement drafted and tested. Days 36-60, scale — Ring 2 rollout in two waves with a gate between them, support team running the break-fix workflow daily, stakeholder updates biweekly. Days 61-80, complete — Ring 3, servers on their hardened track, all-hands communication, final gate. Days 81-90, harden and hand over — exception inventory audited, reports automated, documentation finished, project retrospective, transition to steady-state operations.

Worked example — the plan's risk register, the section most plans skip. Risk one: executive's unapproved tool gets blocked, executive escalates over IT. Mitigation: exec one-pager signed in week one, plus a 1-hour VIP approval SLA. Risk two: a critical legacy app breaks in Ring 3 that never appeared in earlier rings. Mitigation: application inventory interviews with every department before Ring 2, plus the Tier 1 rollback plan rehearsed. Risk three: support team overwhelmed by ticket volume. Mitigation: break-fix runbook written before Ring 1, temp help approved if tickets exceed 15 per week, gate criteria include resolution time. Risk four: Learning Mode window misses monthly processes. Mitigation: three-week window including a month-end, finance interviewed about periodic workflows. A plan without a risk register is a wish; the register is what makes it a plan.

Common mistakes: the plan that ends at 'deployment complete' — the 81-90 hardening phase is where the project becomes sustainable operations; skipping it leaves a deployed platform with no owner. The plan with no dates — 'phase 2 follows phase 1' drifts forever; put calendar dates on every gate. And the plan nobody reads — a 40-page document that the team ignores. Keep the plan to ten pages: timeline, rings, gates, comms, risks, metrics, owners. If it does not fit in a 30-minute walkthrough, it is too long to execute.

Run the retrospective with the whole project team within two weeks of day 90, while memories are fresh. The format is fixed: what worked (keep doing), what broke (fix the process), what surprised us (update the risk-register template for next time), and what we would tell the next team (the handover wisdom). Write it down — the retrospective document is the most valuable artifact of the project for the organization, more than the plan itself, because the next deployment starts from it instead of from zero. Include the numbers: final metrics, total tickets, total exceptions, hours spent. End with the ownership transfer: who owns the platform now, what their first 30 days look like, and when you check back. Projects end; operations continue — the retrospective is the bridge.

cards.front: What does each pilot ring prove? (Rings 0-3)
cards.back: Ring 0 (IT): platform behavior with zero business risk. Ring 1 (volunteers): real workflows with cooperative users. Ring 2 (half fleet): scale effects and weird combinations. Ring 3 (all): proven policies, experienced support.

cards.front: What is Learning Mode's purpose in a deployment?
cards.back: Observe-before-enforce baselining: the agent records normal application behavior without blocking, so the baseline can be reviewed and converted into initial policies.

cards.front: How long should a baselining window run, and why?
cards.back: At least two to three weeks covering a full business cycle including month-end — so periodic processes like payroll are observed, not missed.

cards.front: What three questions does the exec one-pager answer?
cards.back: What are we doing and why (business terms), what disruption to expect, and what is needed from leadership (visible sponsorship).

cards.front: What three questions does the user announcement answer?
cards.back: What is changing on my computer, what to do when something legitimate is blocked, how fast support will respond.

cards.front: What four things does a go/no-go gate check?
cards.back: Breakage rate and trend, resolution time vs commitment, exception quality (narrow/owned/reviewed), user sentiment (do users understand the process?).

cards.front: What are the three rollback tiers under deny-by-default?
cards.back: Tier 1: revert policy to last known-good. Tier 2: halt the rollout wave. Tier 3: pause enforcement to monitor-only for the affected scope.

cards.front: Why is mass uninstallation NOT a rollback tier?
cards.back: It destroys visibility exactly when you need it most; policy revert restores service without surrendering the security boundary.

cards.front: Name the five deployment success metrics.
cards.back: Coverage, block volume by category, exception inventory health, ticket trends, time-to-approve.

cards.front: What should block volume do over a healthy rollout?
cards.back: Spike at enforcement start (discovering shadow IT), then settle to a low baseline — a rising trend means policies or communication are failing.

cards.front: What are the five phases of the 90-day plan?
cards.back: Foundation (days 1-14), pilot (15-35), scale (36-60), complete (61-80), harden and handover (81-90).

cards.front: Why does the plan need a risk register?
cards.back: A plan without named risks and mitigations is a wish — the register (exec escalation, legacy apps, support overload, missed periodic processes) is what makes it executable.

quiz.q: You have 200 endpoints and an executive demanding full deployment this month. What is the operator-correct response?
choices: Deploy to all 200 at once to meet the deadline.
Hold the ring structure: explain that compressing rings moves breakage from pilot into production where it costs ten times more, and propose the fastest safe schedule with dates.
Deploy to the executive's machine first to win support, then everyone else.
Refuse the project.
quiz.explain: The rings are the schedule — skipping them does not save time, it relocates the cost. The professional move is a clear explanation of the tradeoff plus a committed fast schedule, not silent compliance or refusal.

quiz.q: Your Learning Mode window ran over a holiday week. What is the risk?
choices: No risk; the platform learns the same way regardless.
The baseline captures abnormal behavior as 'normal' and misses periodic processes — re-run the window over a representative business period.
The baseline will be more secure.
Agents cannot learn during holidays.
quiz.explain: Baselining during abnormal periods bakes wrong 'normal' into policy and misses the monthly processes that then break on enforcement day. The window must cover a representative business cycle.

quiz.q: Ring 1 gate review: 14 tickets on 20 machines, average resolution 3 hours (commitment 4), 6 narrow exceptions with owners, but 4 of 20 users confused about USB blocks. Decision?
choices: NO-GO — any confusion fails the gate.
Conditional GO — fix the USB communication gap first, then proceed; the gate caught a small problem before it scaled.
GO — confusion is the users' problem.
Skip Ring 2 and go straight to Ring 3 to save time.
quiz.explain: Gates exist to catch exactly this: a small, fixable issue before it becomes 90 confused users. Conditional go with the comms fix is the gate working as designed — neither blind approval nor pointless delay.

quiz.q: Wednesday morning, 12 warehouse machines cannot print after Tuesday's policy tightening. What is the Tier 1 rollback?
choices: Uninstall the agent from all warehouse machines.
Revert the label policy to the previous version for the warehouse group — minutes, printing restored — then diagnose calmly.
Wait to see if it resolves itself.
Push a fleet-wide exception for all printing.
quiz.explain: Tier 1 is policy revert to last known-good: fast, controlled, preserves the security boundary and visibility. Uninstallation destroys visibility; waiting wastes business hours; fleet-wide exceptions are scope creep under pressure.

quiz.q: Which metric trend signals a failing rollout?
choices: Block volume spiking at enforcement start.
Break-fix tickets rising week over week after Ring 2.
Time-to-approve median of 45 minutes.
Coverage at 99 percent.
quiz.explain: Early spikes are expected discovery; rising tickets after scale means policies or communication are failing. The trend is the signal — falling ticket volume is what the gates demand.

quiz.q: A VP's unapproved screen-capture tool gets blocked and they escalate over your head. What should have prevented this?
choices: Nothing — VPs are exempt from policy.
The exec one-pager signed in week one plus a VIP approval SLA, so leadership backs the process instead of overriding it.
Blocking the VP's email.
Pre-approving every application in existence.
quiz.explain: This is the risk-register scenario: visible leadership sponsorship plus a fast VIP path handles it. Without the signed one-pager, every executive exception becomes a political incident that punches holes in the rollout.

quiz.q: The baseline review finds a forgotten remote-access tool on several machines. What do you do?
choices: Approve it — it was in the baseline, so it must be normal.
Investigate: unreviewed baselines allowlist bad habits. Remove the tool if unauthorized; approve narrowly only if legitimate.
Ignore it; baselining handles it.
Extend the baseline window.
quiz.explain: The baseline is observed behavior, not approved behavior — approving everything learned without categorization allowlists the organization's bad habits. The review is where you discover what IT thought the fleet ran versus what it actually runs.

quiz.q: Your canary ring missed a driver-version difference that broke 12 machines in Ring 2. What is the systemic fix?
choices: Larger canary rings only.
Ensure canaries cover the real variant space (driver versions, machine types) and record the lesson: the post-mortem updates the canary selection criteria.
Never update drivers again.
Blame the canary volunteers.
quiz.explain: Canaries must be representative of the variant space, not just numerous. The miss becomes a process improvement: update selection criteria so the next rollout's canaries cover known variants.

quiz.q: The 90-day plan ends at day 80 with 'deployment complete.' What is missing?
choices: Nothing — deployment is the goal.
The harden-and-handover phase (days 81-90): exception audit, automated reports, finished documentation, retrospective, transition to steady-state ownership.
A celebration party.
More rings.
quiz.explain: Days 81-90 convert a deployed platform into sustainable operations with an owner. Skipping handover leaves a working deployment that slowly rots — the most common way good projects die.

quiz.q: Users are working around blocks with portable apps instead of requesting approvals. Which gate check failed?
choices: Breakage rate.
User sentiment — they do not understand or trust the request process, so the communication failed.
Exception quality.
Coverage.
quiz.explain: Workarounds signal that users find the approved path harder than evasion — a communication and process failure, not a technical one. The pulse survey exists to catch this before it becomes culture.

items.prompt: What does each ring (0-3) prove?
items.answer: Ring 0: platform behavior, no business risk. Ring 1: real workflows, cooperative users. Ring 2: scale effects. Ring 3: proven policies, experienced support.
items.explain: Each ring buys knowledge the previous one could not.

items.prompt: How long should Learning Mode baselining run?
items.answer: 2-3 weeks minimum, covering a full business cycle including month-end.
items.explain: Periodic processes must be observed, not discovered on enforcement day.

items.prompt: What does the exec one-pager cover?
items.answer: What and why in business terms, expected disruption with the support plan, what leadership must provide (visible sponsorship).
items.explain: Signed before the rollout, it is your shield when executives escalate.

items.prompt: Name the four gate checks.
items.answer: Breakage rate/trend, resolution time, exception quality, user sentiment.
items.explain: Define criteria before the ring starts, when you can still be objective.

items.prompt: What are the three rollback tiers?
items.answer: Policy revert, wave halt, enforcement pause to monitor-only.
items.explain: Revert policy, not panic — never mass-uninstall.

items.prompt: Name the five success metrics.
items.answer: Coverage, block volume by category, exception inventory, ticket trends, time-to-approve.
items.explain: Track from day one so the final report writes itself.

items.prompt: Ring 2 tickets are rising week over week and resolution time just breached the commitment. What do you do?
items.answer: Invoke the gate: pause the next wave, diagnose whether it is policy quality, support capacity, or communication — fix the cause, then re-gate. Do not push into Ring 3 hoping it improves.
items.explain: Rising tickets after scale is the failing-rollout signal; gates without teeth are ceremonies.

items.prompt: The baseline categorized 214 apps; 9 are unknown. Walk through handling them.
items.answer: Investigate each: identify the software and its business purpose, remove what is unauthorized (like the forgotten remote-access tool), approve narrowly what is legitimate, document every decision.
items.explain: Unknown is not a category — it is a to-do list. The review is where shadow IT gets found.

items.prompt: A department was never interviewed and their legacy app breaks in Ring 3. What failed in the plan?
items.answer: The application inventory step — every department gets interviewed before Ring 2. Now: Tier 1 rollback for that group, diagnose, narrow exception, and add the interview to the pre-rollout checklist.
items.explain: This is the risk-register scenario; the mitigation was the inventory interviews.

items.prompt: Two machines sit in storage with no agent. Coverage reads 198/200. How do you report this?
items.answer: Report 99% with the two machines named, explained (in storage, documented), and tracked for reimaging — never round up to 100% silently.
items.explain: Every coverage gap gets a named reason; silent rounding is how gaps become permanent.

items.prompt: Time-to-approve median is 6 hours against a 2-hour commitment. What is the business risk?
items.answer: Users experience security as obstruction and start working around it — approve faster (staffing, pre-approved patterns) or watch workaround culture grow.
items.explain: Approval speed measures whether security enables or obstructs the business.

items.prompt: Write the one-paragraph executive summary of Meridian's 90-day results.
items.answer: 'In 90 days we moved 200 endpoints to deny-by-default: 1,900+ unauthorized executions denied, zero reported malware incidents, 23 tracked exceptions all owned and reviewed, approval median 45 minutes against a 2-hour commitment, 198/200 agents healthy.'
items.explain: Evidence, not adjectives: coverage, blocks with outcomes, exceptions governed, speed, gaps named.

handsOnLab.title: Write a 90-day deployment plan for a fictional 200-endpoint company
handsOnLab.brief: Produce the complete deployment plan package for Meridian Logistics (fictional, 200 endpoints): timeline with gates, ring design, baselining plan, both communications, rollback plan, metrics dashboard, and risk register. This is the document you would defend in front of a panel.
steps: Write the company profile: Meridian Logistics, 200 endpoints — 150 office, 40 warehouse across two buildings, 10 servers. Note the business rhythms that matter: month-end close, warehouse shipping peaks, the legacy label printer.
Design the four rings with machine counts, selection criteria for Ring 1 volunteers, and what each ring must prove. Put calendar dates on every ring assuming a week-1 start.
Write the Learning Mode baselining plan: duration, which machines, the review categories (approve, scope, updater-rule, reject, investigate), and who attends the review.
Draft the exec one-pager: the business why, honest disruption expectations, the support plan, and the specific ask of leadership. Keep it to one page.
Draft the user announcement for Ring 2: what changes, what to do when blocked, the response commitment, the workaround warning, the one-sentence why.
Define the gate criteria numerically: max tickets per machine per ring, resolution-time commitment, exception quality bar, sentiment survey threshold. Write the gate review template.
Write the three-tier rollback plan with the exact steps for Tier 1 (policy revert), who can authorize each tier, and the rehearsal you will run before Ring 1.
Build the metrics dashboard template: the five metrics, where each number comes from, the healthy trend for each, and the threshold that triggers concern.
Write the risk register: at least six risks (executive escalation, legacy app, support overload, missed periodic process, driver variants, user workarounds) with a mitigation for each.
Lay out the 90-day timeline: foundation, pilot, scale, complete, harden-and-handover — with every gate and communication marked on the calendar.
Write the day-90 executive summary as if the project succeeded: fill it with the realistic numbers from this module's worked example.
Save the package as deployment-plan.md and read it end to end as the skeptical executive. Fix anything that would not survive their questions.
handsOnLab.deliverable: deployment-plan.md containing the company profile, ring design with dates, baselining plan, exec one-pager, user announcement, gate criteria and template, rollback plan, metrics dashboard, risk register, 90-day timeline, and the day-90 executive summary.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every ring has dates and gate criteria; both communications answer their three questions; the rollback plan names who authorizes each tier; the risk register has six risks with mitigations; the plan survives a 30-minute skeptical read.

videos.title: ThreatLocker official YouTube channel
videos.blurb: Official deployment walkthroughs and best-practice content — use it to see how the vendor frames rollout phases and baselining, then compare against the operator discipline in this module. Channel; duration varies.

mockTask.q: Panel question: the CEO asks, 'Why should we pay for a project to block things that already work?' Give your two-minute answer.
choices: 'Because ransomware is scary and the news says so.'

'Because what 'works' today includes every unapproved installer, personal app, and malicious attachment your users run — last year one attachment cost three days of downtime. Deny-by-default blocks what is not approved before it executes: our pilot data shows hundreds of unauthorized executions stopped per week with legitimate work approved in under an hour. You pay to convert unknown risk into a governed list.'
'Because compliance requires it.'
'Because our competitors have it.'
mockTask.explain: The winning answer translates to business terms: names the actual cost (downtime), explains the mechanism in one line (blocks unapproved before execution), cites pilot evidence, and frames the outcome (unknown risk becomes a governed list). Fear, compliance, and peer pressure are weak closes; quantified risk reduction is the strong one.

title: MIT 6.858: Threat Models & Security Architecture
summary: The first-principles habit from MIT's computer systems security course, taught in our own words: what a threat model is, how to reason about assets, adversaries, attack surface, and trust boundaries, and how to apply that reasoning to an endpoint fleet. Independent study aligned to the course's public topic map — no affiliation claimed.
objectives: Define a threat model using its four parts: assets, adversaries, attack surface, trust boundaries.
Apply first-principles security reasoning: goals, adversary model, mechanism, iteration.
Classify adversaries by capability and match defenses to the realistic threat, not the scariest one.
Enumerate an attack surface by counting entry points systematically.
Threat-model a small business file server end to end as a worked example.
Translate threat modeling to fleet scale: what changes when you protect 200 endpoints instead of one server.

notes.title: What a threat model is: assets, adversaries, surface, boundaries
notes.body:
A threat model is a structured answer to four questions. What are you protecting — the assets: data, systems, availability, reputation. Who are you protecting it from — the adversaries: their capabilities, their motivations, their resources. Where can they attack — the attack surface: every entry point, every interface, every trust assumption. And where does trust change — the trust boundaries: the lines across which data or control passes from a trusted zone to a less-trusted one. Without all four, security decisions are vibes: you buy tools for threats you do not face and miss the ones you do.

Worked example: your home router. Assets: your internet traffic, the devices on your network, the router's admin interface. Adversaries: opportunistic internet scanners probing for default passwords; a houseguest who might snoop; a determined attacker targeting you specifically (unlikely — note how you consciously set this aside). Attack surface: the WAN port facing the internet, the Wi-Fi network, the admin web page, WPS if enabled, outdated firmware with known bugs. Trust boundaries: internet versus LAN, guest network versus main network, admin interface versus regular traffic. The model immediately suggests actions: change the default admin password (kills the scanner adversary), enable the guest network (contains the houseguest), disable remote admin from the WAN (shrinks the surface), update firmware. Every action traces to a specific part of the model — that traceability is the whole point.

Common mistakes: the asset list that says 'everything' — if everything is critical, nothing is, and you cannot prioritize. The adversary list with one entry, 'hackers' — too vague to design against; capabilities and motivations change the defense completely. And the model that is written once and filed: threat models decay as systems change, so date them and revisit when the architecture changes. A threat model is a living document, not a compliance artifact.

When everything feels critical, rank assets by asking two questions: what does losing it cost (money, legal exposure, operational halt), and what does protecting it cost? Assets where loss-cost dwarfs protection-cost are the priority; assets where protection costs more than the loss are candidates for acceptance — and acceptance is a documented decision with an owner, not an oversight. Revisit the ranking when the business changes, because asset value moves: the archive nobody cared about becomes critical during litigation, the dev server becomes critical when it holds the only copy of the new product. Ranking is not a one-time sorting; it is a living judgment about what the business cannot afford to lose.

notes.title: First-principles reasoning: the security design habit
notes.body:
The core habit this course teaches — in our own words, as independent study — is reasoning from first principles instead of from checklists. The loop has four steps. First, state the security goal precisely: not 'be secure' but 'only the billing team can read the invoice database, even if an attacker controls a workstation.' Second, define the adversary: what can they do, what can they not do — be explicit, because every unstated assumption is a future vulnerability. Third, design the mechanism: the actual technical control that achieves the goal against that adversary — authentication, isolation, cryptography, policy. Fourth, iterate: attack your own design on paper, find where the goal, adversary, or mechanism mismatch, and refine. Then repeat, because the first design is always wrong somewhere.

Worked example: goal — 'a malicious email attachment must not be able to encrypt the file server's shared drive.' Adversary — controls a user's workstation via a phishing document; can run code as the user; cannot break cryptography or guess admin passwords. Mechanism candidate one: antivirus on the workstation. Iterate — attack it: the adversary's brand-new malware is not in any signature database, so the mechanism fails against this adversary. Mechanism candidate two: the file server only accepts connections from known application processes, and workstations run deny-by-default application control so the unknown malware never executes. Iterate — attack it: the adversary could steal a user's credentials and log in directly... which the goal did not cover. Refine the goal: add 'and stolen credentials alone cannot reach the share without the managed device.' Now the mechanism needs device authentication too. Each iteration made the goal sharper and the mechanism stronger — that is the loop working.

Common mistakes: starting from the tool ('we bought X, therefore we are secure against Y') instead of from the goal — tools serve mechanisms, mechanisms serve goals. Another is the unstated adversary: designing against 'an attacker' without saying what they can do produces mechanisms that fail against slightly stronger attackers. And skipping iteration: the first design always has a hole; the discipline is attacking your own work before reality does. Write the loop down for every significant design decision — the document is short and the clarity is enormous.

Apply the loop to purchasing decisions to kill shelfware. Goal: state precisely what the tool must achieve against which adversary — 'detect ransomware-affiliate tooling on workstations within minutes' is a goal; 'improve security' is not. Adversary: name the tier from this module's taxonomy. Mechanism: how does the tool actually achieve the goal — technically, not per the datasheet? Iterate: attack the claim — what does it miss, what are its blind spots, what does it assume? Then compare against not buying it: can existing controls, configured better, achieve the goal? Half of security purchases fail this loop, which is exactly why running it saves money. Bring the one-page loop analysis to every procurement discussion; it ends vague enthusiasm with specific questions.

notes.title: Adversary capability levels: match the defense to the threat
notes.body:
Not all adversaries are equal, and defenses designed for the wrong level either waste money or fail silently. Think in four rough tiers. Opportunistic: automated scanners, mass phishing, commodity malware — low skill, high volume, defeated by hygiene (patching, defaults changed, basic filtering). Targeted criminal: ransomware affiliates, business-email-compromise crews — moderate skill, motivated by money, defeated by layered controls and tested backups. Determined professional: advanced persistent threats, well-funded — high skill, patient, defeated only by architecture: least privilege, segmentation, monitoring, and assume-breach design. Insider: the trusted employee or contractor — the hardest, because they start inside your trust boundary; defeated by separation of duties, auditing, and least privilege.

Worked example: the same asset — the law firm's document archive — against three adversaries. Opportunistic: a botnet scanning for exposed file shares. Defense: the share is not internet-facing, firewall denies inbound, done — cheap and sufficient. Targeted criminal: a ransomware affiliate phishes a paralegal. Defense: deny-by-default on endpoints so the payload never executes, Ringfencing so a hijacked app cannot reach the share, offline backups tested monthly — because this adversary will try again. Insider: a departing employee copying client files to a personal drive. Defense: Storage Control blocking unapproved removable media, access logging on the archive, and a termination checklist that revokes access the same day. Notice how each tier demands a different investment — and how defending against the insider with only the opportunistic controls would fail completely.

Common mistakes: designing for the movie-plot adversary while ignoring the likely one — most organizations are breached by the targeted criminal, not the nation-state, and money spent on exotic defenses while backups go untested is money wasted. The reverse error: assuming 'we are too small to be targeted' — ransomware affiliates automate targeting and do not care about your size. And forgetting the insider entirely: every trust boundary you draw should prompt the question 'what if someone on the trusted side goes bad?' Least privilege is the answer, and it is covered in depth in module 15.

Stay current without drowning: build a threat-intel diet with three tiers. Daily skim: one reputable security news source, headlines only, five minutes — watching for your industry and your stack. Weekly read: one deep analysis of a campaign or technique relevant to your adversary tiers — this is where you learn the ransomware affiliate's current tooling. Quarterly review: revisit your adversary list itself — has the business changed, have you become interesting to a new tier? Unsubscribe from everything else; intel you do not read is noise that trains you to ignore intel. And always translate: every item should end with 'so we should...' — a control to check, a detection to verify, or a conscious 'not our tier.'

notes.title: Attack surface: counting the doors
notes.body:
The attack surface is the set of all points where an adversary can interact with your system — and you cannot defend what you have not counted. Enumerating it is mechanical: list every network service listening on every interface, every user account and what it can reach, every application users can launch, every file share and its permissions, every USB port and what may connect, every web form and API endpoint, every vendor remote-access path. Then for each entry, ask: does this need to exist, does it need to be reachable from where it is reachable, and is it at its least privilege? The surface always turns out larger than expected — that discovery is the value of the exercise.

Worked example: a small business file server. Enumeration: SMB file sharing on the LAN (needed), RDP open to the internet for the vendor (questionable), an old FTP service nobody remembers installing (remove), the backup agent's management port (needed, but reachable from anywhere — restrict to the backup server), local admin accounts on five workstations with the same password (rotate to unique), a file share called 'Everyone-Temp' with write access for all staff (audit and restrict), USB ports unrestricted on the server itself (block via policy), the router's remote admin enabled (disable). Count before: roughly a dozen entry points, several unjustified. Count after the exercise: six, each justified and restricted. The attack surface shrank by half in an afternoon of enumeration — no new tools purchased, just counting and questioning.

Common mistakes: counting only the network — the USB port and the disgruntled employee's legitimate access are surface too. Another is the one-time inventory: new services appear with every software install, so surface enumeration belongs in the change process. And the 'it is internal so it is safe' fallacy — internal services are reachable by every compromised workstation and every insider; the trust boundary between LAN and server still needs justification. Count everything, justify everything, re-count on change.

Enumerate the shadow-IT surface: the SaaS apps nobody approved, the personal cloud storage syncing company data, the departmental database running on someone's desktop. Find them by asking the network (DNS logs reveal the SaaS domains), the endpoints (installed-software inventory), and finance (the credit-card subscriptions). Each discovery gets the same three questions: must it exist, must it be reachable, is it least-privilege? Most shadow IT exists for a legitimate reason the official process failed to serve — so the fix is often approving and governing it, not just banning it. The surface you do not know about is the surface you cannot defend; the enumeration is uncomfortable precisely because it works.

notes.title: Trust boundaries and where they break
notes.body:
A trust boundary is a line across which the level of trust changes: internet to DMZ, DMZ to LAN, user workstation to server, application to database, employee to contractor. Security architecture is largely the art of placing these lines well and guarding the crossings. Data crossing a boundary gets validated; code crossing a boundary gets verified; users crossing a boundary get authenticated — and the strength of each check matches the trust drop across the line. Boundaries break in predictable ways: the crossing with no check (the internal API that trusts all callers), the boundary that moved without anyone noticing (the 'temporary' firewall rule from 2019), and the confused boundary (treating the corporate LAN as trusted when every workstation is a potential beachhead).

Worked example: the intern's laptop on the LAN. The old mental model draws the trust boundary at the office firewall: inside is trusted, outside is not. The intern clicks a phishing link; the laptop is now adversary-controlled — and it sits inside the 'trusted' zone with line-of-sight to the file server, the printer with its ancient firmware, and the database's management port. The boundary was drawn in the wrong place: the real boundary is between each device and the network, not between the office and the internet. The fix is the zero-trust redrawing: every device authenticates, every connection is authorized, the file server does not trust the laptop because of its IP address. This is the architectural idea behind endpoint-level controls: when the network boundary cannot be trusted, each endpoint becomes its own boundary.

Common mistakes: drawing boundaries around networks instead of around trust relationships — IP addresses are locations, not identities. Another is the unguarded crossing: the vendor VPN that lands directly on the LAN with no jump host, the API with no authentication 'because it is internal.' And boundary erosion: exceptions accumulate — 'just open this port temporarily' — until the boundary is decorative. Every crossing needs a named guard (authentication, validation, policy), and every temporary exception needs the expiry discipline from module 11.

Treat every internal API as a trust-boundary crossing, because it is one. The mobile app calling the backend, the web frontend calling the microservice, the scheduled job calling the database — each crosses from one trust zone to another, and each needs its guard: authentication (who is calling), authorization (may they do this), and validation (is the input sane). The 'it is internal' exemption is how breaches propagate: the compromised web tier calls the internal API with no authentication, and the attacker rides it straight to the data. When you review an architecture, draw every API call as a boundary crossing and demand its guard by name. Unguarded internal APIs are the trust-boundary failure you will find most often.

notes.title: Worked example: threat-model a small business file server
notes.body:
Let us run the full loop on a concrete target: a Windows file server at a 30-person accounting firm, holding client tax records. Step one, assets: the client records themselves (confidentiality, integrity — altered tax data is a disaster), the server's availability during tax season (a week of downtime in April is existential), and the firm's reputation (a breach notice to clients ends relationships). Rank them: confidentiality and integrity of records first, April availability second, reputation as the consequence of losing the first two.

Step two, adversaries: opportunistic scanners (internet-facing RDP — check if it is), a ransomware affiliate via phishing (the realistic headline threat), a disgruntled employee (tax season layoffs happen), and the curious insider (an employee browsing client files they have no business seeing). Explicitly set aside: nation-state targeting — no evidence this firm is that interesting; note the assumption so it can be revisited.

Step three, attack surface: SMB shares on the LAN, RDP (is it internet-facing?), the backup software's agent, USB ports on the server, the admin's workstation used for server management, the cloud backup sync account, and every workstation that maps the share. Step four, trust boundaries: internet/LAN at the firewall, workstation/server at the share permissions, employee/employee at the folder ACLs, admin/standard-user at the management tools.

Step five, mitigations mapped to the model: RDP off the internet onto a VPN with MFA (kills the scanner); deny-by-default on workstations plus tested offline backups (blunts the ransomware affiliate); Storage Control on the server's USB plus share-permission audit (contains the disgruntled employee); folder ACLs by engagement team plus access logging (catches the curious insider). Every mitigation names its adversary — nothing is 'best practice' floating unattached. Step six, residual risks written honestly: a zero-day in the backup agent, a determined insider with legitimate access, the admin's workstation as a single point of compromise. The model does not eliminate risk; it makes the remaining risk explicit and owned. That document — two pages — is worth more than any tool purchase made without it.

Run the file-server model as a tabletop drill with the team: one person plays each adversary tier and narrates their attack path step by step while the defenders check whether the mitigations actually stop it. The ransomware affiliate's player will find the gaps the document missed — 'your backups are on the same network segment, so I encrypt those too.' The insider's player will find the permission the audit overlooked. The drill takes ninety minutes and produces more improvements than a month of document reviews, because adversarial thinking is a skill exercised, not a document written. Record the findings, update the model, and schedule the next drill after the next architecture change. The model lives in the drill, not on the page.

notes.title: Threat-modeling an endpoint fleet: what changes at scale
notes.body:
Threat-modeling one server is a whiteboard exercise; threat-modeling 200 endpoints is an operations program — and the differences matter. First, heterogeneity: the fleet is not one machine but dozens of software combinations, user behaviors, and risk profiles. Your asset inventory becomes a classification (executives with sensitive data, finance with money-movement access, warehouse kiosks with almost nothing) rather than a list. Second, the adversary shifts: at fleet scale you are defending against the phishing campaign that hits everyone at once, the wormable vulnerability, the malicious insider with broad access — correlated attacks, not single-machine incidents. Third, the attack surface is dominated by the user: every workstation is a boundary crossing, every USB port a door, every installed application a potential weapon.

Worked example: applying the loop to Meridian's 200 endpoints. Assets by class: finance workstations (money movement), executive laptops (sensitive strategy data, travel exposure), the file server and backups (shared data, availability), warehouse systems (operational continuity). Adversaries: the ransomware affiliate via mass phishing (primary), the opportunistic malware from personal browsing on work machines, the departing employee (quarterly layoffs in logistics), the vendor with remote access. Surface: 200 user behaviors, USB ports, email attachments, the VPN, the vendor's remote tool. Boundaries: device/network (zero-trust: no implicit trust by location), user/data (least-privilege share access), app/system (Ringfencing: allowed apps cannot reach beyond their job).

Mitigations at fleet scale are architectural, not individual: deny-by-default everywhere so mass phishing fails at execution; Ringfencing so a compromised app cannot move laterally; Storage Control so the departing employee cannot walk out with the data; Network Control so the compromised laptop cannot become a beachhead; centralized logging so the correlated attack is visible as one incident, not 200 tickets. The threat model for a fleet is what justifies the platform: each module maps to an adversary and a boundary from the model. When the CFO asks why the project costs what it costs, this mapping — adversary to boundary to control — is the answer. Scale does not change the loop; it changes what the loop outputs: architecture instead of tweaks.

Build the asset-class matrix as the fleet's standing reference: rows are asset classes (finance workstations, executive laptops, servers, kiosks), columns are the model elements (ranked assets, primary adversary tier, key surface entries, trust boundaries, assigned controls). Fill it once, review it quarterly. New systems get classified into the matrix before deployment — 'which row is this?' becomes the intake question for every new project. The matrix turns threat modeling from a per-project effort into organizational muscle memory: the reasoning is done once per class, then applied by reference. When the panel asks how you would secure their fleet, sketching this matrix from memory shows you operate at scale.

notes.title: Common mistakes: threat-model theater
notes.body:
Threat modeling fails in predictable ways, and recognizing the failure modes is part of the skill. Theater mode one: the vague adversary — 'hackers might attack us' produces no design decisions; capabilities and motivations or it did not happen. Theater mode two: the model that justifies the purchase — starting from the tool you already bought and writing a model that conveniently requires it. Run the loop honestly first, then see which tools the mitigations actually call for. Theater mode three: ignoring the insider — every model with only external adversaries has a blind spot exactly where the most damaging attacks come from. Theater mode four: the one-and-done — a model written for last year's architecture, now describing a system that no longer exists.

Worked example of catching theater: a team presents a threat model for a new customer portal. Assets: 'customer data.' Adversaries: 'hackers.' Surface: 'the internet.' Mitigations: 'we bought a WAF.' The review questions that expose it: which customer data — names, payment details, session tokens? Each has different protections. Which hackers — opportunistic scanners or credential-stuffing crews with breach databases? The defenses differ. What is the surface — the login form, the password reset flow, the API, the admin panel? Each needs separate analysis. What about the support staff who can look up any customer — where is the insider? The WAF might be fine, but the model as presented justifies nothing and examines nothing. The fixed version answers each question specifically, and usually discovers that the password-reset flow and the support tooling were the real risks — neither of which the WAF addresses.

The discipline that prevents theater: write the model before choosing tools, name capabilities not costumes, include the insider always, date the document, and re-run the loop when the architecture changes. A two-page honest model beats a fifty-page theater production every time — and in the October interview, walking a panel through a crisp threat model of their endpoint fleet is one of the strongest moves you can make.

Invite attack on your own models: the red-team review. Hand your threat model to a sharp colleague and ask them to break it — find the missing adversary, the unguarded crossing, the mitigation that does not actually mitigate. Reward the findings publicly; the reviewer who finds the hole you missed just saved you from the incident that would have found it. Do this before every major deployment, and rotate reviewers so fresh eyes see it each time. A model that survives a hostile review is worth ten that survived only their author's optimism. This is the iterate step made social — and the fastest way to build a team that thinks adversarially by habit.

cards.front: What four questions does a threat model answer?
cards.back: What are the assets? Who are the adversaries? Where is the attack surface? Where are the trust boundaries?

cards.front: What are the four steps of first-principles security reasoning?
cards.back: State the goal precisely, define the adversary explicitly, design the mechanism, iterate by attacking your own design.

cards.front: Name the four adversary tiers.
cards.back: Opportunistic (scanners, mass phishing), targeted criminal (ransomware affiliates), determined professional (APT), insider (trusted employee/contractor).

cards.front: Why must adversary capabilities be explicit?
cards.back: Every unstated assumption is a future vulnerability — defenses designed against a vague 'attacker' fail against slightly stronger ones.

cards.front: How do you enumerate an attack surface?
cards.back: List every listening service, account, launchable app, share, USB port, web form, API, and vendor path — then ask of each: must it exist, must it be reachable from there, is it least-privilege?

cards.front: What is a trust boundary?
cards.back: A line across which trust changes (internet/DMZ, user/server, app/database) — crossings get validated, verified, or authenticated according to the trust drop.

cards.front: Why is 'the LAN is trusted' a dangerous boundary?
cards.back: IP addresses are locations, not identities — one phished laptop puts the adversary inside the 'trusted' zone with line-of-sight to everything.

cards.front: In the file-server worked example, what were the ranked assets?
cards.back: 1) Confidentiality and integrity of client tax records. 2) Availability during tax season. 3) Reputation as the consequence of losing the first two.

cards.front: What changes when threat-modeling a 200-endpoint fleet vs one server?
cards.back: Assets become classes, adversaries become correlated (campaigns, worms), the user dominates the surface — so mitigations become architectural (deny-by-default, ringfencing, segmentation) not individual.

cards.front: What is 'threat-model theater'?
cards.back: Vague adversaries, models that justify pre-bought tools, ignored insiders, and one-and-done documents — modeling that examines nothing and justifies nothing.

cards.front: Why date a threat model?
cards.back: Models decay as architectures change; the date forces revisits and exposes one-and-done theater.

cards.front: What is the correct order: threat model first or tool purchase first?
cards.back: Model first, then see which tools the mitigations actually call for — tools serve mechanisms, mechanisms serve goals.

quiz.q: A team says their asset is 'everything' and their adversary is 'hackers.' What is the modeling failure?
choices: There is no failure; this covers all cases.
Both are too vague to design against — 'everything' cannot be prioritized and 'hackers' has no capabilities or motivations to match defenses to.
They should add more adversaries.
They need a longer asset list.
quiz.explain: Vague assets cannot be ranked and vague adversaries produce no design decisions. The fix is specificity: which data, which capabilities, which motivations — that is what turns a model into mitigations.

quiz.q: Your mechanism is antivirus against an adversary using brand-new custom malware. The first-principles loop says:
choices: Buy a second antivirus.
Iterate: attack your own design — signature-based detection fails against unknown malware, so the mechanism does not achieve the goal against this adversary. Redesign.
Accept the risk silently.
Blame the adversary for being unfair.
quiz.explain: The iterate step exists to kill mechanisms that do not match the adversary. Antivirus vs. novel malware is the textbook mismatch — the loop forces you to confront it on paper instead of in an incident.

quiz.q: Which adversary tier is defeated primarily by tested offline backups?
choices: The curious insider browsing files.
The targeted criminal running ransomware — backups blunt the extortion when deny-by-default and ringfencing are bypassed or fail.
Opportunistic scanners.
The nation-state.
quiz.explain: Ransomware's leverage is denying you your data; tested offline backups remove that leverage. Each tier has a different decisive defense — matching the defense to the tier is the skill.

quiz.q: During surface enumeration you find an old FTP service nobody remembers installing. What is the correct action?
choices: Leave it; it might be needed.
Investigate, and remove it if unjustified — unjustified services are pure attack surface with zero business value.
Add it to the threat model as an asset.
Open it to the internet for easier access.
quiz.explain: Enumeration's value is finding exactly this: entry points with no owner and no purpose. Every unjustified service removed shrinks the surface for free — no tool purchase required.

quiz.q: The intern's phished laptop sits on the LAN with line-of-sight to the file server. What boundary error does this expose?
choices: The firewall is misconfigured.
Drawing the trust boundary at the office perimeter instead of per-device — the laptop was 'inside' the trusted zone, so the server trusted it by location.
The intern should not have a laptop.
Phishing is unstoppable.
quiz.explain: Location is not identity. The zero-trust redrawing puts the boundary between each device and the network: every device authenticates, every connection is authorized, and the server never trusts by IP address.

quiz.q: In the file-server worked example, why was the nation-state adversary explicitly set aside?
choices: Nation-states do not attack small firms.
There was no evidence this firm is that interesting — and the assumption was written down so it can be revisited, which is honest modeling.
The model only allows three adversaries.
It was forgotten.
quiz.explain: Explicitly scoping out an adversary with a written, revisitable assumption is disciplined — it focuses investment on the realistic threats (ransomware affiliate, insider) instead of spreading it thin over movie plots.

quiz.q: At fleet scale, why do mitigations become architectural rather than individual?
choices: Architecture sounds more impressive.
Because adversaries correlate — one phishing campaign hits everyone at once — so per-machine tweaks cannot keep up; you need fleet-wide controls like deny-by-default and segmentation.
Individual fixes are forbidden at scale.
Auditors prefer architecture.
quiz.explain: Correlated attacks defeat uncorrelated defenses. The fleet threat model is what justifies platform-level controls: each module maps to an adversary and a boundary from the model.

quiz.q: A threat model for a customer portal lists mitigations as 'we bought a WAF.' What is wrong?
choices: Nothing — a WAF is a good mitigation.
The model justifies the pre-bought tool instead of examining the actual risks — the password-reset flow and support tooling, which the WAF does not address, were never analyzed.
WAFs do not work.
The model is too short.
quiz.explain: Tool-first modeling is theater: it examines nothing and justifies the purchase. Honest modeling would analyze each surface element separately and usually finds the real risks where the bought tool does not reach.

quiz.q: Which residual risk statement shows honest modeling?
choices: 'Our controls eliminate all risk.'
'Remaining risks: a zero-day in the backup agent, a determined insider with legitimate access, the admin workstation as a single compromise point — each explicitly owned.'
'We follow best practices.'
'Risk is low.'
quiz.explain: Threat models do not eliminate risk; they make the remaining risk explicit and owned. Named residual risks with owners are the mark of a model that was actually reasoned through.

quiz.q: When must a threat model be revisited?
choices: Never — it is a point-in-time artifact.
When the architecture changes: new services, new integrations, new data flows, new trust relationships — the dated document triggers the review.
Only after a breach.
Every decade.
quiz.explain: Models decay as systems change; a model describing last year's architecture is theater. Dating the document and tying reviews to architectural change keeps it alive.

items.prompt: Name the four parts of a threat model.
items.answer: Assets, adversaries, attack surface, trust boundaries.
items.explain: Miss one and security decisions become vibes.

items.prompt: What are the four first-principles steps?
items.answer: Precise goal, explicit adversary, mechanism design, iterate by self-attack.
items.explain: The first design is always wrong somewhere — the loop finds it.

items.prompt: Name the four adversary tiers.
items.answer: Opportunistic, targeted criminal, determined professional, insider.
items.explain: Match the defense to the tier, not the movie plot.

items.prompt: What three questions do you ask of each surface entry?
items.answer: Must it exist? Must it be reachable from there? Is it least-privilege?
items.explain: Enumeration plus interrogation shrinks the surface for free.

items.prompt: What guards a trust-boundary crossing?
items.answer: Validation for data, verification for code, authentication for users — scaled to the trust drop.
items.explain: Every crossing needs a named guard.

items.prompt: Why is 'the LAN is trusted' dangerous?
items.answer: IP addresses are locations, not identities; one compromised device is inside with line-of-sight to everything.
items.explain: Draw boundaries around trust relationships, not networks.

items.prompt: What is threat-model theater?
items.answer: Vague adversaries, tool-justifying models, ignored insiders, one-and-done documents.
items.explain: Theater examines nothing and justifies nothing.

items.prompt: A vendor asks for always-on remote access directly to your LAN. Threat-model the request.
items.answer: Asset: every system reachable from the LAN. Adversary: compromised vendor (or their stolen credentials). Surface: a permanent inbound path. Boundary: vendor/LAN with no guard. Verdict: deny as stated; counter with time-boxed, MFA'd jump-host access with session logging — or reject.
items.explain: Run the four questions on every access request; the model makes 'no' defensible and the counter-offer concrete.

items.prompt: Your firm is considering disabling USB ports fleet-wide. Which adversary does this primarily address, and what is the residual risk?
items.answer: Primarily the insider (data theft via removable media) and opportunistic malware via USB. Residual: determined insiders will use network exfiltration or phones — pair with Storage Control plus egress awareness, not USB policy alone.
items.explain: Name the adversary the control serves, then name what it does not cover — honest residual risk.

items.prompt: Someone proposes 'we are too small to be targeted by ransomware.' Reframe with the model.
items.answer: Ransomware affiliates automate targeting and do not care about size — the adversary tier is 'targeted criminal,' capability moderate, motivation money. Small firms are targeted precisely because defenses are weaker.
items.explain: Capabilities and motivations, not flattery, set the adversary list.

items.prompt: You discover the 'temporary' firewall rule from 2019 is still open. What modeling failure is this?
items.answer: Boundary erosion — an unguarded crossing with no expiry. Fix: close or re-justify it, and add expiry discipline so temporary exceptions cannot become permanent silently.
items.explain: Boundaries decay; the model must be re-run when the architecture drifts.

items.prompt: Threat-model the October 13 interview itself: what is the asset, adversary, surface?
items.answer: Asset: the offer and your credibility. Adversary: a sharp panel probing for bluffing. Surface: every claim on your resume and every answer you give. Mitigation: honest scoping ('here is what I know, here is how I would find out'), crisp models, no invented facts.
items.explain: The loop applies anywhere — even to the interview. Panels respect explicit scoping over confident bluffing.

items.prompt: A colleague's model has no insider adversary. What do you say?
items.answer: 'Every trust boundary needs the question: what if someone on the trusted side goes bad? Add the insider with their actual access, then check separation of duties, auditing, and least privilege.'
items.explain: Missing insiders are the most common blind spot — and the most damaging attacks.

handsOnLab.title: Threat-model your home lab network
handsOnLab.brief: Run the full first-principles loop on a network you control: diagram it, inventory assets, name adversaries with capabilities, enumerate the surface, mark trust boundaries, assign mitigations, and write the residual risks honestly. Two pages that prove you can reason, not just recite.
steps: Draw your home lab or home network: router, every device, the internet connection, any cloud services, remote-access paths. Label every connection.
List your assets and rank them: which data or availability loss would hurt most? Write one sentence per asset saying why it matters.

Name your adversaries in tiers with explicit capabilities: the opportunistic scanner, the targeted criminal (are you interesting?), the insider (housemates? guests?), and anyone you consciously scope out — with the assumption written down.
Enumerate the attack surface mechanically: listening services per device, admin interfaces, Wi-Fi networks, USB ports, cloud consoles, port forwards. Count them.
Mark the trust boundaries on your diagram: internet/LAN, guest/main network, device/device, user/admin. For each crossing, name the guard or mark it unguarded.
For each adversary, write the attack path in one paragraph: how they get from outside to the asset, step by step, naming the surface entries and boundary crossings they use.
Assign mitigations mapped to adversary and boundary: each mitigation names what it stops. Be specific — 'change the router admin password' not 'harden the router.'
Write the residual risks honestly: what remains after your mitigations, who owns each risk, and what would trigger revisiting it.
Date the document and add the review trigger: 'revisit when I add a device, open a port, or start hosting a service.'
Read it as an attacker: find the weakest path you left and either mitigate it or justify accepting it in writing.
Condense the whole model to a 3-minute spoken walkthrough — practice delivering it aloud, as you would to the October 13 panel.
Save as threat-model.md with the diagram (ASCII is fine), the ranked assets, adversaries, surface count, boundaries, mitigations, and residual risks.
handsOnLab.deliverable: threat-model.md with a labeled network diagram, ranked assets, tiered adversaries with capabilities, enumerated attack surface, marked trust boundaries, mapped mitigations, honest residual risks, and the date plus review trigger.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every asset has at least one adversary and one mitigation; every mitigation names its adversary; residual risks are explicit and owned; you can deliver the 3-minute walkthrough without notes.
