title: MIT 6.858: Control Hijacking & Buffer Overflows
summary: How attackers hijack a program's control flow — stack layout, return addresses, buffer overflows — taught conceptually with worked walkthroughs, plus the defenses that blunt them: canaries, DEP/NX, ASLR. You will finish understanding why allowlisting changes the exploitation game even when a bug exists. Independent study in our own words; no affiliation claimed.
objectives: Explain how programs use the stack: frames, local variables, and return addresses.
Describe what a buffer overflow is and how overlong input corrupts adjacent memory.
Walk through how overwriting a return address hijacks control flow, conceptually.
Explain stack canaries: how the check works and what it catches.
Explain DEP/NX and ASLR: what each denies the attacker and why they compose.
Argue why allowlisting and Ringfencing blunt exploitation even when a memory bug exists.

notes.title: How programs use the stack: frames and return addresses
notes.body:
To understand control hijacking, you first need the machine's-eye view of a function call. When a program calls a function, it needs somewhere to put the function's local variables, and it needs to remember where to resume when the function returns. That somewhere is the stack: a region of memory organized as last-in-first-out, growing downward in most systems. Each function call gets a stack frame — a contiguous chunk holding the function's local variables, bookkeeping data, and crucially the return address: the instruction address in the caller where execution should continue after the function finishes. Call a function, push a frame; return from it, pop the frame and jump to the return address.

Worked example — trace it by hand. The program is executing main at instruction address 0x1000 and calls process_input at 0x2000. The call instruction pushes the return address (0x1004, the next instruction in main) onto the stack, then jumps to 0x2000. process_input's frame is created: space for its local buffer (say 64 bytes), then the saved bookkeeping, then the return address 0x1004 sitting just above the frame. The function runs, fills its buffer, finishes, and executes return: the processor pops 0x1004 off the stack and resumes main right where it left off. This happens millions of times per second in every program you run. The security-relevant insight: the return address — the thing that decides where the program goes next — lives in writable memory, right next to the program's own data buffers. That adjacency is the entire story of this module.

Common misconceptions: that the stack is some abstract concept — it is concrete memory with addresses you can inspect in a debugger. Another is that 'the program knows where to return' as if by magic — no, it reads the return address from the stack, trusting that nothing modified it. That trust is exactly what the attacker violates. Keep this picture — buffer, then bookkeeping, then return address, all adjacent in writable memory — fixed in your mind; everything else in the module is a consequence of it.

See it in a debugger to make it concrete: break at a function's entry and inspect the frame — the saved registers, the locals' addresses, and the return address sitting at a specific stack location. Dump the raw stack words and watch the return address as just another value among the data. This is not exploit development; it is literacy — the operator who has seen the return address as a memory value understands viscerally why an overflow reaches it. Spend thirty minutes with a debugger and a toy program; the abstract diagram becomes a physical place, and every defense in this module becomes obviously necessary rather than theoretically nice.

notes.title: What a buffer overflow is
notes.body:
A buffer is a fixed-size region of memory set aside to hold data — a 64-byte character array for a username, for instance. An overflow happens when the program writes more data into the buffer than it can hold, and the excess spills into whatever memory sits adjacent. In a safe language this cannot happen; in C and C++, the workhorse languages of operating systems and performance-critical software, the language does not check — it trusts the programmer to get the sizes right, and programmers get them wrong constantly. The overflow itself is just a bug; whether it becomes a security catastrophe depends on what the spilled bytes overwrite.

Worked example — conceptually, with illustrative pseudocode. A function declares a 64-byte local buffer and copies user input into it with an unchecked copy operation: copy(buffer, user_input) with no length check. The user supplies 80 bytes. Bytes 0-63 fill the buffer as intended. Bytes 64-79 keep writing — into the adjacent stack memory: first the saved bookkeeping, then the return address. The program did not intend this; it just kept copying because nobody told it to stop. With 80 bytes of the letter 'A', the program likely crashes when it tries to return to address 0x41414141 (the hex for 'AAAA') — a crash is a denial of service, annoying but not yet a hijack. The critical realization: the attacker controls those overflowing bytes. They are not random; they are chosen. And what they choose to overwrite — and with what values — is the difference between a crash and a takeover.

Common mistakes: thinking overflows only come from 'hackers typing long input' — they come from any untrusted data: network packets, file contents, environment variables, database fields. Another is assuming modern software is immune — memory-unsafe languages still underpin operating systems, browsers, and embedded devices, and new overflow bugs are found regularly. And the dangerous comfort: 'it just crashes.' A crash proves the attacker can corrupt memory; corruption the attacker controls is one step from control of execution. Treat every overflow-class bug as potentially exploitable until proven otherwise.

Meet the overflow's cousin: the integer overflow, where arithmetic wraps around instead of spilling. A program computes a buffer size from user input; with a huge input the multiplication wraps to a small number, the program allocates the small buffer, then copies the full amount into it — an overflow born from arithmetic, not from a long string. The lesson generalizes: memory unsafety is a family — overflows, integer wraps, use-after-free, format-string bugs — all violating the programmer's mental model of memory. Defenses must therefore be systemic (canaries, DEP, ASLR, safe languages, sandboxing) rather than bug-specific. When you hear of a new memory-bug class, ask which defense layer catches it — the answer tells you whether your architecture is deep or merely decorated.

notes.title: From overflow to control hijack
notes.body:
Here is the conceptual leap: if the attacker controls the overflowing bytes, and the overflow reaches the return address, then the attacker controls where the function returns to. Instead of resuming the caller, the processor jumps to an address of the attacker's choosing. That is control hijacking — the attacker's first and most powerful primitive. What they do with it varies: classically, they point the return address at their own injected code (the overflowed input itself contains machine instructions, placed in a writable-and-executable memory region), so the function 'returns' into the attacker's code. The program is now executing attacker instructions with the program's privileges.

Worked example — the narrative, step by step. The vulnerable function has its 64-byte buffer; the attacker sends 76 bytes. Bytes 0-63: filler. Bytes 64-71: more filler overwriting bookkeeping. Bytes 72-75: the new return address — not 0x41414141 this time, but the address of the attacker's choosing. Where does it point? In the classic version, it points back into the buffer itself, where bytes 0-63 contain not filler but machine code the attacker wrote — code that, say, launches a command shell. The function returns; the processor jumps to the attacker's code; a shell opens with the privileges of the vulnerable program. If that program was a network service running as a privileged user, the attacker now has a privileged shell. Three ingredients made it work: a writable buffer the attacker fills, an adjacent return address they overwrite, and a memory region that is both writable and executable so their injected code can run. Defenses target each ingredient — which is why the next three notes exist.

Common misconceptions: that hijacking requires the attacker to 'break encryption' or 'guess passwords' — no, it subverts the program's own machinery using the program's own privileges. Another is that this is historical: the specific classic shape is largely defeated on modern systems, but the principle — corrupt control data, redirect execution — recurs in every generation of exploitation, including return-oriented programming, which chains together snippets of the program's own code instead of injecting new code. Understand the principle deeply; the variants are commentary.

Understand return-oriented programming conceptually, because it is the adaptation that defines modern exploitation. DEP killed injected code, so attackers stopped injecting: instead they overwrite the return address to point at tiny snippets of the program's own code — each ending in a return instruction — chaining them so each snippet's return lands on the next. Like words forming a sentence, the snippets compose attacker behavior from the program's own vocabulary. The defense implications: DEP alone is insufficient, ASLR matters enormously (the attacker must know where the snippets live), and verifying that returns go to legitimate callers becomes the next frontier. Defenses do not end exploitation; they escalate it, and each escalation demands the next layer.

notes.title: Defense: stack canaries
notes.body:
If the problem is silent corruption of the return address, one defense is to make the corruption detectable before the return happens. A stack canary is a secret random value placed on the stack between the local buffers and the return address — named for the canary in the coal mine, which died to warn miners of gas. The function prologue (its setup code) writes the canary; the function epilogue (its teardown code) checks that the canary still holds its original value before returning. A normal execution leaves the canary untouched. An overflow that reaches toward the return address must overwrite the canary first — and when the epilogue finds the canary changed, it aborts the program instead of returning to the attacker's address.

Worked example — watch it work. Without a canary: the 76-byte overflow silently rewrites the return address, the function returns into attacker code. With a canary: the stack layout is now buffer, then canary (a random 4- or 8-byte value the attacker cannot predict), then bookkeeping, then return address. The attacker's 76 bytes overwrite the canary with filler before reaching the return address. At function exit, the epilogue compares the canary to its saved copy — mismatch. The program terminates immediately with a stack-smashing error. The attacker's carefully chosen return address never gets used, because the program refused to return at all. The defense does not fix the bug — the overflow still happened — but it converts silent hijack into a loud crash, which is a vastly better outcome.

Limits, honestly stated: canaries only protect the return address, and only if the overflow actually passes through the canary — an overflow that precisely targets other control data, or an attacker who can learn the canary's value (via a separate memory-disclosure bug), can bypass it. Some overflows corrupt adjacent local variables without ever touching the canary. So canaries are one layer: they raise the bar from 'trivially exploitable' to 'needs an additional information leak,' which is real progress but not a complete fix. Defense in depth means stacking this with the next two defenses, each attacking a different ingredient of the exploit.

Notice the canary's clever detail: canary values typically include null bytes, and that is not an accident. Many overflow vectors are string operations that stop at null bytes — so a canary containing nulls is harder to overwrite precisely without terminating the copy early, and harder to leak via string disclosure. This is defense design at its finest: the mechanism exploits the attacker's own tools' limitations. The broader lesson: good defenses are not just walls but traps shaped by attacker constraints. When you evaluate any mitigation, ask what attacker capability it specifically taxes — the canary taxes precise memory writes, DEP taxes code injection, ASLR taxes address knowledge. Each tax compounds; the attacker's budget is finite.

notes.title: Defense: DEP/NX and ASLR
notes.body:
Recall the hijack's three ingredients: attacker-controlled bytes in memory, a corrupted return address, and a place to put executable code. Canaries guard the second. DEP — Data Execution Prevention, also called NX for 'no-execute' — kills the third: it marks memory regions as either writable or executable, never both. The stack, where the attacker's input lives, is marked non-executable. Now even if the attacker overwrites the return address to point at their injected code, the processor refuses to execute it — the jump lands in non-executable memory and the program faults. The classic 'return into my buffer' attack dies at this step.

Worked example — reason through the composition. Attack attempt one: inject code into the buffer, overwrite the return address to point at it. DEP stops it: the buffer is not executable. Attack attempt two (the adaptation): do not inject code at all — instead, overwrite the return address to point at code that already exists in the program, like the function that launches a shell, which lives in an executable region. DEP cannot stop this; the target code is legitimately executable. This is where ASLR — Address Space Layout Randomization — enters: it randomizes where the stack, heap, libraries, and program code load in memory each time the program runs. The attacker no longer knows the address of the shell-launching function — it is somewhere different on every run. Their overwritten return address points at a guessed location that is almost certainly wrong, and the program crashes instead of yielding a shell.

Limits, honestly stated: ASLR's protection dies if the attacker learns the layout — a single memory-disclosure bug that leaks one address can defeat the randomization, and on 32-bit systems the address space is small enough to brute-force by crashing and retrying. DEP's protection dies against return-oriented programming, which never needs injected code. Neither fixes the underlying bug. But stacked — canary plus DEP plus ASLR — the attacker needs an overflow plus a memory disclosure plus a code-reuse strategy, all without crashing the target first. Each layer multiplies the attacker's work. This compounding is the entire philosophy of defense in depth, and it is why modern exploitation is a discipline of chaining weaknesses rather than finding one magic bug.

Grasp the entropy intuition: on 64-bit systems the address space is astronomically larger than on 32-bit, so ASLR has vastly more room to randomize — guessing a randomized address goes from feasible-with-patience to effectively impossible. This is why the 64-bit transition was a bigger security upgrade than most realize: it did not just add memory, it multiplied attacker uncertainty. The lesson for operators: architecture choices — 64-bit everywhere, strong ASLR defaults verified with your own checks from the lab — are security decisions, not just performance ones. When you standardize the fleet, standardize the strong defaults. Entropy is a resource, and you want the maximum your platform offers.

notes.title: Why allowlisting changes the exploitation game
notes.body:
Now connect this course's two halves. Memory-corruption defenses make exploitation harder; allowlisting changes what exploitation can achieve. Follow the attacker's plan against a hardened endpoint: suppose they find a buffer overflow in an allowed application and hijack its control flow despite canaries, DEP, and ASLR — a serious, skilled achievement. What next? The classic payoff is executing something: dropping a payload binary and running it, or launching a script interpreter to download stage two. But the endpoint runs deny-by-default application control. The payload binary is not on the allowlist — denied at execution. The script interpreter launch is not the application's permitted behavior — Ringfencing denies it. The attacker's hijacked process can thrash inside its own sandbox, but every path to useful action crosses a policy boundary that says no.

Worked example — the kill chain, stopped late but stopped. A user opens a malicious document; the document exploits an overflow in the document viewer and hijacks control flow. On an unprotected machine, the next steps are: launch PowerShell, download the ransomware, execute it, encrypt the file shares. On the allowlisted machine: the hijacked viewer tries to launch PowerShell — Ringfencing denies it, because the viewer has no legitimate need to spawn script interpreters. It tries to write an executable to disk — denied, the viewer may only write document files. It tries to reach an external server — denied, the viewer has no network permission. Detect logs each denied attempt, and the security team gets indicators of compromise from a failed attack rather than a ransom note from a successful one. The memory bug still existed. The exploitation still technically succeeded at the control-flow level. And it achieved nothing, because the endpoint's architecture assumed compromise and contained it.

The operator's takeaway: you will never patch every memory bug — they live in code you did not write and cannot rewrite. What you can do is architect the endpoint so that a successful hijack is a dead end: the exploited process cannot execute new code, cannot reach the network, cannot touch what it should not. That is the deep reason deny-by-default and Ringfencing matter: they are exploitation mitigations at the architectural layer, complementing the compiler and OS mitigations at the code layer. Defense in depth, from the stack canary all the way up to the application policy.

Value the detection bonus: every denied exploit attempt is a free indicator of compromise. The hijacked viewer denied at the script-interpreter launch tells you which machine, which document, which technique — intelligence you would never get from a silent successful compromise. Feed these denies into the detection workflow: the single attempt gets investigated via the incident-response path, the pattern across machines triggers the campaign response. This inverts the usual economics: the exploitation attempt becomes your sensor. Brief the team accordingly — 'blocked' does not mean 'ignore'; it means an adversary just showed their hand.

notes.title: Common misconceptions and the road ahead
notes.body:
Close with the misconceptions that trap even experienced techs. 'Modern systems are immune to buffer overflows' — they are resistant, not immune; the defenses raise the bar, and skilled attackers chain a disclosure bug with a corruption bug to clear it. Resistance is not immunity, and the history of exploitation is attackers adapting to each new defense: canaries led to information leaks, DEP led to code reuse, ASLR led to disclosure-assisted bypasses. 'Only C programs are affected' — mostly true in the strict sense, but memory-unsafety also lives in unsafe blocks of otherwise safe languages, in firmware, in just-in-time compilers, and anywhere performance trumped safety. 'Crashes are just bugs' — a crash from memory corruption is evidence of attacker-controlled memory writes until proven otherwise; triage it as potentially exploitable.

Worked example — the triage habit. A server process crashes with a memory error twice in a week. The lazy response: restart it, note 'flaky,' move on. The operator response: capture the crash, check whether the input that triggered it was attacker-influenced (network data? file upload?), determine whether the corruption is bounded or potentially control-relevant, patch or isolate, and watch for probing — repeated crashes with varying inputs smell like someone developing an exploit. You may never prove it was an attack; you do not need to. The habit is treating corruption as hostile until the evidence says otherwise, because the cost of the wrong assumption is total compromise.

Where this leads: the next two modules build on this foundation. Privilege separation (module 15) asks: if a network-facing program is likely to contain a memory bug, how do we architect it so the bug yields minimal privilege? Sandboxing (module 16) asks: how do we confine what even a hijacked process can do? Each is the same philosophy as this module's final note — assume the bug, contain the blast radius — applied at the software-design and OS layers. The through-line of the entire 6.858 arc: perfect code is impossible, so architecture must assume imperfection.

Follow the supply chain: your software's memory bugs are often your dependencies' memory bugs. The document library, the image codec, the network stack — written in memory-unsafe languages, maintained by someone else, updated on their schedule. Your threat model must therefore include the dependency's patch cadence: a critical overflow in a library you embed is your vulnerability until you ship their fix. Maintain a software bill of materials for critical systems, subscribe to the dependencies' security advisories, and test their updates in your canary ring like any other change. The modern exploit often enters through the library you forgot you shipped — supply-chain hygiene is memory-safety hygiene.

cards.front: What three things live in a stack frame?
cards.back: Local variables, bookkeeping data, and the return address — the instruction address where execution resumes after the function returns.

cards.front: Why is the return address's location security-relevant?
cards.back: It lives in writable memory adjacent to the program's data buffers — so a buffer overflow can reach and rewrite it.

cards.front: What is a buffer overflow, in one sentence?
cards.back: Writing more data into a fixed-size memory region than it can hold, spilling into adjacent memory — unchecked in C/C++.

cards.front: What turns a crashing overflow into a hijack?
cards.back: The attacker choosing the overflowing bytes to overwrite the return address with an address they select — controlling where the function 'returns' to.

cards.front: What are the three ingredients of the classic hijack?
cards.back: Attacker-controlled bytes in memory, a corrupted return address, and a writable-and-executable region to run injected code.

cards.front: How does a stack canary work?
cards.back: A secret random value sits between buffers and the return address; the function epilogue verifies it before returning — a mismatch aborts the program instead of jumping to the attacker's address.

cards.front: What does a canary NOT protect against?
cards.back: Overflows that avoid the canary, attackers who learn its value via a memory disclosure, and corruption of non-control data — it guards the return address only.

cards.front: What does DEP/NX deny the attacker?
cards.back: Executable memory that is also writable — injected code on the stack cannot run because the stack is marked non-executable.

cards.front: What does ASLR deny the attacker?
cards.back: Knowledge of where code lives — stack, heap, libraries, and program code load at randomized addresses each run, so guessed return targets are almost certainly wrong.

cards.front: What defeats ASLR?
cards.back: A memory-disclosure bug that leaks the layout, or brute-forcing on 32-bit systems with small address spaces.

cards.front: What is return-oriented programming, conceptually?
cards.back: Hijacking without injected code: chaining snippets of the program's own executable code to build attacker behavior — the adaptation that DEP forced.

cards.front: Why does allowlisting blunt exploitation even when a memory bug exists?
cards.back: The hijacked process cannot execute new payloads (deny-by-default) or misuse its permissions (Ringfencing) — every path to useful action crosses a policy boundary that denies it.

quiz.q: A function with a 64-byte buffer receives 80 bytes via an unchecked copy. What happens to bytes 64-79?
choices: They are discarded safely.
They spill into adjacent stack memory — bookkeeping, then the return address — because the language does not check the length.
They trigger an automatic exception.
They are written to the heap.
quiz.explain: In memory-unsafe languages the copy keeps writing past the buffer into whatever is adjacent on the stack. That adjacency — buffer, bookkeeping, return address — is the physical fact the whole module builds on.

quiz.q: Why does overwriting the return address give the attacker control?
choices: It corrupts the program's source code.
The processor reads the return address from the stack to decide where to resume — a chosen value redirects execution to the attacker's target.
It disables the firewall.
It grants administrator privileges directly.
quiz.explain: Return is not magic; it is a jump to an address read from writable memory. Control the bytes, control the destination — that is the entire hijack primitive.

quiz.q: With 80 bytes of 'A' (0x41), the program crashes returning to 0x41414141. What does the crash prove?
choices: The system is now secure.
The attacker can corrupt stack memory with chosen bytes — a crash is evidence of controlled corruption, one step from a hijack, not a benign bug.
The program has no vulnerability.
Only denial of service is possible.
quiz.explain: A crash from 'AAAA' proves the attacker controls the overwritten bytes. Replace the A's with a chosen address and the crash becomes a redirect — triage corruption as potentially exploitable until proven otherwise.

quiz.q: How does the stack canary convert a hijack into a crash?
choices: It encrypts the return address.
The overflow must overwrite the canary before reaching the return address; the epilogue detects the changed canary and aborts instead of returning.
It randomizes the stack layout.
It marks the stack non-executable.
quiz.explain: The canary is a tripwire between the buffer and the return address. Detection happens before the return instruction uses the corrupted address — so the attacker's chosen destination never gets jumped to.

quiz.q: DEP is enabled. The attacker overwrites the return address to point at their injected code in the buffer. What happens?
choices: The injected code runs normally.
The processor faults — the stack is marked non-executable, so the jump into attacker code fails.
The canary is bypassed.
ASLR is disabled.
quiz.explain: DEP kills the third ingredient: writable-and-executable memory. The corrupted return address still gets used, but its target — injected code on a non-executable stack — cannot run.

quiz.q: DEP is enabled and the attacker instead points the return address at an existing shell-launching function. Which defense answers this adaptation, and how?
choices: Canaries — they encrypt function addresses.
ASLR — the function's address is randomized per run, so the attacker's guessed target is almost certainly wrong.
Firewalls.
Antivirus signatures.
quiz.explain: This is the code-reuse adaptation DEP forced. ASLR answers by denying the attacker knowledge of where executable code lives — without a disclosure bug, the guessed address misses and the program crashes.

quiz.q: An attacker chains an overflow with a memory-disclosure bug. What does the disclosure buy them?
choices: Nothing; disclosures are harmless.
The memory layout — defeating ASLR — and possibly the canary value, removing two layers at once.
Faster network access.
A valid user password.
quiz.explain: Modern exploitation is chaining: the disclosure defeats randomization (and maybe the canary), the overflow provides the corruption. Each defense falls to a different bug class — which is why depth requires layers from different families.

quiz.q: A hijacked document viewer on an allowlisted endpoint tries to launch PowerShell, write an executable, and reach an external server. What happens?
choices: All three succeed; the hijack is complete.
Ringfencing denies each — the viewer has no legitimate need for script interpreters, executable writes, or network access — and Detect logs the attempts as indicators of compromise.
The viewer crashes immediately.
The actions succeed but are logged.
quiz.explain: This is the architectural layer of defense: even with control flow hijacked, every path to useful action crosses a policy boundary. The failed attack produces IOCs for the security team instead of a ransom note.

quiz.q: Why is 'it just crashes' a dangerous conclusion about a memory-corruption bug?
choices: Crashes are always exploitable.
A crash proves attacker-influenced memory corruption; whether it is controllable determines exploitability — assuming benignity risks missing a developing exploit.
Crashes damage hardware.
It is not dangerous at all.
quiz.explain: The operator habit: treat corruption as hostile until evidence says otherwise. Repeated crashes with varying inputs especially smell like exploit development — capture, analyze, and watch.

quiz.q: What is the through-line connecting canaries, DEP, ASLR, privilege separation, and Ringfencing?
choices: They all fix bugs.
Assume imperfection and contain the blast radius: each layer makes the attacker's next step harder, so exploitation requires chaining multiple weaknesses instead of one mistake.
They are all compiler features.
They replace patching.
quiz.explain: None of these fix the underlying bug — they compound the attacker's work. The philosophy across all layers, from stack to architecture, is that perfect code is impossible so the system must assume compromise and limit what compromise achieves.

items.prompt: What three things are in a stack frame?
items.answer: Local variables, bookkeeping, return address.
items.explain: The return address in writable memory, adjacent to buffers, is the key fact.

items.prompt: What is a buffer overflow?
items.answer: Writing past a fixed-size region into adjacent memory; unchecked in C/C++.
items.explain: The language trusts the programmer; programmers err.

items.prompt: What makes an overflow a hijack rather than a crash?
items.answer: Attacker-chosen bytes overwriting the return address with a chosen destination.
items.explain: Control the bytes, control where the function returns.

items.prompt: How does a stack canary work?
items.answer: Secret random value between buffer and return address; epilogue verifies it before returning, aborting on mismatch.
items.explain: Converts silent hijack into loud crash.

items.prompt: What does DEP/NX enforce?
items.answer: Memory is writable or executable, never both — injected code on the stack cannot run.
items.explain: Kills the writable-and-executable ingredient.

items.prompt: What does ASLR randomize, and what defeats it?
items.answer: Randomizes load addresses of stack, heap, libraries, code per run; defeated by memory disclosure or 32-bit brute force.
items.explain: Denies the attacker knowledge of where code lives.

items.prompt: Why does allowlisting blunt a successful hijack?
items.answer: The hijacked process cannot execute new payloads or misuse permissions — Ringfencing and deny-by-default block every path to useful action.
items.explain: Architectural containment assumes the bug and limits the blast radius.

items.prompt: A vendor says 'our software is written in a memory-safe language, so buffer overflows are impossible.' What is the careful response?
items.answer: Largely true for the safe code, but unsafe blocks, FFI to C libraries, firmware, and JIT compilers can still harbor memory-unsafety — verify the claim's scope rather than accepting it absolutely.
items.explain: Memory-safety is a property of code regions, not marketing claims; the boundary with unsafe code is where bugs live.

items.prompt: You see repeated crashes of a network service with varying input lengths. What do you suspect and do?
items.answer: Suspect exploit development (probing for control). Capture crashes, check if input is attacker-influenced, isolate or patch the service, watch for patterns — treat as hostile until proven otherwise.
items.explain: Varying inputs plus crashes is the signature of someone mapping the corruption.

items.prompt: An attacker has a memory-disclosure bug but no overflow. What is their next move, defensively speaking?
items.answer: They will hunt for the corruption primitive to pair with it — so your priority is finding and patching overflow-class bugs in the same component before the chain completes.
items.explain: Think in chains: each bug class the attacker holds tells you which complementary bug to hunt.

items.prompt: Explain to a manager why patching alone is not the strategy for memory bugs.
items.answer: 'We cannot rewrite or patch every dependency's memory bugs — some live in code we do not control. So we layer: compiler/OS mitigations raise the exploit cost, and allowlisting plus Ringfencing ensure even a successful hijack cannot execute payloads or move laterally.'
items.explain: Translate depth into business terms: patching is necessary but insufficient; architecture contains what patching misses.

items.prompt: A legacy app cannot be recompiled with canaries or ASLR. How do you protect it?
items.answer: Compensate architecturally: run it with least privilege, Ringfence it tightly (no child processes, no network beyond need), keep it off direct attacker input where possible, and prioritize its replacement.
items.explain: When code-layer defenses are unavailable, the architecture layer carries the weight — containment substitutes for hardening.

items.prompt: Detect logs show a hijacked-viewer pattern: denied PowerShell launch, denied executable write, denied external connection — all from one machine. What is your incident response?
items.answer: The containment worked, but treat as an active attempt: isolate the machine, recover the malicious document, check for lateral movement attempts in Network Control logs, hunt the same indicators fleet-wide.
items.explain: Blocked does not mean over — the attempt proves a live adversary; the IOCs are a gift, use them.

handsOnLab.title: Observe exploit mitigations on your own machine
handsOnLab.brief: Using only safe, standard tools on a Linux machine or VM, observe the real mitigations from this module in action: check ASLR and NX status, compile a small C program with and without stack protectors, and compare the binaries. You touch no exploits — you observe defenses.
steps: Verify you are on a Linux machine or VM you own. Confirm with uname -a and confirm you will only inspect your own files and processes.
Check ASLR status: run cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space and record the value (2 means full randomization).
Observe ASLR in action: run cat /proc/self/maps twice in a row and compare — note how the library load addresses differ between runs.
Check NX on a system binary: run readelf -W -l /bin/ls | grep -i stack and record whether GNU_STACK is marked RWE or RW (RW means non-executable stack).
Write a tiny C program (buffer-test.c) with a function containing a local char buffer — ten lines, no exploit code, just the structure from the notes.
Compile it twice: once normally (gcc -o normal buffer-test.c) and once with protections visibly on (gcc -fstack-protector-strong -o protected buffer-test.c). Both are safe local binaries.
Compare: run objdump -d protected | grep -i stack_chk and objdump -d normal | grep -i stack_chk — record which binary references the canary check and which does not.
Run both binaries with normal input and confirm both work identically — the canary is invisible until an overflow occurs.
Write up what each mitigation would do against the classic hijack: one paragraph each for canary, NX, ASLR, referencing your observed outputs.
Add the allowlisting paragraph: describe what would happen on a deny-by-default endpoint if this program were hijacked — which actions would be denied and why.
Save everything as mitigations-report.md: commands run, outputs observed, and your four paragraphs.
Clean up: delete the test binaries, keeping only the report and the .c source.
handsOnLab.deliverable: mitigations-report.md with the ASLR/NX observations, the with/without protector comparison, and four paragraphs mapping each mitigation (canary, NX, ASLR, allowlisting) to the hijack it defeats.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The report shows differing library addresses between runs (ASLR live), GNU_STACK without execute permission (NX on), the canary reference present only in the protected binary, and a correct allowlisting-containment paragraph.

title: MIT 6.858: Privilege Separation & Capabilities
summary: Least privilege as a software design discipline: splitting programs into privileged and unprivileged parts, capabilities as unforgeable tokens of authority, and the confused-deputy problem. You will map these ideas directly onto Elevation Control and Ringfencing. Independent study in our own words; no affiliation claimed.
objectives: Apply least privilege to software design: give each component only the authority its job requires.
Design a privilege-separated program: split privileged operations from unprivileged parsing and input handling.
Explain capabilities as unforgeable, delegable tokens of authority and contrast them with ambient authority.
Diagnose the confused-deputy problem in a realistic scenario.
Map privilege-separation concepts onto Elevation Control's just-in-time elevation model.
Map capability thinking onto Ringfencing policies that bound what each application may do.

notes.title: Least privilege in software design
notes.body:
Least privilege is simple to state and hard to practice: every component of a system should hold only the authority it needs to do its job, and no more. The reason is blast-radius arithmetic from module 14 — if a component is compromised, the attacker inherits exactly its authority, so excess authority is pre-authorized damage. A program running with full administrative rights because 'it needs to write one config file at startup' hands every one of its bugs the keys to the kingdom. The discipline is asking, for each component: what authority does this actually require, for how long, and what is the smallest grant that satisfies it?

Worked example: a backup tool. As commonly written, it runs as a full administrator 24/7 because it needs to read all files. Least-privilege redesign: the tool's scheduler and network code — the parts exposed to input and most likely to contain bugs — run as an unprivileged user. Only a tiny, audited helper holds the read-all-files authority, and it exposes exactly one operation: 'read this path,' validating the path against the backup set before serving it. A bug in the network parser now yields an unprivileged shell instead of a kingdom. The helper is small enough to audit line by line; the big complex code holds no privilege worth stealing. The total authority in the system did not change — it was redistributed so that the likely-to-be-buggy parts hold none of it.

Common mistakes: confusing least privilege with 'run as a non-admin user' and stopping there — a non-admin program that can still read every user's documents violates least privilege just as badly. Another is all-or-nothing thinking: 'it needs admin sometimes, so run it as admin always.' The 'sometimes' is the design opportunity — grant the authority for the operation, not for the lifetime. And the audit trap: least privilege is not achieved by reviewing permissions once; authority creeps with every feature, so the question belongs in every design review, not just the security review.

Apply least privilege to secrets and credentials, because credentials are authority in concentrated form. Audit where your systems store them: the config file with the database password readable by every developer, the API key baked into the mobile app, the service account whose password has not rotated in years. Each is ambient authority waiting to be stolen — and stolen credentials bypass every privilege-separation design downstream. The fixes are the same principles: scope secrets to the component that needs them, rotate them on a schedule, and prefer short-lived issued credentials over long-lived stored ones. A beautiful privilege-separated architecture with a hardcoded admin password is a vault with the combination written on the door.

notes.title: Privilege separation: splitting programs
notes.body:
Privilege separation is least privilege made structural: divide a program into a small privileged part and a large unprivileged part, with a narrow, well-defined channel between them. The privileged part — sometimes called the monitor — performs only the operations that truly need privilege, and it distrusts everything the unprivileged part sends it, validating each request. The unprivileged part handles all the dangerous work: parsing network input, rendering untrusted files, running complex logic — the code most likely to contain the next buffer overflow. When (not if) the unprivileged part is compromised, the attacker is trapped in a low-privilege compartment and must separately defeat the monitor's validation to gain anything more.

Worked example — design narrative for a network daemon that authenticates users and then serves files. Monolithic design: one process, running privileged, parses network input, checks passwords, and reads files. A single overflow in the packet parser yields full privilege. Separated design: the unprivileged worker handles all network parsing and authentication attempts — it can ask the monitor exactly one question, 'is this username/password valid?', and receives only yes or no. After authentication, the worker asks the monitor to open a specific file; the monitor checks the path against the user's authorized directories, opens it, and passes back a handle the worker can read but not re-target. The monitor is a few hundred lines, auditable, and never parses untrusted input directly. The worker is thousands of lines of risky parsing — and holds no privilege. An overflow in the parser now yields an unprivileged process that can only ask the monitor politely for things the monitor will refuse.

Common mistakes: splitting without distrust — if the privileged part blindly obeys the unprivileged part's requests ('open whatever path it names'), the separation is theater; the monitor must validate every request against policy. Another is a chatty interface: dozens of privileged operations exposed 'for convenience' recreates the monolith's attack surface in the monitor. Keep the privileged interface tiny — a handful of operations, each validated. And the performance excuse: 'separation is too slow' — measure first; the context-switch cost is usually negligible next to network latency, and the security gain is architectural.

Recognize the pattern in the wild: modern browsers separate into a privileged browser process and unprivileged renderer processes, one per tab — the renderer parses the hostile web with no privilege and asks the browser process for the few operations it needs through a validated channel. A renderer exploit yields a useless unprivileged process; the attacker must separately defeat the browser process to escape. This is this module's design running on billions of devices — proof that privilege separation scales to the most attacked software on earth. When you advocate for separation in your own designs, point at the browser: the pattern is not academic, it is why web exploitation is hard instead of trivial.

notes.title: Capabilities as unforgeable tokens
notes.body:
Most systems use ambient authority: your authority comes from who you are — your user identity, your group memberships — and every program you run inherits all of it. A capability system flips this: authority comes from holding an unforgeable token that names a specific object and the operations permitted on it. Think of it like a valet key versus a master key: the valet key starts the car but cannot open the trunk, and you can hand it to someone without giving them your whole keyring. In software, a classic capability is a file descriptor: it names one specific open file and the operations allowed, it cannot be forged or guessed, and a process can hand it to another process to delegate exactly that authority — no more.

Worked example: two designs for a log-processing service that reads application logs and writes summaries. Ambient-authority design: the service runs as a user with read access to the whole log directory and write access to the reports directory. A bug in its parsing lets an attacker read any log file — including the authentication logs with their sensitive entries — because the authority was ambient: 'this user can read logs.' Capability design: at startup, a privileged launcher opens exactly the log files for today and hands the service descriptors for those files only, plus a descriptor for the single output file. The service never holds a directory handle, never holds a path it can re-target. A parsing bug now yields access to today's logs and one output file — the authority the job actually required. Delegation is equally precise: the service can pass the output descriptor to a helper without granting anything else.

Common mistakes: confusing capabilities with passwords or API keys — a password proves identity (ambient authority follows from who you are); a capability IS the authority, bound to the specific object. Another is forgeability: if the 'token' is a guessable filename or an integer the attacker can increment, it is not a capability — unforgeability is the defining property. And the revocation question: capabilities are easy to grant and delegate but need a revocation story (expiry, indirection through a revocable table) — design it upfront, because 'we will figure out revocation later' means it never happens.

Know the lineage briefly: capability thinking comes from operating-system research stretching back decades — systems built around unforgeable tokens rather than user identities, where every access names its capability explicitly. The ideas survived because the problems they solve never went away: ambient authority keeps producing confused deputies in every generation of software. You do not need the history's details, but knowing the lineage helps you recognize capability-shaped solutions in modern systems — file descriptors, scoped API tokens, per-app mobile permissions — and advocate for them with the confidence that the concept has been battle-tested far beyond any single product.

notes.title: Ambient authority and the confused deputy
notes.body:
The confused deputy is the classic failure of ambient authority, and it is worth learning by heart because you will see it in the wild. A deputy is a privileged program that acts on behalf of less-privileged requesters — a compiler service, a backup daemon, a web app writing files. The confusion: the deputy cannot tell which authority it is exercising — its own, or the requester's — so an attacker tricks it into using its superior authority for the attacker's purpose. The deputy is not malicious and not buggy in the ordinary sense; it is doing exactly what it was asked. It was just asked by the wrong party, and it had no way to know.

Worked example: a shared 'document converter' service runs with write access to the company's report archive. Any employee can submit a document and name an output path — the service converts and writes the result. An attacker submits a conversion with the output path set to the archive's billing summary, and the input crafted so the 'converted' output overwrites it with garbage. The service, holding archive-write authority ambiently, happily destroys the billing summary on the attacker's behalf. The service was confused about whose authority it wielded: it used its own (write the archive) when it should have used the requester's (write only the requester's own files). The capability fix: the service receives from each requester a capability for the destination — a token the requester legitimately holds. The attacker holds no capability for the billing summary, so the write is refused. The deputy is no longer confused because it never wields its own authority on a requester's behalf — it only exercises the authority the requester delegated.

Operator relevance: you will meet confused deputies in endpoint policy. A backup agent with write-everywhere authority that takes instructions from user-writable config files is a deputy waiting to be confused. When you scope Ringfencing and Storage Control policies, ask of every privileged application: 'who can instruct this program, and can a lesser party aim its authority at something they should not reach?' If yes, narrow the authority or the instruction channel. The confused deputy is not a coding curiosity — it is a design-review question.

Spot the web's confused deputy: cross-site request forgery. Your browser holds your ambient authority as a logged-in session, and a malicious site tricks your browser into wielding it — submitting a transfer, changing your settings — while you merely visited a page. The browser was the confused deputy, unable to distinguish your intent from the attacker's. The fixes are capability-shaped: per-session anti-forgery tokens bind the authority to the legitimate page, and cookie policies stop the ambient authority from traveling cross-site. Every time you implement or review these defenses, you are applying this module's lesson — the deputy problem is not a historical curiosity but a daily web reality.

notes.title: How this shows up in Elevation Control
notes.body:
Now map the theory onto the platform. The standing-local-admin problem is ambient authority at the endpoint: every program the user runs inherits administrative power, so every bug in every program is a privilege-escalation bug waiting to happen. Elevation Control applies privilege separation to the whole endpoint: the user — and everything they run — operates unprivileged by default. When a specific application legitimately needs elevation, the platform grants just-in-time elevation delegated to that application via policy — a capability-like grant: this application, this operation, now, for this long. The authority is no longer ambient ('the user is an admin, so everything is admin'); it is a scoped token issued per need.

Worked example: an accounting application needs to update itself, which requires writing to a protected directory. Old world: the user is a local admin, so the updater — and everything else on the machine, including the user's browser with its twenty tabs of untrusted content — runs with full privilege. New world: the user is standard. The updater launches; the platform recognizes the approved updater identity and elevates just that process for the update operation per policy. The browser, the document viewer, the chat app — all still unprivileged. A phishing document exploiting the viewer now yields an unprivileged process, and there is no ambient admin authority to steal. The elevation was a capability: bound to the specific application, issued just in time, gone when the operation completes. If the updater itself is later compromised, the damage is bounded by what the elevation grant permitted — which is why the grant must be narrow, not 'elevate everything this vendor ships.'

Operator gotchas: the broad elevation grant — 'elevate anything signed by Vendor X' recreates ambient authority with extra steps; scope elevation to the specific application and operation. Another is elevation without expiry discipline: just-in-time must actually end; review what stays elevated. And user experience: if legitimate elevation takes ten minutes of approval latency, users will demand admin rights back — the approval path must be fast (module 10's support discipline) or the architecture loses politically what it gained technically.

Design the approval workflow with two paths: the fast path for known-good patterns (pre-approved application identities elevate in seconds, logged for audit) and the deliberate path for the novel (unknown requests get human review with the business justification). The fast path keeps the business moving — this is what prevents the 'give me admin back' revolt. The deliberate path is where judgment lives — and where you collect the data to promote patterns into the fast path over time. Measure both paths' latency like the deployment module's time-to-approve metric, because the workflow's speed is the architecture's political survival. A just-in-time system with multi-hour latency is just-in-time in name only.

notes.title: How this shows up in Ringfencing
notes.body:
Ringfencing is capability thinking applied per application: instead of each program wielding the user's full ambient authority, each allowed application gets exactly the authority its job requires — and the platform enforces the boundary. The document viewer may read documents and write to the documents folder; it may not launch script interpreters, edit the registry, or open network connections. Those denials are not punishments; they are the application operating under least privilege. When the viewer's parser is exploited (module 14's scenario), the hijacked process finds its capability set is precisely the viewer's job description — and a shell, a network exfiltration, or a registry persistence mechanism is not in it.

Worked example — writing a Ringfencing policy as capabilities. Application: the firm's PDF reader. Job analysis: it needs to read PDF files from user directories and the document share, write nothing except print spooling, launch no child processes, touch no registry keys beyond its own settings, and reach no network addresses. The policy expresses exactly that: read allowed on the document paths, write denied except the spool path, child-process execution denied, registry writes denied outside its key, network denied. Each rule is a capability grant or refusal. Test it against the confused deputy: can a malicious PDF instruct the reader to write an executable somewhere? The write rules say no — the reader holds no write capability beyond the spool path, so there is nothing for the attacker to aim. Can it be tricked into launching a helper that does the damage? Child execution is denied — no deputy to confuse.

Common mistakes: the 'allow everything the app asks for' policy — learning what an app touches and permitting all of it just re-creates ambient authority with paperwork; the job analysis must be normative (what SHOULD it need), not merely descriptive. Another is forgetting the updater: the reader's updater legitimately needs network and install-path writes — that is a separate, narrower policy for the updater identity, not a hole in the reader's policy. And policy drift: applications gain features, features need new capabilities, and nobody reviews whether the old grants are still minimal — the review-date discipline from module 11 applies to Ringfencing policies too.

Think of per-application Ringfencing as a firewall where the 'network' is the operating system: just as a network firewall defines which hosts may talk to which, the application policy defines which resources each application may touch. The mental model transfers directly — default deny, explicit allows, rules scoped to identity (the application, not the address), and denied attempts logged as intelligence. When you explain Ringfencing to network engineers, use their vocabulary: it is a host firewall for application behavior. The analogy is honest because the principles are identical; only the enforcement point moved. And like firewall rules, application rules need the same hygiene: reviewed, minimal, documented, with expiry on the temporary.

notes.title: Design exercise: privilege-separating a fictional updater
notes.body:
Let us do the full design exercise, because this is the skill the interview panel will probe. Target: 'QuickPatch,' a fictional third-party updater that downloads and installs application updates. Current design: runs as a privileged service, fetches manifests over HTTPS, parses them, downloads binaries, executes installers — all as one privileged process parsing untrusted network input. Threat model: the update server could be compromised, a network attacker could tamper with manifests, and the manifest parser is complex code facing untrusted data. A single bug anywhere yields full system privilege.

Separated design, step by step. Identify the truly privileged operations: writing to the install directories and executing the installer. Everything else — fetching, parsing, verifying — needs no privilege. Split: an unprivileged fetcher/parser downloads the manifest and binaries, parses them, and verifies signatures against pinned vendor keys. It then asks the privileged installer a single narrow question: 'install this verified package,' passing a capability — a handle to the downloaded, signature-verified file, not a path it could swap. The installer validates: is the signature valid, is this package in the approved set, is the target directory the application directory? Only then does it write and execute. The channel between them carries exactly one operation with exactly one validated payload.

Now attack your own design (the iterate step from module 13). Attack one: compromise the update server and serve a malicious manifest — defeated, the parser verifies signatures against pinned keys and the installer re-validates. Attack two: exploit the parser with a malformed manifest — yields an unprivileged process that can only ask the installer to install signature-valid packages; the installer refuses. Attack three: swap the file between verification and install (time-of-check to time-of-use) — defeated by passing a handle, not a path; the installer validates the handle's contents. Residual risks, stated honestly: a bug in the small installer itself, a compromised vendor signing key, a malicious but properly signed update from the vendor. Each residual is explicit and owned — which is the honest endpoint of the exercise. Practice delivering this design aloud in five minutes: it is exactly the shape of a strong panel answer.

Practice the whiteboard narrative until it is smooth, because the panel will ask for exactly this shape: 'Design something secure.' Open with the threat model (thirty seconds), sketch the split (one minute), define the narrow channel and its validation (one minute), attack your own design out loud (one minute), and close with honest residuals (thirty seconds). The self-attack is the differentiator — most candidates present a design; few volunteer its weaknesses before being asked. Bring a marker-friendly diagram: two boxes, one arrow, the validation checks labeled on the arrow. Five minutes, one whiteboard, zero bluffing — that is the performance this module has been building toward.

cards.front: State the principle of least privilege.
cards.back: Every component holds only the authority its job requires — excess authority is pre-authorized damage when the component is compromised.

cards.front: What is privilege separation, structurally?
cards.back: Splitting a program into a small privileged monitor (few validated operations, distrusts input) and a large unprivileged worker (handles dangerous parsing/input with no privilege).

cards.front: What must the privileged part do with every request from the unprivileged part?
cards.back: Validate it against policy — blind obedience recreates the monolith's risk; the monitor must distrust the worker.

cards.front: What is a capability?
cards.back: An unforgeable token naming a specific object and permitted operations — authority comes from holding the token, not from identity.

cards.front: Contrast ambient authority with capabilities.
cards.back: Ambient: authority from who you are (user/groups), inherited by everything you run. Capabilities: authority from which tokens you hold, each scoped to an object and delegable precisely.

cards.front: Give a classic real capability example.
cards.back: A file descriptor: names one open file, permits specific operations, cannot be forged or guessed, and can be handed to another process to delegate exactly that authority.

cards.front: What is the confused deputy problem?
cards.back: A privileged program acting for requesters cannot distinguish its own authority from the requester's, so an attacker tricks it into wielding superior authority for malicious ends.

cards.front: What is the capability fix for the confused deputy?
cards.back: The deputy exercises only authority the requester delegated via capabilities — it never wields its own ambient authority on a requester's behalf.

cards.front: How is Elevation Control capability-like?
cards.back: It replaces ambient local-admin with just-in-time elevation granted per application via policy — a scoped, temporary authority token instead of standing privilege.

cards.front: How is Ringfencing capability thinking?
cards.back: Each allowed application gets exactly the authority its job requires (read/write/execute/network scoped per app) instead of the user's full ambient authority.

cards.front: What is the defining property of a capability, and what breaks it?
cards.back: Unforgeability — if the token is guessable (a filename, an incrementable integer), it is not a capability.

cards.front: In the QuickPatch design, why pass a file handle and not a path to the installer?
cards.back: To defeat time-of-check-to-time-of-use swaps: the installer validates the handle's actual contents rather than trusting a path the parser could change after verification.

quiz.q: A program runs as full administrator 24/7 because it writes one config file at startup. What is the least-privilege redesign?
choices: Keep it as is; rewriting is expensive.
Run unprivileged; use a tiny audited helper holding only the config-write authority, exposing one validated operation.
Run as administrator but add a firewall.
Split it into two administrators.
quiz.explain: Redistribute authority so the big, buggy, input-facing code holds none of it. The helper is small enough to audit; the 'sometimes needs privilege' becomes a scoped grant, not a lifetime one.

quiz.q: In a separated design, the privileged monitor opens whatever path the unprivileged worker names. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing — separation is achieved.
The separation is theater: the monitor blindly obeys, so compromising the worker still yields arbitrary file access. The monitor must validate every request.
It is too slow.
Workers should be privileged instead.
quiz.explain: Splitting without distrust changes nothing — the attacker aims the monitor's authority through the worker. Validation of every request against policy is what makes separation real.

quiz.q: Why is a file descriptor a capability but a filename is not?
choices: Filenames are longer.
A descriptor is an unforgeable reference to a specific open object with fixed operations; a filename is guessable, re-targetable ambient naming — anyone can name any file.
Descriptors are encrypted.
There is no difference.
quiz.explain: Unforgeability is the defining property. A filename can be guessed or swapped (symlink attacks); a descriptor cannot be minted by the holder and names exactly one object.

quiz.q: The document-converter service overwrites the billing summary because the attacker named it as the output path. What failed?
choices: The converter has a buffer overflow.
Confused deputy: the service wielded its own archive-write authority for a requester who held no such authority. Fix with per-request destination capabilities.
The billing summary permissions.
The network firewall.
quiz.explain: The service was not buggy in the ordinary sense — it could not distinguish its authority from the requester's. Capabilities fix it by ensuring the deputy only exercises delegated authority.

quiz.q: A user is a local admin, so their browser runs with full privilege. What does Elevation Control change, architecturally?
choices: It makes the browser faster.
It removes ambient admin: everything runs unprivileged by default; only specific applications get just-in-time scoped elevation via policy — a phishing exploit now yields an unprivileged process.
It blocks the browser.
It encrypts the disk.
quiz.explain: The architectural move is ambient-to-scoped: standing privilege becomes per-application, just-in-time grants. Exploitation still happens, but the inherited authority — the real prize — is gone.

quiz.q: Your Ringfencing policy for the PDF reader permits everything the reader was observed doing, including launching a helper updater with network access. What is the flaw?
choices: There is no flaw; observation is policy.
Descriptive-only policy re-creates ambient authority with paperwork — the updater needs a separate narrow policy; the reader's job analysis should be normative (what it SHOULD need).
PDF readers do not need policies.
Updaters should be banned.
quiz.explain: Permitting all observed behavior confuses description with authorization. Separate identities get separate policies, each scoped to the job — that is capability thinking, not behavior recording.

quiz.q: An elevation grant reads 'elevate anything signed by Vendor X.' Why is this dangerous?
choices: Vendor signatures are worthless.
It recreates ambient authority with extra steps — any current or future Vendor X binary, including a compromised updater, inherits elevation. Scope to the specific application and operation.
Elevation should never be granted.
It is too slow.
quiz.explain: Broad grants defeat the purpose of just-in-time scoping. The grant must name the application and operation — otherwise one compromised vendor binary escalates everything.

quiz.q: In the QuickPatch design, the parser verifies signatures and the installer re-validates. Why validate twice?
choices: Redundancy for compliance.
Defense in depth across the trust boundary: the unprivileged parser's verification can be bypassed if the parser is compromised, so the privileged installer must independently validate before acting.
It is faster.
Single validation is illegal.
quiz.explain: The installer distrusts the worker — that is the separation contract. Each side of a trust boundary validates independently, because the other side may already be compromised.

quiz.q: A capability system has no revocation story. What is the risk?
choices: No risk; capabilities are perfect.
Delegated authority cannot be taken back — a compromised holder keeps its power indefinitely. Design expiry or indirection upfront.
Capabilities stop working.
It becomes ambient authority.
quiz.explain: Easy grant and delegation without revocation is a one-way ratchet. 'We will figure out revocation later' means never — build expiry or revocable indirection into the design.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the module's through-line?
choices: Privilege is necessary, so accept the risk.
Assume components will be compromised; architect so each holds minimal authority — separation, capabilities, and per-app policies bound what any single compromise can achieve.
Remove all privileges from all software.
Trust but verify.
quiz.explain: The through-line from least privilege through separation and capabilities to Elevation Control and Ringfencing: design for compromise, bound the blast radius architecturally, never rely on any single component's correctness.

items.prompt: State least privilege in one sentence.
items.answer: Each component holds only the authority its job requires.
items.explain: Excess authority is pre-authorized damage.

items.prompt: What are the two parts of a separated program, and what does each do?
items.answer: Small privileged monitor (few validated operations) + large unprivileged worker (dangerous parsing, no privilege).
items.explain: The monitor distrusts and validates everything the worker sends.

items.prompt: Define a capability.
items.answer: Unforgeable token naming a specific object and permitted operations.
items.explain: Authority from holding the token, not from identity.

items.prompt: What is the confused deputy?
items.answer: A privileged program tricked into wielding its own authority for an attacker's purpose, unable to distinguish its authority from the requester's.
items.explain: Fixed by exercising only delegated capabilities.

items.prompt: How is Elevation Control capability-like?
items.answer: Just-in-time per-application elevation via policy replaces ambient local admin — scoped, temporary authority tokens.
items.explain: Standing privilege becomes per-need grants.

items.prompt: How is Ringfencing capability thinking?
items.answer: Each app gets exactly its job's authority (read/write/execute/network scoped) instead of the user's ambient authority.
items.explain: A hijacked app finds only its job description in its capability set.

items.prompt: Why must the monitor validate every worker request?
items.answer: Blind obedience lets a compromised worker aim the monitor's authority arbitrarily — separation without distrust is theater.
items.explain: Validation is the separation contract.

items.prompt: A backup agent takes its include-list from a user-writable config file and runs with read-all-files authority. Diagnose.
items.answer: Confused deputy: a lesser party (any user editing the config) can aim the agent's superior authority at files they should not reach. Fix: privileged launcher validates the config against policy, or the agent reads only via capabilities it is granted per job.
items.explain: Ask of every privileged app: who can instruct it, and can a lesser party aim its authority?

items.prompt: Your team proposes running the new chat app as admin 'because it needs to update itself.' Counter with the separated design.
items.answer: App runs standard; a tiny audited updater holds install-path write authority, invoked only for signature-verified packages via a narrow channel — the chat parser never holds privilege.
items.explain: 'Needs admin sometimes' is the design opportunity, not the verdict.

items.prompt: An API uses incrementing integer IDs as 'capabilities' for customer records. What is wrong?
items.answer: They are forgeable — incrementing the integer accesses another customer's record. Real capabilities must be unforgeable (unguessable tokens bound to the object).
items.explain: Guessable IDs are ambient naming with extra steps; the confused-deputy and IDOR families live here.

items.prompt: Elevation approvals take 20 minutes and users demand admin rights back. What is the real problem?
items.answer: The approval path is too slow — architecture loses politically what it gained technically. Fix the support latency (fast verification, pre-approved patterns), not the architecture.
items.explain: Security that obstructs the business gets routed around; speed the legitimate path.

items.prompt: A Ringfencing policy has not been reviewed in two years and the app gained three features. What do you do?
items.answer: Re-run the job analysis: map each new feature to required capabilities, prune grants the job no longer needs, set the review date — policy drift silently re-creates ambient authority.
items.explain: Authority creeps with features; the review-date discipline exists for exactly this.

items.prompt: Deliver the 5-minute QuickPatch design to a panel. What is the structure?
items.answer: Threat model (compromised server, parser bugs) → split (unprivileged fetch/parse/verify, tiny privileged installer) → narrow channel (one validated operation, handle not path) → self-attack (malicious manifest, parser exploit, TOCTOU swap) → honest residual risks.
items.explain: Model, split, validate, self-attack, residuals — the shape of a strong design answer.

handsOnLab.title: Least-privilege review of three everyday programs
handsOnLab.brief: Pick three programs you actually use, inventory the authority each holds versus what its job requires, and sketch a privilege-separated redesign for one of them. You produce the kind of review a security architect would commission.
steps: Choose three everyday programs: e.g., a document viewer, a chat application, and a backup or sync tool. Prefer ones you genuinely run.

For each, build the holds-vs-needs table: columns for authority (files it can read/write, processes it can launch, network it can reach, privilege level it runs at), what it holds today, what its job actually requires, and the gap.
Be honest about the gaps: mark every 'holds but does not need' cell — these are the pre-authorized damage if the program is compromised.
Pick the program with the worst gap. Write its threat model in four lines: asset, adversary, surface, boundary (module 13's loop).

Sketch the separated redesign: name the privileged operations (the tiny set), describe the unprivileged worker and what it handles, and define the narrow channel between them (operations, validation rules).
Run the confused-deputy check on your design: who can instruct the privileged part, and can a lesser party aim its authority somewhere wrong? Fix what you find.
Define the capability inventory for the redesign: what tokens the worker holds at startup, what it can delegate, and the revocation/expiry story.
Write the residual risks honestly: what your redesign does not fix (e.g., a bug in the tiny privileged part, a compromised signing key).
Map your redesign onto platform controls: which parts would Elevation Control and Ringfencing enforce on a real endpoint, and what the policies would roughly scope.
Condense the redesign to a 5-minute spoken walkthrough and practice it aloud.
Save as least-privilege-review.md with the three tables, the redesign, the deputy check, capabilities, residuals, and the platform mapping.
handsOnLab.deliverable: least-privilege-review.md with holds-vs-needs tables for three programs, a full privilege-separated redesign of the worst offender, the confused-deputy check, capability inventory with revocation, honest residuals, and the Elevation Control/Ringfencing mapping.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every program has a holds/needs/gap table; the redesign's privileged interface is tiny and validated; the deputy check found and fixed at least one aiming path; residuals are explicit and owned.
