title: MIT 6.858: Sandboxing & Isolation
summary: Confinement as a security primitive: sandboxing native code, seccomp syscall filtering, the isolation spectrum from processes to containers to VMs, and the performance-security tradeoff. You will map every concept onto Ringfencing policies you can actually write. Independent study in our own words; no affiliation claimed.
objectives: Explain what a sandbox guarantees: bounded authority for untrusted or compromised code.
Describe why sandboxing native code is hard: system calls as the escape hatch.
Sketch a seccomp-style syscall filter policy for a realistic application.
Compare processes, containers, and VMs on the isolation spectrum and choose correctly.
Reason about the performance-security tradeoff with concrete overhead thinking.
Write a Ringfencing-style sandbox policy that blocks defined attack scenarios while preserving the workflow.

notes.title: What sandboxing is: bounded authority for dangerous code
notes.body:
A sandbox is a confined execution environment: code runs inside it with strictly bounded authority, so that even if the code is malicious or compromised, the damage cannot escape the box. The sandbox defines what the code may do — which files it can touch, which network addresses it can reach, which system operations it may invoke — and enforces the boundary. Your browser does this every day: the JavaScript on a random website runs in a sandbox that cannot read your files, and the tab rendering an untrusted page is isolated from your banking tab. The guarantee is never absolute — sandboxes have escapes, which is why the last note in this module exists — but a good sandbox converts 'any bug is total compromise' into 'a bug plus a sandbox escape is compromise,' multiplying the attacker's work.

Worked example — the email attachment viewer. Without a sandbox: the viewer parses the attachment with full user authority; a parser bug (module 14) yields code execution with everything the user can do — read all documents, reach the network, install persistence. With a sandbox: the viewer runs in a box whose policy says 'read this one attachment file, render it, write the rendered output here, nothing else.' The same parser bug now yields code execution inside the box — and the box denies the file reads, the network, the persistence. The attacker must additionally find a sandbox escape to do anything useful. Notice the relationship to module 15: sandboxing is least privilege enforced at runtime around code you do not trust, while privilege separation is least privilege designed into code you wrote. Same philosophy, different application point.

Common misconceptions: 'sandboxed means safe' — sandboxes reduce and bound risk; they are bypassed regularly by skilled attackers chaining a code-execution bug with a sandbox-escape bug. Treat the sandbox as one layer, not a verdict. Another is confusing sandboxing with virtualization alone — a VM is one sandbox technology, but sandboxing also includes OS-level mechanisms (syscall filters, capability sandboxes, application policies) that are lighter and more precise. And the deployment fallacy: a sandbox with a sloppy policy ('allow everything except known-bad') is not a sandbox — the policy must be deny-by-default to deserve the name.

Look at your phone: mobile platforms sandbox every app by default — each app gets its own storage, must request permission for the camera or contacts, and cannot read other apps' data. That is sandboxing as consumer infrastructure on billions of devices, and it is why phone malware is rarer and less damaging than desktop malware was at the same age. The desktop endpoint is catching up through application sandboxing. When users ask why their desktop app 'cannot just' do something, the phone analogy lands instantly: your phone's apps work the same way — they ask permission because the alternative is any app reading everything. Familiar examples make the abstract policy concrete.

notes.title: Sandboxing native code: the hard parts
notes.body:
Sandboxing scripts or bytecode is relatively tractable — the interpreter mediates everything. Sandboxing native code — compiled machine code running directly on the processor — is genuinely hard, and understanding why makes you respect every working sandbox. The problem: native code can issue system calls directly, and system calls are the operating system's front door to everything interesting — files, network, processes, memory. A sandbox for native code must therefore interpose on system calls: every attempt by the sandboxed code to ask the OS for something passes through the sandbox's policy check. Miss one path to the kernel — an obscure syscall, a shared-memory channel, a hardware feature — and the sandbox has a hole. The policy itself must also be complete: allowing 'file reads' in general re-opens the data-theft door you were trying to close.

Worked example — sandboxing a font parser. Font files are a classic attack vector: complex format, parsed by privileged code, historically full of memory bugs. The sandbox design: the parser runs as native code but under a syscall filter. Allowed: read the single input font file, allocate memory, write the rendered output to a designated pipe, exit. Denied: everything else — no other file opens, no network sockets, no process creation, no executable memory mapping. The policy is derived from the job analysis (module 15's normative question: what SHOULD it need). Now the exploit narrative: a malicious font triggers the parser bug and hijacks control flow — inside the sandbox. The attacker's code tries to open the user's documents: the open syscall is denied by the filter. Tries to create a network socket: denied. Tries to map executable memory for stage two: denied. The hijack succeeded and achieved nothing — the sandbox held because the policy was derived from the job, not from observed behavior.

Common mistakes: the permissive policy — allowing broad syscall classes ('file access') instead of specific ones ('read this file') recreates the risk inside the box. Another is the trusted-parser fallacy: 'the parser is ours, so it needs less sandboxing' — the parser faces untrusted input, which makes it the most dangerous code in the system, not the least. And forgetting side channels: the sandbox controls syscalls, but shared caches, timing, and other covert paths can leak data across the boundary — the sandbox bounds authority, not information flow, unless explicitly designed for it.

Confront the just-in-time compilation problem to appreciate the difficulty: JIT compilers — in browsers, in runtimes — legitimately need to write machine code and then execute it, which is exactly what write-xor-execute forbids. The solutions are intricate dances: separating the writing from the executing across processes, or toggling permissions in narrow windows — each dance a potential vulnerability. This is why browser JITs are among the most attacked components on earth: they live at the exact tension point of the sandbox model. The lesson: wherever legitimate functionality conflicts with the security invariant, the engineering gets subtle and the bugs get valuable. Identify those tension points in your own systems — they are where the next escape will come from.

notes.title: seccomp and syscall filtering: policy at the kernel door
notes.body:
seccomp — secure computing mode — is the Linux mechanism that lets a program voluntarily restrict which system calls it (and its children) may invoke. In its strict form, a process declares a filter: a list of permitted syscalls, optionally with argument constraints ('allow open, but only with read-only flags'). Once installed, the filter cannot be removed by the process — the kernel enforces it, killing the process on violation. This is sandboxing at the narrowest choke point: no matter what the code does internally — no matter how thoroughly it is hijacked — it cannot ask the OS for anything outside the filter. The power is in the irreversibility and the kernel enforcement: the policy is not a suggestion the code follows, it is a cage the code cannot open.

Worked example — a filter policy sketch for the font parser from the last note. The parser's legitimate needs: read the input file, allocate working memory, write rendered output, exit. The filter: allow read, write (constrained to the output pipe's descriptor), open/openat (constrained to read-only, and in a stricter version, only the pre-opened input descriptor is used at all), mmap (constrained to non-executable mappings), brk, exit/exit_group, and the handful of startup syscalls the runtime needs. Deny: socket, execve, open with write flags outside the output path, mprotect with execute permission, ptrace, and everything else by default. Argument constraints do the heavy lifting: 'allow openat but only read-only' is far stronger than 'allow openat.' The exercise of writing the filter forces the job analysis — every allowed syscall must be justified, and the justification is the documentation.

Operator gotchas: the filter that is too tight breaks the application in production — the classic failure is forgetting the runtime's own needs (thread creation syscalls, locale file reads, DNS for no good reason). Test under the filter with real workloads, not just hello-world. Another is filter-everything-once thinking: libraries update and gain new syscall dependencies, so filters need maintenance alongside software updates. And seccomp is Linux-specific vocabulary — the concept (syscall interposition with irreversible kernel-enforced policy) generalizes: other platforms have their own mechanisms, and application-level sandboxes like Ringfencing enforce analogous boundaries at the policy layer rather than the syscall layer.

Study the progressive pattern used by well-engineered network services: the network-facing code runs unprivileged and, after the dangerous phases complete, sandboxes itself further — shedding even the system calls it no longer needs. The principle generalizes beautifully: sandboxing can tighten over a program's lifetime, from parsing untrusted input (needs file reads) to serving validated requests (needs almost nothing). When you design sandboxes, ask whether the policy can shrink as the program progresses — the parser needs file reads during startup but not after. Progressive tightening means a late-stage compromise inherits an even smaller box. The best sandbox is the one that keeps getting smaller.

notes.title: The isolation spectrum: processes, containers, VMs
notes.body:
Isolation mechanisms sit on a spectrum of strength versus cost, and choosing correctly is an operator skill. Processes: the OS separates memory and gives each process its own file-descriptor table and user identity — cheap (microseconds to create), but a compromised process still shares the kernel, the filesystem view, and the network stack with everyone else. Containers: OS-level virtualization that adds namespaces (separate views of processes, network, filesystem mounts) and resource limits around groups of processes — still sharing one kernel, but with a much smaller visible world per container; cheap enough to run dozens per host. Virtual machines: a hypervisor emulates hardware, and each VM runs its own full kernel — the strongest isolation on the list, because a compromised VM must escape the hypervisor rather than just the OS; but heavy (gigabytes of memory, seconds to boot) and operationally complex.

Worked example — three ways to isolate a risky document converter, and the reasoning for each. As a sandboxed process with a syscall filter: cheapest, fastest, sufficient if the threat is parser bugs and the policy is tight — the converter never legitimately needs the network, so the filter denies it outright. As a container: better when the converter needs a whole toolchain (fonts, libraries, temp space) — the container gives it a private filesystem and no network namespace, containing both the exploit and the mess. As a VM: justified when the documents come from active adversaries and the converter handles the CEO's inbox — the hypervisor boundary means even a kernel exploit in the guest stays in the guest. The choice follows the threat model (module 13): match the isolation strength to the adversary tier and the blast radius, and do not pay VM costs for process-level threats.

Common mistakes: container-as-security-boundary thinking — containers share the kernel, so a kernel vulnerability breaks all containers on the host; containers are a packaging and weak-isolation tool, not a VM. Another is VM sprawl: isolating everything in VMs 'to be safe' creates an unmanageable, unpatched fleet of mini-servers — each VM is a machine you must maintain. And the performance cop-out: 'VMs are too slow so we will not isolate' — measure; the spectrum exists precisely so you can pick the cheapest mechanism that meets the threat.

Know the middle ground: microVMs — virtual machines stripped to the minimum, booting in milliseconds with tiny memory footprints — built for the 'VM isolation at container speed' use case. They do not replace the spectrum's reasoning; they add a point on it, letting you buy near-VM isolation for workloads that could never afford full VMs. The operator lesson is not the technology but the habit: revisit your isolation choices as the mechanisms evolve, because a choice that was correct three years ago may be wrong today. The spectrum moves; your architecture should move with it, guided always by the threat model rather than by novelty.

notes.title: The performance-security tradeoff, honestly
notes.body:
Every isolation mechanism costs something — CPU cycles, memory, latency, operational complexity — and pretending otherwise produces security designs nobody deploys. The honest approach is quantifying the cost against the threat. Context switches between a sandboxed process and its monitor cost microseconds; for a network service handling thousands of requests per second, that can be measurable but is usually dwarfed by network latency. Syscall filtering adds per-call overhead in the nanoseconds — negligible for most workloads, noticeable only in syscall-heavy hot loops. Containers add near-zero runtime overhead (no emulation, just kernel bookkeeping) — their cost is operational: image management, orchestration, patching the fleet of images. VMs add real overhead: emulated or virtualized hardware, duplicated kernels in memory, I/O indirection — single-digit to double-digit percentage performance costs plus minutes of provisioning time.

Worked example — reasoning it through for the endpoint fleet. Should every workstation application run in its own VM? The security gain is real (hypervisor isolation per app), but the cost is absurd: hundreds of VMs per user, unmanageable patching, destroyed battery life and user experience — the design fails the deployability test. Should the PDF reader get a Ringfencing policy (application-layer sandbox)? Cost: near zero at runtime, some policy-maintenance effort. Gain: the reader's parser bugs are contained to the reader's job description. The tradeoff is overwhelmingly favorable — this is why application-layer sandboxing won on endpoints. Should the browser's renderer get OS-level sandboxing with a tight syscall filter? Cost: engineering effort by the browser vendor, modest runtime overhead. Gain: the most-attacked code on the machine (web content parsing) is contained. Also favorable — which is why modern browsers do exactly this. The method: name the cost, name the threat it addresses, and check that the ratio makes sense — security economics, not security vibes.

Common mistakes: the 'performance is paramount' veto that kills all isolation — usually asserted without measurement; measure first, then decide. The reverse: gold-plating low-risk components with VM-grade isolation while the actual crown jewels run unconfined — the threat model should allocate the isolation budget, not habit. And ignoring operational cost: a sandbox nobody can maintain becomes a sandbox with a stale, hole-ridden policy — the cheapest mechanism you will actually maintain beats the perfect one you will abandon.

Use the latency-budget method for services: start from the user-visible budget — say two hundred milliseconds per request — allocate it across components, and give security mechanisms their explicit slice. If the sandbox costs two milliseconds of a two-hundred-millisecond budget, the discussion is over — it fits. If it costs fifty, you negotiate: can the check be cached, moved off the hot path, or applied selectively to untrusted inputs? The budget turns 'too slow' from a veto into an engineering problem with numbers. And it exposes the real tradeoffs: teams routinely spend large slices on analytics tracking while vetoing slivers of sandboxing — the budget makes the priorities visible, which is often the actual problem.

notes.title: Mapping sandboxing onto Ringfencing policies
notes.body:
Here the course converges: Ringfencing is sandboxing at the application-policy layer, and everything in this module maps onto writing better Ringfencing policies. The sandbox guarantee becomes the policy's promise: this application may do exactly its job, nothing more. The syscall-filter mindset becomes the rule-writing discipline: enumerate what the application legitimately needs — which files, which registry areas, which network destinations, which child processes — and deny everything else by default. The job analysis from module 15 becomes the policy's source document: normative (what it should need), not merely descriptive (what it was observed doing). And the escape mindset from the next note becomes the review question: 'if this application were fully hijacked, what could it still do under this policy?'

Worked example — a Ringfencing-style policy for the firm's PDF reader, written as a sandbox spec. Identity: the reader's executable. File rules: read allowed on user document directories and the shared drive; write denied everywhere except the print spool path; execute denied for any file the reader writes (no drop-and-run). Process rules: child process creation denied entirely — the reader has no legitimate children; the updater is a separate identity with its own narrow policy. Registry rules: writes allowed only under the reader's own key. Network rules: denied — the reader never legitimately needs the network; updates come through the separate updater. Now the attack scenarios. Malicious PDF exploits the parser: the hijacked reader tries to write a payload — denied except spool path, and spool writes are not executable. Tries to launch PowerShell — child creation denied. Tries to exfiltrate via the network — denied. Tries to persist via registry run keys — denied outside its own key. The policy holds because each rule was derived from the job, and the job never included those actions.

Operator gotchas: the policy written from observation alone — 'the reader touched these 200 files, allow them all' — is a sandbox in name only; normative analysis must prune it. The forgotten updater path: updates need network and install writes, so give the updater its own tight policy rather than punching holes in the reader's. And the 'temporary' loosening — 'allow network for now, we will tighten later' — later never comes; write the tight policy first and loosen only with the exception discipline from module 11.

Review policies with a checklist, quarterly per application: is the identity still correct (no renames, no updater drift)? Is every allow still in the job description (prune the cruft)? Are the denies still holding (spot-check the block logs for the actions that should be denied)? Has the application gained features needing new analysis? Is there a temporary loosening past its expiry? The checklist takes twenty minutes per app and prevents the two slow killers: policy drift (accumulating cruft) and bit rot (rules that stopped matching reality). Assign each application's review to a named owner — policies without owners are policies without maintenance, and unmaintained sandboxes are decorative.

notes.title: When sandboxes fail: the escape mindset
notes.body:
Close the module where serious operators live: assuming the sandbox will be tested and thinking like the escape artist. Sandboxes fail in a taxonomy worth memorizing. Policy gaps: the filter allows a syscall the designer forgot is dangerous — the classic is allowing an obscure syscall with powerful side effects, or argument constraints with a loophole. Trusted-component compromise: the sandbox's own enforcement code has a bug — the monitor, the filter loader, the policy parser. Side channels: the sandbox bounds syscalls but the attacker exfiltrates data via timing, shared caches, or other channels the policy never considered. Composition failures: two sandboxes, each sound alone, interact badly — the classic is a sandboxed process that can ask an unsandboxed helper to do its dirty work (the confused deputy again, wearing a sandbox costume). And the oldest: the sandbox was never actually enabled in production — deployed in monitor mode, or disabled for 'compatibility' and never re-enabled.

Worked example — auditing a sandbox with the escape mindset. Target: the PDF reader policy from the last note. Policy gaps: does 'write allowed to the spool path' let the attacker write a malicious file the print spooler then executes? Check what consumes the spool path — the boundary moved, not disappeared. Trusted components: who parses the policy, and does the parser face untrusted input? Composition: the reader is denied network, but can it write a file to a synced cloud folder that exfiltrates on sync? The cloud sync app is a separate identity with network rights — the reader just found a deputy. Side channels: can the hijacked reader encode stolen data in the printed output? Possibly — printing is allowed, and the information flow was never bounded, only the syscall set. Each finding does not necessarily kill the design, but each must be answered: tighten, monitor, or explicitly accept and document. The escape mindset is not paranoia — it is the iterate step of module 13 applied to your own sandbox.

Final synthesis of the 6.858 arc: threat modeling taught you to reason from goals and adversaries; control hijacking showed what memory bugs give attackers; privilege separation and capabilities showed how to bound authority by design; sandboxing showed how to bound it at runtime. The through-line never changed: perfect code is impossible, so architecture assumes compromise and contains it. On the endpoint, that architecture has a name — deny-by-default application control with per-application boundaries — and you now understand it from the silicon up to the policy. That is operator-grade depth, and it is exactly what the October 13 panel is hoping to hear.

Think like the escape researcher for a day: their workflow is recon (map the sandbox's boundary — which syscalls, which IPC channels, which helpers), differential analysis (what does the sandboxed app do differently — the differences are the policy), and chaining (the parser bug gets code execution, the helper's permissive channel gets the escape — two medium bugs become one critical). Borrow the workflow defensively: recon your own sandbox's boundary, enumerate its helpers and their authority, and ask which two-bug chain breaks it. Researchers publish their escapes; read them as free audits of the patterns you deploy. Every public sandbox escape is a lesson someone else paid for — collect them.

cards.front: What guarantee does a sandbox provide?
cards.back: Bounded authority: even compromised or malicious code cannot act outside the box the policy defines — though escapes exist, so it is one layer, not a verdict.

cards.front: Why is sandboxing native code harder than sandboxing scripts?
cards.back: Native code runs directly on the processor and can issue system calls — the OS front door — so the sandbox must interpose on every syscall path without missing one.

cards.front: What is seccomp, in one sentence?
cards.back: A Linux mechanism letting a process irreversibly restrict its own (and children's) permitted system calls, with argument constraints, enforced by the kernel.

cards.front: Why is seccomp's irreversibility important?
cards.back: The policy is a cage, not a suggestion — once installed, the sandboxed code cannot remove its own restrictions even when fully hijacked.

cards.front: What makes a syscall filter strong vs weak?
cards.back: Argument constraints ('open, read-only only') and job-derived minimalism make it strong; broad syscall classes ('file access') make it weak.

cards.front: Order processes, containers, VMs by isolation strength and state the cost of each.
cards.back: Processes (cheapest, share kernel/filesystem/network view) < containers (namespaces + limits, still one kernel) < VMs (own kernel via hypervisor; strongest, heaviest: memory, boot time, patching burden).

cards.front: Why are containers not a VM-grade security boundary?
cards.back: They share the host kernel — one kernel vulnerability breaks every container on the host.

cards.front: How do you honestly evaluate the performance-security tradeoff?
cards.back: Name the cost (cycles, latency, operational burden), name the threat it addresses, check the ratio — measure rather than assert, and let the threat model allocate the isolation budget.

cards.front: How does Ringfencing map to sandboxing?
cards.back: It is sandboxing at the application-policy layer: each allowed app gets exactly its job's authority (files, registry, network, child processes) with deny-by-default — the policy is the sandbox.

cards.front: What is the normative vs descriptive question in policy writing?
cards.back: Normative: what SHOULD the app need (prunes the policy). Descriptive: what was it observed doing (re-creates ambient authority with paperwork). Policies must be normative.

cards.front: Name four sandbox failure modes.
cards.back: Policy gaps (forgotten dangerous syscalls), trusted-component bugs, side channels (timing, caches), composition failures (sandboxed code aiming an unsandboxed deputy) — plus the classic: never actually enabled.

cards.front: What is the through-line of the four 6.858 modules?
cards.back: Perfect code is impossible, so architecture assumes compromise and contains it — from threat models through hijacking, privilege separation, to sandboxing.

quiz.q: A sandboxed font parser is hijacked via a parser bug. It tries to open the user's documents, create a network socket, and map executable memory. The filter allows only: read the input file, write the output pipe, allocate non-executable memory, exit. What happens?
choices: All three attacker actions succeed; the sandbox failed.
All three are denied by the filter — the hijack succeeded but achieved nothing, because the policy was derived from the job.
The parser crashes before the hijack.
The filter is bypassed automatically.
quiz.explain: This is the sandbox guarantee working: control flow was hijacked, but every path to useful action crossed the filter and died. Job-derived minimalism is what makes the box hold.

quiz.q: Why must native-code sandboxes interpose on system calls?
choices: System calls are slow.
Syscalls are the OS front door to files, network, processes, and memory — any unmediated path to the kernel is a sandbox hole.
It improves performance.
Compilers require it.
quiz.explain: Native code's power is direct kernel access. The sandbox boundary IS the syscall boundary — miss one path (an obscure syscall, a shared-memory channel) and the box leaks.

quiz.q: Your seccomp filter allows 'openat' without argument constraints. What is the weakness?
choices: None — openat is safe.
The filter allows file opens generally instead of read-only opens of specific targets — argument constraints are what make the filter strong; without them it is a weak, broad permission.
It will crash the program.
openat does not exist.
quiz.explain: Broad syscall classes re-create the risk inside the box. 'Allow openat but read-only' versus 'allow openat' is the difference between a sandbox and a suggestion.

quiz.q: You need to isolate a document converter handling attachments from active adversaries, aimed at the CEO's inbox. Which isolation and why?
choices: A sandboxed process — cheapest.
A VM — the adversary tier (targeted, high value target) justifies hypervisor isolation; a kernel exploit in the guest stays in the guest.
No isolation — the converter is trusted.
A container is always sufficient.
quiz.explain: The threat model allocates the isolation budget: active adversaries plus a high-value target justify the VM's cost. Containers share the kernel — insufficient against an adversary who may bring kernel exploits.

quiz.q: A team rejects all sandboxing as 'too slow' without measurements. What is the operator response?
choices: Accept the veto; performance is paramount.
Measure first: syscall filtering costs nanoseconds per call, containers near-zero runtime overhead — the veto is usually asserted without data, and the spectrum offers cheap options.
Insist on VMs for everything.
Abandon security.
quiz.explain: Security economics, not vibes: quantify the cost against the threat. The isolation spectrum exists so you can pick the cheapest mechanism that meets the threat — most objections evaporate on measurement.

quiz.q: Your Ringfencing policy for the PDF reader was built purely from observed behavior — 200 files allowed. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; observation is accurate.
It is descriptive, not normative — it re-creates ambient authority with paperwork. Prune to what the job SHOULD need.
200 is too few.
Readers do not need policies.
quiz.explain: Permitting everything observed confuses description with authorization. The job analysis must be normative — otherwise the 'sandbox' permits whatever the app happened to touch, including the attacker's paths.

quiz.q: The PDF reader is denied network, but it can write to a cloud-synced folder, and the sync app has network rights. What failure mode is this?
choices: A policy gap.
Composition failure — the sandboxed reader aims an unsandboxed deputy (the sync app) to exfiltrate; the boundary moved, not disappeared.
A side channel.
No failure; sync is legitimate.
quiz.explain: The confused deputy in sandbox costume: each component's policy is sound alone, but together they compose an exfiltration path. Audit the deputies your sandboxed apps can reach.

quiz.q: The sandbox policy was deployed in monitor-only mode 'temporarily' six months ago. What is this, and the fix?
choices: Best practice; leave it.

The classic never-enabled failure — a monitor-mode sandbox enforces nothing. Fix: enforce now, handle the breakage with the exception discipline, and never deploy security in permanent 'temporary' mode.
It is still protecting via logging.
Delete the policy.
quiz.explain: Monitor-only is visibility, not containment. 'Temporary' without an expiry is permanent — enforce, manage the breakage properly, and put expiry discipline on every temporary relaxation.

quiz.q: A hijacked reader encodes stolen data in its allowed printed output. Which sandbox property does this defeat?
choices: The syscall filter.
None directly — the sandbox bounded authority (syscalls), not information flow; exfiltration via allowed outputs is a side/covert channel the policy never considered.
The VM boundary.
The canary.
quiz.explain: Sandboxes bound authority, not information flow, unless explicitly designed for it. Allowed outputs are legitimate channels that can carry stolen data — the escape mindset asks about flows, not just calls.

quiz.q: What connects this module back to module 13's first-principles loop?
choices: Nothing; sandboxing is purely practical.
The escape mindset IS the iterate step: define the sandbox's goal and adversary, design the policy mechanism, then attack your own design (policy gaps, deputies, side channels) and refine.
Threat models are only for networks.
Sandboxing replaces threat modeling.
quiz.explain: The loop never left: goal (bound the app's authority), adversary (hijacked app), mechanism (the policy), iterate (escape-mindset audit). First-principles reasoning applies to sandboxes exactly as to networks.

items.prompt: What does a sandbox guarantee, and what does it not?
items.answer: Bounded authority for code inside; not absolute safety — escapes exist, so it is one layer.
items.explain: Converts 'any bug is total compromise' into 'bug plus escape is compromise.'

items.prompt: Why must native sandboxes interpose on syscalls?
items.answer: Syscalls are the kernel's front door; any unmediated path is a hole.
items.explain: The sandbox boundary is the syscall boundary.

items.prompt: What is seccomp and why does irreversibility matter?
items.answer: Irreversible, kernel-enforced syscall restriction; the cage cannot be opened by the code inside.
items.explain: Policy as cage, not suggestion.

items.prompt: Order processes, containers, VMs by isolation strength.
items.answer: Processes < containers (share kernel) < VMs (own kernel via hypervisor).
items.explain: Match strength to adversary tier; do not pay VM costs for process threats.

items.prompt: Why are containers not VM-grade boundaries?
items.answer: Shared kernel — one kernel bug breaks all containers on the host.
items.explain: Packaging and weak isolation, not a security boundary.

items.prompt: How is Ringfencing sandboxing?
items.answer: Application-policy-layer sandbox: each app gets exactly its job's authority, deny-by-default.
items.explain: The policy is the sandbox.

items.prompt: Name four sandbox failure modes.
items.answer: Policy gaps, trusted-component bugs, side channels, composition failures (+ never enabled).
items.explain: The escape-mindset audit checklist.

items.prompt: Write the syscall-allow list for a log-uploader that reads one log file and POSTs it to a fixed HTTPS endpoint. Justify each entry.
items.answer: read (the log), write (sockets + logs), openat read-only (the log path), socket/connect (TCP to the fixed endpoint only — ideally constrained), TLS needs (getrandom), mmap non-exec, exit. Denied: execve, open-write elsewhere, ptrace. Each entry traces to the job: read log, send log, nothing else.
items.explain: Job-derived minimalism with argument constraints; every allow must be justified.

items.prompt: The uploader's library update starts needing a new syscall and breaks under the filter. What is the maintenance discipline?
items.answer: Treat filter updates like policy changes: verify the new syscall is legitimate (not the library phoning home unexpectedly), constrain its arguments, canary-test, document — filters evolve with software.
items.explain: Filters need maintenance alongside updates; a breakage is a review prompt, not just an annoyance.

items.prompt: A vendor's 'sandboxed' app runs with full network, all files readable, and no syscall filter — but in a container. Assess.
items.answer: Sandbox theater: the container adds namespaces but the policy inside is ambient authority. Demand the actual confinement policy (syscall filter, file/network scoping) or treat it as unsandboxed.
items.explain: Containers are not magic; without a deny-by-default policy inside, the box is decorative.

items.prompt: Your Ringfencing policy blocks the PDF reader's new 'cloud save' feature users love. Walk through the decision.
items.answer: Job analysis: is cloud save in the reader's legitimate job? If yes, scope it — specific domains, specific account, via the reader identity only, with Storage Control awareness. If it is feature creep, say no with the business reason. Either way, exception discipline: narrow, owned, reviewed.
items.explain: Features change the job; re-run the normative analysis rather than reflex-allowing or reflex-denying.

items.prompt: Audit finds the spool-path write rule lets the reader drop files the spooler service executes. What do you do?
items.answer: Boundary moved, not disappeared: constrain writes to non-executable formats, verify the spooler's consumption, or route through a sanitizing intermediary — then re-run the attack scenarios against the tightened rule.
items.explain: Follow the data past your boundary: who consumes what you allow, and with what authority?

items.prompt: Explain the whole 6.858 arc in 60 seconds to the panel.
items.answer: 'We assume code has bugs, so we architect containment: threat models tell us what matters and who attacks; understanding hijacking tells us what bugs give away; privilege separation and capabilities bound authority by design; sandboxing bounds it at runtime. On the endpoint that architecture is deny-by-default with per-app boundaries — so even a successful exploit hits a wall.'
items.explain: The arc in one breath: assume compromise, bound the blast radius, at every layer from silicon to policy.

handsOnLab.title: Write a Ringfencing-style sandbox policy for a document viewer
handsOnLab.brief: Pick a real document viewer, derive its job normatively, and write a complete sandbox policy spec — file, process, registry, and network rules — then attack your own policy with three scenarios and verify the legitimate workflow survives. A policy document a real admin could implement.
steps: Choose a real document viewer you use (a PDF reader, an office viewer). Install nothing new — use what you have.
Write the normative job analysis: in one paragraph, what SHOULD this viewer need? List every legitimate capability: which files it reads, what it writes, whether it needs children, network, registry.

Inventory the descriptive reality: check what the viewer actually touches (recent files, its install directory, temp paths, any network calls you can observe). Note every gap between descriptive and normative.
Write the file rules: read-allowed paths (enumerated), write-allowed paths (minimal — spool/temp only), execute denied on anything the viewer writes.
Write the process rules: child process creation allowed or denied, with the justification. If the viewer has an updater, specify it as a separate identity with its own narrow rules.
Write the registry/configuration rules: which keys the viewer may write (its own settings), everything else denied.
Write the network rules: allowed destinations enumerated or fully denied, with the justification tied to the job analysis.

Attack scenario 1: a malicious document exploits the viewer. Walk through what the hijacked process attempts (payload write, process launch, exfiltration, persistence) and verify each is denied by your rules.

Attack scenario 2: the confused deputy — can the viewer be aimed at something through an allowed path (cloud-synced folders, spool consumers, helper apps)? Document what you find and tighten the rules.
Attack scenario 3: the updater — verify the updater's narrow policy cannot be abused to grant the viewer new capabilities (scope, signature checks, separate identity).
Positive test: walk through the legitimate workflow (open, read, print, save-as) under your policy and confirm nothing breaks. Adjust with exception discipline if needed.
Save as sandbox-policy.md: job analysis, the four rule sections, the three attack walkthroughs with verdicts, the positive test, and review-date discipline.
handsOnLab.deliverable: sandbox-policy.md with the normative job analysis, file/process/registry/network rule sections, three attack-scenario walkthroughs with deny verdicts, the positive workflow test, and the review schedule.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All three attack scenarios are denied by specific rules you can name; the legitimate open/read/print/save workflow survives; the updater is a separate identity; every rule traces to the job analysis.

mockTask.q: Panel question: 'We ringfenced the PDF reader — no child processes, no network — and now users complain it cannot print. Walk me through it.'
choices: Loosen the policy to allow child processes so printing works.

Diagnose first: check the block events to confirm printing is what is actually denied (vs. a coincidental issue), identify the exact mechanism the reader uses to print (spool path writes vs. a helper process), then permit narrowly — e.g., write to the spool path only — verify printing on a canary, and keep the child-process and network denials intact.
Tell users printing is a security risk and remove printers.
Disable Ringfencing for the reader until the vendor fixes it.
mockTask.explain: The panel tests whether you reflex-loosen or diagnose-then-narrow. The strong answer verifies the actual denied action, finds the minimal legitimate mechanism (spool writes, not child processes), and preserves the rest of the sandbox — sandbox judgment under user pressure, which is the daily reality of the role.
